title: AI compute & model internals
summary: From tracking Claude Code token cost to why capacity is scarce, why inference keeps getting cheaper, how transformers and MoE actually work, how models are trained, and what might replace the transformer.

concepts.title: Compute economics
concepts.summary: Why capacity is scarce, how fast demand grows, and when it might ease
concepts.overview: Compute economics is the story of why frontier AI capacity is scarce in 2026 and when that might change. Two exponentials are running against each other. On the demand side, the stock of AI chip compute is growing about **3.4× per year** ([Epoch AI](#c/epoch)), and Nvidia describes demand rising ~1,000,000× in two years as chatbots became [reasoning agents](#c/reasoning-load). On the supply side, the [binding constraint](#c/capacity) keeps moving, from power to chips to transformers and switchgear, and 30–50% of planned 2026 capacity is projected to [slip to 2028](#c/slip). Meanwhile the cost of reaching a *fixed* capability keeps collapsing. So "AI got cheaper" and "the frontier got more expensive" can both be true. [Fable 5's gating](#c/fable-gating) behind usage credits is one concrete case. The chat's hedged best guess is that the premium squeeze eases around 2027–28, but only if demand growth slows too.

concepts.title: Why inference gets cheaper
concepts.summary: What the famous cost-decline numbers measure, and what drives them
concepts.overview: This theme untangles one of the most misread statistics in AI: Epoch's finding that the cost of inference at a fixed level of performance falls roughly **100× per year**. The fixed thing is a benchmark score, not a model. The figure measures how quickly newer, smaller models [re-reach old capability bars](#c/fixed-capability). A frozen model such as a particular Sonnet also gets cheaper to serve, but by much smaller steps, through [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts), [new hardware](#c/hardware-gens) and [distillation](#c/distillation). How big the decline looks depends heavily on method. Controlled estimates are ~5–10×/year for frontier price-for-performance and ~3×/year for [algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress) alone. The eye-catching 900× comes from frozen proprietary list prices. The list price you pay moves on yet another schedule, set by business decisions.

concepts.title: Inside a transformer
concepts.summary: Tokens, attention, heads, layers, the KV-cache and position
concepts.overview: Every frontier LLM today is a **decoder-only transformer**, and this part of the map opens one up, using DeepSeek-V3's public `config.json` as the worked example because closed models don't publish their shapes. Text is chopped into [tokens](#c/tokenizer) (vocabulary 129,280), each token becomes a 7,168-wide [embedding](#c/embedding) vector, and that vector rises through a [stack of 61 layers](#c/layer-stack). Each layer does two things: [attention](#c/attention), where tokens read from one another through 128 query/key/value heads, and a [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) that works on each token alone (here a Mixture of Experts). Only after the last layer does the [output head](#c/output-head) turn the vector into next-token probabilities. Around this core sits a family of efficiency tricks (GQA, MLA, sparse attention, FlashAttention, PagedAttention, KV quantization, prefix caching, RoPE scaling) that the chat sorted into two kinds: ones baked in at training time and ones that make an already-frozen model cheaper to serve.

concepts.title: Mixture of Experts
concepts.summary: How sparse experts decouple capacity from cost, and where the idea came from
concepts.overview: **Mixture of Experts** is the idea that lets a model's knowledge capacity grow without its per-token cost growing with it. The [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) in each transformer layer is split into many parallel sub-networks, and a small [router](#c/router) sends each token to only a few of them, so a model like [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) holds 671B parameters but does arithmetic with about 37B per token. This topic traces the idea from the [1991 'Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts' paper](#c/moe-1991) through [sparse gating in 2017](#c/sparse-moe), [GShard](#c/gshard) and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch), to the balancing and granularity fixes ([auxiliary loss](#c/lb-loss), [loss-free bias balancing](#c/aux-free), [fine-grained plus shared experts](#c/fine-grained)) that made it the open-weight default by 2025. It also corrects two common misconceptions: that experts are topic specialists, and that MoE is a recent breakthrough rather than a decade of incremental engineering on a 1991 idea.

concepts.title: Open model landscape
concepts.summary: What the published open models are made of
concepts.overview: This topic surveys what published models are actually made of, from the dense scaling era to the MoE-dominated open landscape of 2025–26. Parameter counts rose 1000× from [GPT-1](#c/gpt-1) (117M) to [GPT-3](#c/gpt-3) (175B) in two years, then about 10× more to an estimated ~1.8T for [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4). After that the trend [reversed](#c/r-smaller): frontier models got smaller, and [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) split *total* parameters (capacity) from *active* ones (cost). The open flagships, among them [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4), [Qwen3](#c/qwen3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-5](#c/glm-5), all use MoE, but they differ on expert granularity, whether to keep a shared expert, and attention type (GQA, MLA, sparse or linear). A recurring lesson is that [recent architecture changes mostly bought efficiency](#c/c-arch-efficiency), while the quality gains came from post-training. Newer releases (GLM-5.1, GLM-5.2) come with self-reported and sometimes contradictory benchmark claims.

concepts.title: Training
concepts.summary: Pre-training, post-training, RL and fine-tuning
concepts.overview: Training is how a model's weights get their values, and for modern LLMs it happens in two broad phases. [Pre-training](#c/pretraining) teaches next-token prediction over trillions of tokens. It is the expensive part, where knowledge and raw capability come from. [Post-training](#c/post-training) is a much cheaper sequence of stages (SFT, preference learning, reinforcement learning) that turns the resulting base model into an assistant. It is where behaviour, alignment and, since 2025, most headline reasoning gains are shaped. Around these phases sit decisions about how to spend compute ([Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla)), whether to update every weight or only small adapters ([LoRA](#c/lora)), and whether to train one generalist or [specialists that are later merged](#c/merging). The chat noted a clear shift: recent architecture changes mostly bought efficiency, while the quality gains came from the training recipe, especially scaled-up RL.

concepts.title: Data
concepts.summary: What goes into training corpora and how they're refined
concepts.overview: Data covers what goes into a model's training sets and how that raw material is refined. For pre-training, the backbone is a [filtered web crawl](#c/web-crawl): Common Crawl text run through extraction, deduplication and [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter). Aggressive pipelines like DCLM and FineWeb-Edu discard roughly 90% of the crawl. Code, papers, books, Wikipedia and math are then mixed in, and choosing the proportions is a craft of its own. Post-training data is smaller but costs far more per example. It consists of demonstrations ([synthetic SFT responses](#c/synthetic-sft)), preference pairs (increasingly labelled by an LLM judge) and [verifiable problems](#c/verifiable-problems) for RL, all decontaminated against benchmarks. Flagship labs keep their data secret, so most of what is known comes from fully open efforts such as Dolma, FineWeb, DCLM and [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3).

concepts.title: Beyond the transformer
concepts.summary: Hybrids, state-space models, byte-level, diffusion and concept models
concepts.overview: The standard LLM recipe is a tokenized, autoregressive decoder-only transformer: stacked attention and feed-forward blocks, emitting one token at a time. This cluster collects the serious attempts to change one of those assumptions. [State-space models](#c/ssm) and [Mamba](#c/mamba) replace quadratic attention with a fixed-size recurrent state; [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids) and linear / hybrid attention keep a minority of full-attention layers for precise recall. The [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/blt) removes the tokenizer, [diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm) drop left-to-right decoding, and the [Large Concept Model](#c/lcm) and latent reasoning try to think at a level other than tokens. The chat's verdict as of June 2026: hybrids and byte-level models are the most validated at scale, diffusion LMs have shipped but their quality parity is narrow and self-reported, and concept and latent models remain speculative. Historically these alternatives get partly absorbed into the transformer rather than replacing it.

concepts.title: Sources
concepts.summary: Who the numbers come from, and how independent they are
concepts.overview: Every number in this graph came from somebody, and the chat kept asking who and with what stake. Its rough ranking runs from neutral to interested. [Epoch AI](#c/epoch) and academic papers are the most neutral, and their growth *rates* are measured from disclosed data. Analyst shops such as [SemiAnalysis](#c/semianalysis) and [McKinsey](#c/mckinsey) give directional estimates that get re-reported across many outlets, which can make one estimate look like several. Parties with a position, such as [Nvidia](#c/nvidia) (it sells the chips) and [JLL](#c/jll) (real estate), give the softest numbers, especially dollar forecasts and timing calls. The same scrutiny applies to model claims: [vendor announcements](#c/vendor-claims) are self-reported, and fast-moving launch coverage can contradict itself within days. The chat's rule of thumb: trust agreement on *direction* more than any single number.

concepts.title: Fable 5 gated behind usage credits
concepts.summary: Pulled from subscription plans June 23 and billed at API rates ($10/$50 per M tokens); return is capacity-gated
concepts.overview: On **June 23, 2026**, Anthropic pulled [Claude Fable 5](#c/fable-release) from its subscription plans. Fable 5 stayed usable, but once a user's normal plan limits ran out, further use needed usage credits billed at API rates: **$10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens**. Anthropic said it plans to restore Fable 5 as a standard subscription feature "as soon as possible" and "once capacity allows", and might extend the free window if capacity holds. It gave no committed date. The chat treats this as a concrete example of [frontier scarcity pricing](#c/frontier-price): premium capability is scarce, so it is priced and metered. It also stresses that Anthropic never said what "capacity-driven" means internally. The cause could be accelerators, serving headroom, power or a commercial decision, so the gating can't be pinned on any single layer of the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity).

concepts.title: Capacity constraint
concepts.summary: Not one knob: accelerators, HBM, power and electrical gear bind in turn
concepts.body:
Anthropic doesn't say what "capacity-driven" means internally. Industry-wide, the
binding constraint has **moved**: power (2024–early 2025), then chips (late 2025 –
early 2026), then long-lead electrical gear (from ~May 2026).
concepts.overview: "Capacity" is not one knob. It is at least four constraints that bind one after another. **Accelerators** (GPUs and TPUs) were sold out through the Blackwell generation. **HBM memory** is sold out for 2026 and now takes about 30% of hyperscaler AI spend. **Power and grid** access has left operators holding chips they couldn't energize. **Electrical gear** such as high-voltage transformers now has 36–48-month lead times. The binding layer has moved: power through 2024 and early 2025, chips in late 2025 and early 2026, and electrical gear from about May 2026. This is why the popular idea that [capacity is all about GPUs](#c/m-gpu) is out of date, and why [hyperscaler capex](#c/capex) of $600B+ can't buy the problem away quickly. What any one provider means by "capacity-driven", as with [Fable 5's gating](#c/fable-gating), isn't public. See also [HBM supply](#c/hbm-supply) and [power & grid](#c/power).
concepts.article:
The **capacity constraint** on AI compute is the limit on how much model inference and training the industry can actually run at a given moment. It is often pictured as a simple GPU shortage. In practice it is a chain of physical constraints (accelerators, high-bandwidth memory, power and grid connections, and the electrical equipment that energizes a site), and whichever link is tightest sets the pace. By mid-2026 that link had changed at least three times in about two years.

## The four layers

| Layer | State in the chat (mid-2026) | Why it's slow to fix |
|---|---|---|
| [Accelerators](#c/gpu-supply) | Nvidia record $51.2B data-center quarter; [Blackwell sold out](#c/blackwell) | Fab capacity and packaging take years to add |
| [HBM memory](#c/hbm-supply) | SK Hynix sold out for 2026; memory ~30% of hyperscaler AI spend (up from ~8%) | HBM competes with ordinary DRAM for wafers |
| [Power & grid](#c/power) | Operators held chips they couldn't plug in; interconnection queues | Grid upgrades and connections are multi-year projects |
| [Transformers & switchgear](#c/electrical-gear) | Transformer lead times 36–48 months, up from 12–18 | Specialized heavy manufacturing with few suppliers |

These are *serially binding*. Loosening one just exposes the next. Through 2024 and early 2025 the bottleneck was power, and Satya Nadella described Microsoft holding AI chips it lacked the power to plug in. In late 2025 and early 2026 it swung back to silicon, with chip production described as "a binding constraint on the pace of the AI compute buildout." From around May 2026 the gating factor moved again, to long-lead electrical items like high-voltage transformers and medium-voltage switchgear.

## Why money doesn't fix it quickly

The spending is enormous. Major cloud companies are expected to put over $600 billion into [capex](#c/capex) in 2026, up 36%, with about $450 billion of it for AI infrastructure. Spending doesn't shorten a 36-month transformer lead time or move a site up a grid interconnection queue, though. That is why 30–50% of planned 2026 AI data-center capacity is projected to [slip to 2028](#c/slip), and one estimate has roughly half of planned US 2026 data centers delayed or cancelled. The result is that [available compute](#c/compute-supply) lags well behind what has been paid for.

## Why it matters for prices

When [demand](#c/compute-demand) grows about 3.4× a year and supply is held back by multi-year lead times, the scarce resource gets priced up or rationed. In 2026 that scarce resource is frontier inference capacity. The chat reads [Fable 5's move to usage credits](#c/fable-gating) and its $10/$50 per-million-token pricing as one instance of this [frontier scarcity](#c/frontier-price). The same scarcity sits comfortably alongside falling prices for older capability tiers.

## Newer chips and the inference axis

Newer chips help on two axes that are easy to conflate: raw FLOPs for training, and tokens per dollar per watt for inference. For serving a model to subscribers, the inference axis is what counts, and it is gated as much by memory bandwidth and HBM capacity as by compute, because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). So an HBM shortage can cap the benefit of a new GPU generation even when the chip itself is available.

## When it eases

Delayed projects are expected to come online through 2027 and 2028, stretching component demand across those years rather than peaking in 2026. McKinsey projects [global data-center supply](#c/dc-growth) growing from ~70 GW to ~220 GW within five years. Deeper power fixes such as new nuclear are mostly a post-2035 story. The chat's hedged view is that the premium squeeze most likely eases as [delayed capacity comes online](#c/capacity-relief), but only if demand growth also slows.

## From the chat

- The chat was explicit that it had **no inside information** on what Anthropic means by "capacity-driven" for Fable 5. It could be accelerators, serving headroom, power or a deliberate commercial throttle, and "probably a mix" was labelled as inference.
- It sequenced the binding constraint as power (2024–early 2025), then chips (late 2025–early 2026), then electrical gear (from ~May 2026), and called the "it's all GPUs" framing [out of date](#c/m-gpu).
- Key figures: Nvidia $51.2B record data-center revenue (fiscal Q3 2026); memory ~30% of hyperscaler AI spend in 2026 vs ~8% in 2023–24; HBM using ~23% of DRAM wafer capacity; transformer lead times 36–48 months.
- Sourcing caution: many figures trace back to a few analyst shops (SemiAnalysis, McKinsey, Bloomberg Intelligence) re-reported widely. Treat the percentages as directional, and trust the cross-source agreement on direction more than any single number.
- The chat admitted it was thin on the next-generation chip roadmap, including custom silicon like TPUs and Trainium and inference-specific chips.

concepts.title: Accelerator supply (GPUs/TPUs)
concepts.summary: Blackwell sold out; Nvidia data-center revenue a record $51.2B in a quarter
concepts.overview: Accelerator supply is the number of GPUs and TPUs that can be built and delivered. It is the layer of the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity) people usually mean when they say "compute". In mid-2026 it was still tight. In fiscal Q3 2026 Nvidia reported record data-center revenue of **$51.2 billion**, and Jensen Huang said Blackwell sales were "off the charts" and cloud GPUs were sold out ([Blackwell sold out](#c/blackwell)). Nvidia takes the overwhelming majority of accelerator spend. The chat describes chips as the binding constraint in late 2025 and early 2026, when leading AI companies couldn't get enough of them, before the bottleneck moved on to electrical gear. [Hyperscaler capex](#c/capex) of over $600B in 2026 is what pays for this supply. More accelerators only become [usable compute](#c/compute-supply) once there is HBM to pair with them and power to run them.

concepts.title: HBM memory supply
concepts.summary: SK Hynix sold out for 2026; memory ~30% of hyperscaler AI spend, up from ~8%
concepts.overview: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) is stacked DRAM packaged right next to an accelerator. It holds model weights and the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) during inference. The chat calls it the underappreciated constraint. SK Hynix said all its HBM was sold out for 2026, and Samsung had secured customers for its 2026 output. SemiAnalysis estimates memory could be about **30% of hyperscaler AI spending in 2026, up from ~8%** in 2023–24, and HBM now uses about 23% of all DRAM wafer capacity, which pushes up ordinary DRAM prices too. It matters so much because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound): serving speed is limited mostly by how fast data moves out of HBM, not by arithmetic. So more HBM per chip lowers the [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token), and an HBM shortage caps what a new chip generation can deliver.

concepts.title: Power & grid
concepts.summary: Operators have held chips they couldn't energize; interconnection queues slip projects
concepts.overview: Power and grid access is the layer of the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity) that decides whether installed chips can actually run. Through 2024 and early 2025 it was the binding constraint. Satya Nadella described Microsoft holding AI chips it lacked the power capacity to plug in. Chip manufacturing, power access, land and grid connections are all tightening at once, and grid interconnection queues plus construction bottlenecks are the main reason 30–50% of planned 2026 AI data-center capacity is projected to [slip to 2028](#c/slip). Bigger fixes take longer. McKinsey's [~70 → ~220 GW](#c/dc-growth) projection spans five years, and [new nuclear](#c/nuclear) mostly lands after 2035. The Stanford teaching model adds that an energy breakthrough would simply move the bottleneck to memory bandwidth. Part of the [capex](#c/capex) wave goes into power infrastructure.

concepts.title: Transformers & switchgear
concepts.summary: High-voltage transformer lead times stretched from 12–18 to 36–48 months
concepts.overview: High-voltage transformers and medium-voltage switchgear are the unglamorous equipment that connects a data center to the grid and distributes power inside it. As of about **May 2026** they became the newest chokepoint in the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity). Long-lead electrical items now largely decide whether a site energizes on schedule. Tech Insider reported that lead times for high-voltage transformers had stretched from **12–18 months to as long as 36–48 months** in some cases. A three-to-four-year wait can't be shortened by paying more, which is why the chat and [Accuris](#c/accuris) coverage treat it as a reason the frontier squeeze lasts into [2027–28](#c/c-squeeze). A site can have chips and HBM in hand and still add nothing to [available compute](#c/compute-supply) until its electrical gear arrives.

concepts.title: Available AI compute
concepts.summary: What can actually be energized and served
concepts.overview: Available AI compute is the capacity that can actually be energized and served, as opposed to what has been ordered or announced. It is the output of the whole [capacity constraint](#c/capacity) chain. Accelerators, HBM, power and electrical gear all have to be in place, and the weakest one sets the total. [Construction and interconnection delays](#c/slip) subtract from it, with 30–50% of planned 2026 capacity projected to slip to 2028. Epoch's measure of the installed stock of AI chip compute is growing about 3.4× a year, doubling every ~7 months, which is fast but hasn't been enough. When available compute can't keep up with [demand](#c/compute-demand), the gap shows up as [frontier price and scarcity](#c/frontier-price): rationing, usage credits and premium pricing.

concepts.title: Compute demand
concepts.summary: Grew ~1,000,000× in two years by Nvidia's framing: ~10,000× per request × ~100× usage
concepts.overview: Compute demand is how much processing the world's AI workloads need. By Nvidia's framing at GTC it grew roughly **1,000,000× in two years**, the product of two multipliers. Compute per inference session rose ~10,000× as [chatbots became reasoning and agentic systems](#c/reasoning-load), and [usage](#c/usage-growth) grew ~100×. Treat that framing as coming from an interested party ([Nvidia](#c/nvidia) sells the chips). The more careful anchor is Epoch's measurement that the stock of AI chip compute is growing about **3.4× per year**. Demand is also changing character: [inference is expected to overtake training](#c/inference-shift) in 2027, and inference demand grows with adoption instead of arriving in one-off training runs. Against multi-year supply lead times, this growth is what pushes up [frontier prices](#c/frontier-price).
concepts.article:
**Compute demand** is the total processing that AI workloads call for: training new models and, increasingly, serving them to users and agents. By mid-2026 it was growing faster than any physical supply chain could follow, and it is one of the two exponentials at the heart of [compute economics](#c/t-econ). The other is the falling cost of reaching a fixed capability.

## How fast it is growing

There are two very different ways to put a number on it.

- **The measured rate.** [Epoch AI](#c/epoch) estimates that the total computing power of the installed stock of AI chips has grown about **3.4× per year** since 2022, doubling roughly every seven months ([e-stock](#c/e-stock)). The estimate is built from revenue data, financial disclosures and analyst reports. For comparison, [Moore's law](#c/e-moore) doubles about every two years.
- **The keynote framing.** At GTC, [Nvidia](#c/nvidia) put the growth in computing demand over two years at about **1,000,000×** ([e-demand](#c/e-demand)). That is the product of ~10,000× more compute per inference session and ~100× more usage.

The two numbers measure different things. Epoch counts installed hardware, which is what supply actually delivered. Nvidia's figure is a stylized estimate of what workloads would *want*, and part of the gap between them is why capacity feels short. The chat trusts the measured rate more than the framing.

## What drives it

The multiplication in Nvidia's framing is the useful part. [Reasoning and agentic workloads](#c/reasoning-load) consume vastly more compute *per request*: a reasoning model emits long chains of thought, and an agent makes many model calls to finish one task. That per-request growth stacks on top of [usage growth](#c/usage-growth). Cheaper tokens also feed the loop. By [Jevons' paradox](#c/jevons), efficiency gains get spent on more tokens and more capability, not on smaller bills.

## Training gives way to inference

JLL estimates AI was about a quarter of data-center workloads in 2025, with training driving most of the demand. [Inference is expected to overtake training in 2027](#c/inference-shift), and by 2030 AI could be half of all data-center workloads, with inference as the main driver. This matters because training is a one-time or periodic investment, while inference demand keeps compounding with adoption, so it is stickier.

## Forecasts and their authors

Jensen Huang's own dollar forecasts climbed fast. A year earlier he saw $500 billion in high-confidence demand through 2026. By the time of the chat he saw at least **$1 trillion through 2027**, adding "we are going to be short." The chat flags this as the most interest-conflicted figure in the discussion, though the direction is corroborated elsewhere. JLL also names a fragility in the bull case: the inference supercycle depends on inference applications that don't yet exist at scale.

## When demand growth could slow

The chat treats demand as the bigger swing factor in when the squeeze eases, and the harder one to call. Cooling would need one of three things: growth decelerating naturally as easy gains saturate, the expected inference applications failing to arrive, or returns disappointing enough that [capex](#c/capex) pulls back. The [Stanford teaching model](#c/stanford-toy) shows that if demand growth slowed to ~100% a year, supply could catch up. It is explicitly a toy, not a forecast.

## From the chat

- The chat anchored on Epoch's **3.4×/year** (7-month doubling) as the most trustworthy demand-side number, because it is measured from disclosed data.
- It relayed Nvidia's **~1,000,000× in two years = ~10,000× per request × ~100× usage** as the qualitative explanation for why the curve is *bending up*, while flagging Nvidia as an interested party.
- It noted Huang's demand outlook rising from $500B (through 2026) to at least **$1T (through 2027)**.
- It used JLL for the structural shift: AI ~25% of data-center workloads in 2025, inference overtaking training in 2027, possibly half of workloads by 2030.
- It stated that the growth *rates* are more reliable than any dollar forecast or timing call, including its own.

concepts.title: Reasoning & agentic workloads
concepts.summary: Compute per inference session up ~10,000× as chatbots became reasoning agents
concepts.overview: Reasoning and agentic workloads are the shift from chatbots that answer in one short pass to models that "think" through long chains of intermediate tokens, and to agents that make many model calls to finish a task. By Nvidia's framing, compute per inference session rose about **10,000×** over two years because of this shift. That is the bigger of the two factors behind the claimed ~1,000,000× growth in [compute demand](#c/compute-demand), with [usage growth](#c/usage-growth) supplying the other ~100×. It is also why cheaper tokens don't mean cheaper answers: a reasoning answer uses far more tokens, so the [serving cost per task](#c/cost-per-token) rises even as the cost per token falls. The chat describes this test-time compute as a capability axis separate from parameter count, and as arguably the current paradigm shift sustaining progress. Its cost is also what keeps [frontier capacity scarce](#c/frontier-price).

concepts.title: Usage growth
concepts.summary: ~100× more usage in two years
concepts.overview: Usage growth is the rise in how much people and systems use AI: more users, more requests and more integrations. In Nvidia's GTC framing, usage grew about **100×** over two years. That is the smaller of the two multipliers behind the claimed ~1,000,000× growth in [compute demand](#c/compute-demand); the ~10,000× rise in per-request compute from [reasoning and agents](#c/reasoning-load) is the other. The number is a keynote framing from an interested party ([Nvidia](#c/nvidia)), not a measured statistic, so read it as directional. Usage also responds to price. As the [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) falls, people use more tokens, which is [Jevons' paradox](#c/jevons). Efficiency gains therefore tend to raise total consumption instead of lowering spend.

concepts.title: Frontier inference price & scarcity
concepts.summary: Premium capacity gets priced up or rationed — Fable's $10/$50 is one instance
concepts.overview: This concept covers what happens at the top of the market when demand outruns supply. [Compute demand](#c/compute-demand) grows about 3.4× a year while [supply](#c/compute-supply) is held back by multi-year lead times, so the scarcest thing, frontier inference capacity, gets priced up or rationed. [Fable 5](#c/fable-release) is the chat's concrete example: priced at **$10/$50 per million tokens**, double Opus, and moved behind usage credits on subscription plans. The chat's view is tier-specific. For the frontier it expects higher prices in the near term. For any *fixed* capability it expects prices to keep falling, since today's frontier becomes next year's commodity tier. The result is a widening spread. The chat's hedged guess is that the premium squeeze eases around [2027–28](#c/c-squeeze) as delayed capacity arrives, but only if demand growth slows.
concepts.article:
**Frontier inference price and scarcity** refers to the cost and availability of the newest, most capable models, the part of the AI market where capacity is tightest. The chat's central claim is that there is no single "price of AI". A frontier tier stays expensive, or gets pricier, while each older capability tier keeps getting cheaper, and the spread between them widens.

## The mechanism

Basic supply and demand explains most of it. On the demand side, the stock of AI compute grows about **3.4× per year** ([compute demand](#c/compute-demand)), and per-request compute has exploded with [reasoning and agentic workloads](#c/reasoning-load). On the supply side, the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity) is physical and slow to relieve: HBM sold out for 2026, high-voltage transformers at 36–48-month lead times, and 30–50% of planned 2026 capacity projected to [slip to 2028](#c/slip). When demand compounds and supply is gated by multi-year lead times, the scarce resource gets **priced up or rationed**.

Rationing and pricing look different in practice:

- **Pricing up.** A new flagship launches at a premium. [Claude Fable 5](#c/fable-release) came out at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, double Opus.
- **Rationing.** Access is gated. On June 23, 2026, Fable 5 was [taken out of subscription plans](#c/fable-gating) and made available through usage credits at API rates. Its return was tied to capacity.

## Why the frontier stays expensive while AI gets cheaper

The cost to reach a [fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability) falls very fast, by Epoch's headline around 100× a year and by controlled estimates 5–10× a year for frontier price-for-performance. That doesn't flow through to the frontier, because people don't buy fixed performance. They buy the newest models, and the newest models cost more per query, especially with long reasoning chains. Efficiency gains get *consumed* by capability growth, not passed on as price cuts, which is [Jevons' paradox](#c/jevons). Today's frontier model becomes next year's cheap tier, but by then there is a new frontier.

A second reason is that list [prices aren't serving costs](#c/price-vs-cost). Providers set prices as business decisions. Prices often hold flat through a model's life and step down when a successor launches, so scarcity can show up as a price that simply doesn't fall even while serving cost does.

## When it might ease

The chat was emphatic that this part is forecasting, not reporting.

1. **Supply relief** is roughly a 2027–2028 story, when [delayed capacity comes online](#c/capacity-relief). JLL expects nearly 100 GW of new capacity between 2026 and 2030, and McKinsey projects [~70 → ~220 GW](#c/dc-growth) within five years.
2. **Demand** is the bigger swing factor. The squeeze eases only if frontier demand growth slows, whether from saturation, from the expected inference applications failing to materialize, or from disappointing returns cutting capex.
3. If reasoning and agentic demand keeps compounding at recent rates, the frontier squeeze could last well past 2028, even as commodity inference keeps getting cheaper.

The [Stanford teaching model](#c/stanford-toy) offers scenarios for how the bottleneck could move: if demand growth slows to ~100% a year, supply catches up, and an energy breakthrough shifts the bottleneck to memory bandwidth. It explicitly calls itself a pedagogical toy, not a forecast.

## Who says what

The case for a lasting squeeze leans partly on interested parties. [Nvidia](#c/nvidia)'s "we are going to be short" comes from the company that sells the chips. Supply-side evidence from [Accuris](#c/accuris) and trade press (sold-out HBM, transformer lead times) is more physical and harder to spin. The claim itself is recorded as [Frontier capacity stays scarce until ~2027–28](#c/c-squeeze).

## From the chat

- The chat's direct answer to "will the squeeze drive costs up further?" was **"yes for frontier/premium tiers in the near term, no for equivalent capability over time,"** and it labelled this as reasoning, not reporting.
- It called Fable's $10/$50 pricing (double Opus) and the usage-credit gating "arguably a concrete instance" of scarce premium capability being priced and metered.
- It predicted a **widening spread**: frontier models staying expensive or getting more so, while the trailing tier keeps collapsing in price.
- Its best guess on timing, "heavily hedged", was easing in **2027–2028** only if demand growth decelerates. "I'd distrust anyone who says they do" know.
- It concluded that "AI got cheaper" and "the frontier got more expensive" can both be true indefinitely.

concepts.title: Serving cost per token
concepts.summary: What it costs a provider to produce a token at a given capability
concepts.overview: Serving cost per token is what it actually costs a provider, in hardware time, energy and memory, to generate one token from a given model. It is different from the list price the customer pays (see [Price ≠ serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost)). Several forces push it down. [Serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) such as batching, quantization and better kernels work on frozen weights. [Newer hardware](#c/hardware-gens) brings more memory bandwidth, and Mixture of Experts means only the active parameters do work on each token. [Distillation](#c/distillation) swaps in a smaller model. Because inference is memory-bound, bandwidth and HBM matter more than raw FLOPs. One force pushes the other way: reasoning models emit many more tokens per answer, so the cost per *task* can rise while the cost per token falls. Cheaper tokens also draw in more usage, which is [Jevons' paradox](#c/jevons).
concepts.article:
**Serving cost per token** is the provider's cost to produce one output token (or process one input token) from a particular model on particular hardware. It is the economic core of inference. Every discussion of AI "getting cheaper" is ultimately about this number, the [price](#c/price-vs-cost) charged on top of it, or the [capability](#c/fixed-capability) each token delivers.

## What it is made of

At its simplest, the cost per token is the cost of running an accelerator for a second divided by the number of tokens it produces in that second. The numerator covers amortized hardware (GPUs, HBM, networking), power and cooling, and the data center around them. The denominator, **throughput**, is where most engineering happens. Two facts shape throughput:

- **Inference is memory-bound.** For each generated token, a model has to stream its active weights and the relevant [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) out of HBM. The arithmetic units often sit idle waiting for data ([Inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound)). Memory bandwidth and capacity, not FLOPs, usually set the ceiling.
- **Batching spreads that cost.** When many requests are processed together, one pass over the weights serves all of them, so cost per token falls as concurrency rises, up to the limit of memory. That is why memory for the KV-cache is so contested.

## What lowers it

| Lever | How it helps | Needs retraining? |
|---|---|---|
| [Serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) | [Continuous batching](#c/cont-batching), [quantization](#c/quantization), [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding), FlashAttention, PagedAttention, prefix caching | No: works on frozen weights |
| [Hardware generations](#c/hardware-gens) | More bandwidth and HBM per chip, so more tokens per second and more concurrent requests | No |
| [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) | Per-token compute follows *active* parameters, e.g. 37B of DeepSeek-V3's 671B | Yes: an architecture choice |
| Cache-shrinking attention ([GQA](#c/gqa), [MLA](#c/mla)) | Smaller KV-cache per token, so more concurrency | Yes |
| [Distillation](#c/distillation) / model replacement | Serve a smaller model that matches the old quality | Yes: a new artifact |

The chat stresses the "needs retraining?" column. Only the first two rows explain how a *deployed* model gets cheaper over its life. The rest produce a different model, and most of Epoch's dramatic curve comes from them.

## What raises it

[Reasoning and agentic workloads](#c/reasoning-load) don't necessarily raise the cost per token, but they multiply the tokens per answer. Nvidia's framing puts per-session compute up ~10,000×. So the cost of a *task* can go up while the cost per token falls. Scarcity also feeds back. If the newest chips and HBM are sold out, the efficiency they offer exists on paper but can't fully bring costs down.

## Relation to price

The cost to serve and the price charged move on different schedules. The per-token API rate is a business decision only loosely tied to underlying cost. Prices often hold flat for a model's whole life and then drop in a step when a successor launches, even if serving cost fell gradually in between. At the frontier, scarcity can keep prices high regardless of cost ([Frontier price & scarcity](#c/frontier-price)).

## From the chat

- Asked whether "a particular version of Sonnet" gets 100× cheaper per year, the chat said no. A frozen model does get cheaper, but through serving software and hardware, "in lumps rather than a smooth exponential."
- It called inference software optimization on the same weights **"the biggest lever for a frozen model."**
- It said it has **no visibility** into Anthropic's serving stack, so it couldn't say how much cheaper any specific Sonnet version got.
- It split optimizations into pure serving tricks (FlashAttention, PagedAttention, KV quantization, prefix caching) and those baked in at training (GQA/MQA, MLA). Only the first group explains a deployed model getting cheaper without retraining.
- It linked MoE's total/active split to cost: "The total count buys you capacity; the active count sets your per-token cost". The catch is that all the experts still have to sit in HBM.

concepts.title: Hyperscaler capex
concepts.summary: Over $600B in 2026 (+36%), ~$450B of it AI infrastructure
concepts.overview: Hyperscaler capex is the capital spending by the major cloud companies on data centers, chips, power and networking. Per the chat's sources, it is expected to exceed **$600 billion in 2026, a 36% increase over 2025**, with about **$450 billion** going to AI infrastructure. The chat's graph attributes the +36% figure to [SemiAnalysis](#c/semianalysis) and describes the method as company guidance. Accuris describes the spending as "funded, contracted, and under construction rather than speculative." Capex is what pays for [accelerator supply](#c/gpu-supply) and [power](#c/power) buildout, but the chat's point is that money can't buy its way past physical lead times such as 36–48 months for transformers. That is why spending this large sits alongside [capacity](#c/capacity) that stays scarce. A pullback in capex, if returns disappoint, is one way the chat says the demand squeeze could cool.

concepts.title: Construction & interconnection delays
concepts.summary: 30–50% of planned 2026 AI capacity projected to slip to 2028
concepts.overview: Construction and interconnection delays are the gap between AI capacity that has been planned and capacity that actually switches on. Per [Accuris](#c/accuris), **30–50% of planned 2026 AI data-center capacity is projected to slip to 2028** because of grid interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks. A starker Tech Insider estimate has roughly half of planned US data centers for 2026 delayed or cancelled. Behind the delays are the physical layers of the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity): [power and grid](#c/power) connections and long-lead [electrical gear](#c/electrical-gear) such as transformers. The effect is to lower [available compute](#c/compute-supply) now and push it later. Component demand that was expected to peak in 2026 is instead sustained through 2027 and 2028 as the delayed projects [come online](#c/capacity-relief). This is the main reason the chat places supply relief in that window.

concepts.title: Jevons' paradox
concepts.summary: Cheaper tokens mean more tokens: efficiency gains get consumed by capability and usage, not passed through as price cuts
concepts.overview: Jevons' paradox is the observation, first made by the economist William Stanley Jevons about coal in the 1860s, that making a resource more efficient to use can *increase* total consumption of it, because cheaper use invites more use. In AI it explains why a collapsing cost per token doesn't produce collapsing bills. Epoch measures the cost of reaching a *fixed* capability falling around 100× a year, but people buy the frontier, not fixed capability. The savings get spent on longer [reasoning chains](#c/reasoning-load), agents and more [usage](#c/usage-growth). As the chat put it, efficiency gains are "consumed by capability growth rather than passed through as price cuts." This is how [compute demand](#c/compute-demand) can grow 3.4× a year while [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) falls, and why frontier capacity stays [scarce](#c/frontier-price).
concepts.article:
**Jevons' paradox** is the economic observation that improving the efficiency with which a resource is used can raise total consumption of that resource instead of lowering it. In AI compute economics it is the main reason inference keeps getting cheaper per unit while total spending and [compute demand](#c/compute-demand) keep climbing.

## Origin

The idea comes from William Stanley Jevons's 1865 book *The Coal Question*. Jevons noticed that more efficient steam engines had not reduced Britain's coal consumption. Because they made coal-powered work cheaper, they opened up new uses, and total coal use rose. Later economists called the general effect the "rebound effect". Jevons' paradox is the strong case, where the rebound more than cancels the saving.

## How it works

Efficiency lowers the cost of each unit of useful output. What happens next depends on how demand responds to price:

- If demand is **inelastic** (people want a fixed amount), efficiency cuts total spending.
- If demand is **elastic** (lower prices unlock many new uses), consumption grows faster than cost per unit falls, and total resource use rises.

AI inference in 2024–2026 looks strongly elastic. Every drop in the cost of a capability opens up new applications, longer contexts, more agent steps and more users.

## In AI compute

The chat framed this as two exponentials running against each other:

| Force | Rate quoted in the chat |
|---|---|
| Cost to deliver a fixed capability | falling ~100×/year (Epoch headline; controlled estimates 5–10×) |
| Demand for compute (installed AI chip stock) | growing ~3.4×/year |

If people bought fixed capability, the first line would win and bills would collapse. They don't. They buy the frontier, and the frontier gets more expensive per query. [Reasoning and agentic workloads](#c/reasoning-load) raised compute per session by roughly 10,000× in Nvidia's framing, and [usage](#c/usage-growth) grew about 100× on top. The savings from cheaper tokens are spent on more tokens.

So the collapse in [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability) and the persistent [frontier scarcity](#c/frontier-price) are consistent. Both follow from the same elastic demand. The chat's summary was that "AI got cheaper" and "the frontier got more expensive" can both be true indefinitely.

## Why it matters

- **For forecasting capacity.** Efficiency gains don't by themselves relieve the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity). Cheaper serving can deepen the squeeze by drawing in more demand.
- **For reading your bill.** A 100×/year efficiency statistic doesn't predict a 100× cheaper invoice. Users move to newer models and heavier workloads.
- **For the training-to-inference shift.** As [inference overtakes training](#c/inference-shift), demand grows with adoption, and adoption is exactly what cheaper tokens encourage.

## Limits of the analogy

Jevons' paradox is an empirical tendency, not a law. It holds only while demand stays elastic. The chat names conditions under which demand growth could slow: saturation of easy gains, inference applications failing to materialize at scale, or disappointing returns. Under any of them, efficiency gains would start to show up as lower spending. The paradox describes 2024–2026 well. Whether it holds as the market matures is an open question.

## From the chat

- The chat invoked Jevons directly: "making inference cheaper per token increases total tokens consumed rather than reducing spend."
- It gave this as the reason "your bill doesn't fall 100×". The 100×/year figure holds "at a fixed level of performance", and people don't buy fixed performance.
- It set **~3.4×/year** demand growth against **~100×/year** fixed-capability cost decline as the two opposing exponentials.
- It predicted a widening spread between an expensive frontier and a collapsing trailing tier as the practical consequence.

concepts.title: Inference overtakes training
concepts.summary: Expected in 2027; by 2030 AI could be half of all data-center workloads
concepts.overview: This event is the expected point, around **2027**, when running models (inference) overtakes building them (training) as the main AI load in data centers. The source is [JLL](#c/jll)'s data-center outlook. It estimates AI was about a quarter of data-center workloads in 2025, with training driving most of the demand, and projects that by **2030** AI could be half of all workloads, with inference as the primary driver. The shift matters because the two kinds of demand behave differently. A model is trained once or periodically, but inference demand grows with every user and agent and keeps compounding, so it is stickier. This is also where [Jevons' paradox](#c/jevons) bites: cheaper tokens mean more inference. JLL is a real-estate firm with a stake in the buildout, and it notes the inference boom depends on applications that don't yet exist at scale. Treat 2027 as a forecast. See [compute demand](#c/compute-demand).

concepts.title: Delayed capacity comes online
concepts.summary: The likely window for easing the premium squeeze — if demand growth also slows
concepts.overview: This event is the window, most likely **2027–2028**, when AI capacity delayed from 2026 finally switches on. Because 30–50% of planned 2026 capacity is projected to [slip to 2028](#c/slip), component demand expected to peak in 2026 is instead spread across 2027 and 2028 as those projects land. JLL also expects nearly 100 GW of new capacity between 2026 and 2030. The chat names this as the likely time for the premium squeeze to ease, with an important condition: relief happens only if [frontier demand](#c/compute-demand) growth also slows. If reasoning and agentic demand keeps compounding at recent rates, the frontier could stay [scarce](#c/frontier-price) well past this window even as commodity inference gets cheaper. The chat called its own timing call "heavily hedged". See also [Frontier capacity stays scarce until ~2027–28](#c/c-squeeze).

concepts.title: Data centers: ~70 GW → ~220 GW
concepts.summary: McKinsey: global supply could triple within five years, ~75% of growth from AI
concepts.overview: This is McKinsey's projection that global data-center supply could grow from about **70 GW today to about 220 GW within five years**, with around **75% of that growth driven by AI**. The chat called it "the one to anchor on" for the longer horizon. A roughly threefold increase over five years works out to about 26% a year compounded ([e-dc](#c/e-dc)). That is far slower than the ~3.4×/year growth in AI compute stock, but gigawatts measure power, not chip performance, so the two rates aren't directly comparable. [JLL](#c/jll) gives a more conservative sector figure of ~14% CAGR to 2030 ([e-dc-jll](#c/e-dc-jll)). [McKinsey](#c/mckinsey) is an analyst firm and this is a capacity forecast, not a measurement. It also assumes projects get built, while [slips](#c/slip) are already pushing 2026 capacity back.

concepts.title: New nuclear power at scale
concepts.summary: Most projected US nuclear growth lands after 2035, as small modular reactors mature
concepts.overview: New nuclear power is often pitched as the long-term fix for AI's [power constraint](#c/power), but the chat's sources place it firmly in the next decade. Per Carbon Credits, most of the projected increase in US nuclear capacity happens **after 2035**, as small modular reactors (SMRs) become commercially viable. So nuclear does nothing for the 2026–2028 squeeze. The relief that matters in that window comes from delayed conventional projects [coming online](#c/capacity-relief) and from the grid and [electrical gear](#c/electrical-gear) chain catching up. The chat mentions nuclear briefly, as a reminder that the "deeper-power solutions" are "mostly a next-decade story". It gives no details on specific reactor deals or timelines, and this entry adds none. See [Compute economics](#c/t-econ).

concepts.title: Blackwell sold out
concepts.summary: Nvidia FQ3 2026: record $51.2B data-center revenue, cloud GPUs sold out
concepts.overview: Blackwell is Nvidia's data-center GPU generation, the volume product in 2025–26. In its **fiscal Q3 2026** results (reported around November 2025), Nvidia posted record data-center revenue of **$51.2 billion**, and Jensen Huang said Blackwell sales were "off the charts" and cloud GPUs were sold out. The chat uses this as the main evidence that [accelerator supply](#c/gpu-supply) was the binding constraint in late 2025 and early 2026. It is also the hardware example in [hardware generations](#c/hardware-gens): the same model costs less per token on Blackwell-class chips because of more memory bandwidth and HBM. There's a catch, though. If the new chips are sold out and HBM-constrained, that efficiency exists on paper but can't fully bring costs down. The chat said it was thin on what comes after Blackwell. The source is [Nvidia](#c/nvidia) itself, an interested party, though revenue figures are audited disclosures.

concepts.title: Claude Fable 5 released
concepts.summary: Anthropic's most powerful model, priced at double Opus
concepts.overview: Claude Fable 5 is Anthropic's most powerful model, released publicly in **June 2026**. TechCrunch's headline noted the release came days after Anthropic warned that AI was getting too dangerous. On the API it is priced at **$10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens**, which the chat describes as double Opus. For the economics thread it matters as the case that started the discussion. Fable 5 was offered on subscription plans first, then [pulled into usage-credit billing on June 23](#c/fable-gating), with its return tied to capacity. The chat reads the premium price and the gating together as a concrete instance of [frontier scarcity pricing](#c/frontier-price). It had no inside knowledge of Anthropic's capacity decisions and gave no parameter count or architecture details for Fable 5.

concepts.title: Cost at a fixed capability
concepts.summary: The Epoch metric: the cheapest model that clears a benchmark bar, not a frozen model getting cheaper
concepts.body:
The fixed thing is the **capability** (a benchmark score), not the model. The model that
clears a bar in 2026 is smaller and cheaper than the one that cleared it in 2025. A
frozen set of weights gets cheaper too, but through serving work and hardware, in
lumps, and far more slowly.
concepts.overview: "Cost at a fixed capability" is the metric behind Epoch's famous claim that inference costs fall ~100× a year. The fixed thing is a **capability** (a benchmark score such as a GPQA or MMLU threshold), not a model. For each bar, you track the cheapest model that clears it over time. The model that clears a bar in 2026 is usually smaller and cheaper than the one that cleared it in 2025. So the metric measures how fast the field *re-reaches old capability bars*. It does not mean a given Sonnet gets 100× cheaper ([the misconception](#c/m-sonnet)). A frozen model gets cheaper too, through [serving work](#c/serving-opts) and [hardware](#c/hardware-gens), in lumps and far more slowly. The rate also varies widely: 9× to 900× a year depending on the bar, and ~5–10× once frozen list prices are controlled for ([price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)).
concepts.article:
**Cost at a fixed capability** is the measure behind the most-quoted statistic in AI economics: that inference is getting ~100× cheaper every year. Pick a capability level, usually a benchmark threshold, find the cheapest model that reaches it, and watch how that cheapest price changes over time. It is a useful measure and a widely misread one.

## What is held fixed

The metric holds the **capability** constant, not the model. The claim is that the cheapest model able to hit a given bar keeps getting much cheaper. Behind that, a *different* model is doing the work each year. A task that needed GPT-4-class compute in 2023 might be handled today by something Haiku-sized at a small fraction of the cost. The capability stayed put; the model delivering it shrank.

That makes it a measure of how fast the field re-reaches old bars. It is not the price trajectory of any product you can buy. The common misreading, that [a given Sonnet gets 100× cheaper](#c/m-sonnet), confuses the two.

## How it is measured

[Epoch AI](#c/epoch) builds the curves from model list prices and benchmark scores. Each capability bar (for example a GPQA-Diamond threshold) gives its own line. Three consequences follow:

- **There is no single rate.** Across bars, Epoch found declines ranging from **9× to 900× per year** ([e-price-all](#c/e-price-all)). "100×/year" is a summary of a wide spread.
- **The fastest declines are at the top.** The [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper) found the highest GPQA bin falling **31×/year** and the lowest only **1.7×/year** ([e-price-top](#c/e-price-top)). Frontier bars are new, so the first cheaper model to match them is a huge multiplier. Old bars have already had their cost squeezed out. This runs against the intuition that [higher bars take longer to catch](#c/m-harder).
- **Frozen list prices inflate it.** Proprietary developers rarely cut prices on old models, so an old expensive model's price stays frozen next to a new cheap one, which exaggerates the apparent decline. Controlled estimates are much lower (next section).

## The honest range

| Estimate | Rate | What it isolates |
|---|---|---|
| Pure [algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress) | ~3×/yr | Hardware price declines and competition divided out ([e-price-algo](#c/e-price-algo)) |
| Frontier price-for-performance | ~5–10×/yr | Controlled for frozen prices ([e-price-frontier](#c/e-price-frontier)) |
| Open-weight models | 7–28×/yr, geometric mean ~11.8× | No list-price games; fairly uniform across quality ([e-price-open](#c/e-price-open)) |
| All models, current list prices | up to 100–900×/yr | Headline; confounded and concentrated in the latest year |

## What drives it

The capability-bar decline mostly comes from new, smaller models reaching old quality: [distillation](#c/distillation) of fresh frontier models into smaller students, [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) splitting total from active parameters, better training data, and algorithmic progress. The price-trend paper's authors suggest distillation and MoE may explain why declines are fastest at the frontier. Hardware and [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) contribute too, but they are the only levers that also make a *frozen* model cheaper, and they do so much more slowly.

## Limits

- **It is benchmark-bound.** "Cost to reach capability X" really means "cost to reach benchmark score X". Epoch notes that benchmarks miss many useful capabilities as well as factors like output speed.
- **The fastest rates are recent.** The biggest declines in the 9–900× range happened in the last year, and Epoch flags that they may not persist.
- **It says nothing directly about your bill.** Users buy the frontier, not fixed capability, so per [Jevons' paradox](#c/jevons) the savings get spent on more capability. Actual [prices](#c/price-vs-cost) move on their own schedule.

## From the chat

- The chat called it "one of the most widely misread statistics in the space" and said it does **not** mean a frozen Sonnet gets 100× cheaper a year.
- It described the 100×/year as "the falling cost of *re-reaching old capability bars*, not the falling price of any single shipped product."
- The user hypothesized that higher bars would be slower to catch. The data showed the opposite: fastest at the top (31×/yr), slowest at the bottom (1.7×/yr).
- The chat ranked the numbers from "real underlying tech progress" (~3×) to "headline-grabbing but confounded" (100–900×), and called the 5–12× range the most defensible "real" figure.
- It tied the metric to parameter trends: MoE and the post-2023 decoupling of parameters from capability are "a big part of the machinery behind" the decline.

concepts.title: Price ≠ serving cost
concepts.summary: List prices hold flat through a model's life and step down when a successor launches
concepts.overview: The per-token price a provider charges is a **business decision** only loosely tied to what it costs to serve that token. The two move on different schedules. [Serving cost](#c/cost-per-token) tends to fall gradually over a model's life as [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) and [new hardware](#c/hardware-gens) arrive. List prices usually hold flat for the model's whole life and then step down when a successor launches. This corrects the assumption that [the price you pay tracks the cost to serve](#c/m-price). It also distorts the famous trend data. Proprietary developers rarely cut prices on older models, so headline cost-decline figures built from current list prices are inflated, which is why [open-weight models](#c/e-price-open) give a cleaner read. At the frontier, [scarcity](#c/frontier-price) can hold prices up regardless of cost.
concepts.article:
**Price ≠ serving cost** is the principle that the price a model provider charges per token and the provider's actual cost to produce that token are different quantities, driven by different forces and changing on different schedules. Mixing them up leads to wrong conclusions about both AI economics and the trend statistics built from prices.

## Two different schedules

- **Serving cost** ([serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token)) tends to fall *gradually* over a model's deployed life. Engineers add better batching, [quantization](#c/quantization), attention kernels and cache management ([serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts)), and the fleet moves to [newer hardware](#c/hardware-gens) with more memory bandwidth. None of this changes the weights, and all of it lowers cost.
- **List price** tends to stay *flat* for a model's whole life, then drop in a *step* when a successor launches. The new model often arrives at a lower price for the same or better capability, while the old model's price is left alone.

So between launches, a provider's margin on a given model can widen quietly as serving cost falls under a fixed price. Or it can be spent on subsidizing other tiers. The public price signal says nothing about which is happening.

## Why prices don't track cost

Pricing is a commercial choice shaped by things other than cost:

- **Scarcity.** When capacity is short, providers can price up or ration, as [Fable 5](#c/fable-release) did at $10/$50 per million tokens and with its [usage-credit gating](#c/fable-gating). See [frontier price & scarcity](#c/frontier-price).
- **Competition.** Where there are close substitutes, including open-weight models that anyone can serve, prices get pushed toward cost.
- **Product strategy.** Keeping old prices frozen steers users toward newer models. Launch pricing positions a model against competitors.
- **Subscriptions.** Flat-rate plans decouple per-token price from use entirely. That is why Claude Code's `/cost` shows token usage but not dollars on Max and Pro plans.

## Consequences for trend statistics

Because list prices are what's observable, most public "cost" trends are really *price* trends. That creates a known distortion. [Epoch](#c/epoch)'s headline figures, up to 100–900× a year, use all models at their *current* list prices. Proprietary builders tend not to cut the prices of older models, so a frozen, expensive old price sits next to a cheap new one, and the apparent decline is exaggerated.

Controlled studies try to correct for this:

- The [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper) finds frontier price-for-performance falling about **5–10× a year**, and about **3× a year** for algorithmic efficiency alone, once hardware and competition are divided out.
- The [open-model price analysis](#c/open-price) uses open-weight models, which "avoid proprietary list-price games" because many hosts compete to serve the same weights. It finds a steadier **7–28× a year** (geometric mean ~11.8×).

Even the controlled numbers are still prices, not costs. Nobody outside the labs observes serving cost directly.

## The misconception it corrects

A natural assumption is that [the price you pay tracks the cost to serve](#c/m-price), so falling costs mean falling prices, promptly and in proportion. The chat's correction is that prices step down at successor launches and are only loosely coupled to cost in between. The corollary is that a steady API price doesn't mean serving costs are steady. Also, Epoch's curve is about an idealized cost-to-capability, not directly about either price or serving cost.

## From the chat

- The chat said the per-token API price "is a business decision that's only loosely coupled to underlying cost."
- It said prices "often hold flat across a model's life and then drop as a step when a successor launches, even if serving cost fell gradually in between."
- It relayed LessWrong's point that "proprietary model builders tend not to change the inference price of older models," which inflates all-model trend figures.
- It admitted it had no visibility into Anthropic's actual serving costs, so it couldn't say how much cheaper any specific Sonnet version became to serve.

concepts.title: Serving optimizations
concepts.summary: Batching, quantization, speculative decoding, attention kernels, KV-cache work — frozen weights, cheaper tokens
concepts.overview: Serving optimizations are changes to *how* a model is run, not to its weights, that lower the [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token). The chat calls them "the biggest lever for a frozen model." The main ones are [continuous batching](#c/cont-batching) to keep accelerators saturated, [weight quantization](#c/quantization) to FP8/INT8/INT4, [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding), FlashAttention-style kernels, and KV-cache work such as PagedAttention, KV quantization and prefix caching. Most of them attack the same bottleneck: [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), so the aim is to move less data or move it less often. They stack, and a modern stack runs most of them at once. They are the real answer to whether a particular Sonnet gets cheaper to run. It does, mostly through these, but in lumps and far slower than Epoch's 100×/year capability curve.
concepts.article:
**Serving optimizations** are the engineering techniques that make an already-trained model cheaper and faster to run without changing what it computes, or changing it only slightly. They explain how a *frozen* model (a particular version of Sonnet, say) gets cheaper to serve over its life. The chat singles them out as the biggest lever for a deployed model.

## The bottleneck they attack

Transformer inference is usually [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). Generating each token means streaming the model's weights and the KV-cache from the GPU's large but slow HBM into its small, fast on-chip SRAM. The arithmetic units often sit idle waiting for data. Almost every serving optimization is a way to move less data, move it less often, or do more useful work each time it moves.

## The main techniques

| Technique | What it does | Works on frozen weights? |
|---|---|---|
| [Continuous batching](#c/cont-batching) | Swaps requests in and out of a running batch mid-flight so the accelerator never idles | Yes |
| [Weight quantization](#c/quantization) | Stores weights at FP8/INT8/INT4 instead of 16-bit, cutting bytes moved per token | Yes (sometimes with calibration) |
| [Speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding) | A small draft model proposes tokens; the big model verifies several at once | Yes, given a draft model |
| [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn) | Tiles and fuses the attention computation so the full score matrix never goes to HBM | Yes: output mathematically identical |
| [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) | Stores the KV-cache in fixed-size pages, removing fragmentation so more requests fit | Yes |
| [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant) | Stores keys and values in 8-bit or lower | Yes |
| [Prefix / prompt caching](#c/prefix-cache) | Computes a shared prefix's KV-cache once and reuses it across requests | Yes |

The chat draws a sharp line between these pure serving tricks and optimizations that must be **baked in at training time**, such as [GQA](#c/gqa)/MQA and MLA, which shrink the KV-cache at the source. Only the first group explains a deployed model getting cheaper without retraining.

## How they compose

They stack instead of competing. The chat describes a typical modern stack: a GQA model with FlashAttention kernels, running under PagedAttention memory management, with prefix caching and often KV quantization on top, and continuous batching keeping the accelerator saturated. Each attacks a different facet: kernel efficiency, memory fragmentation, cache size, cache precision and redundant recomputation.

Much of the payoff comes through **concurrency**. When the KV-cache takes less memory, more requests fit on one GPU at a time, one pass over the weights serves more of them, and tokens per GPU-second go up. That is the quantity that drives [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) down.

## How big the gains are

The chat gave no specific multiplier for any provider. It stressed that serving gains arrive **in lumps**, as each technique is deployed, not as a smooth exponential. They are also far smaller than the ~100×/year headline for [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability), which is dominated by new, smaller models reaching old quality bars. Serving work is one ingredient in the "algorithmic" slice of cost declines, alongside [hardware generations](#c/hardware-gens) and [distillation](#c/distillation).

The chat also frames this category as the kind of incremental work that makes up most sustained cost declines ([Sustained cost declines come mostly from incremental work](#c/c-incremental)). Each technique is modest, but together they add up.

## Trade-offs

- **Quality.** Quantization and KV quantization can cost some accuracy. Keys tend to be more sensitive than values. FlashAttention and PagedAttention are exact.
- **Complexity.** Each layer of optimization adds engineering and debugging cost to the serving system.
- **Opacity.** Closed labs don't publish their stacks, so which techniques a given provider runs can only be inferred.

## From the chat

- The chat called inference software optimization on the same weights "the biggest lever for a frozen model" and "the real answer to 'does Sonnet get cheaper to run'."
- It listed the core set as better batching, quantization (FP8/INT8/INT4, "often with negligible quality loss"), speculative decoding, better attention kernels and KV-cache optimizations.
- It linked prefix caching to the ~90%-off cached-input pricing seen on APIs.
- It cautioned that these mechanics are well established from open research and systems like vLLM, but that it could not say which combination Anthropic, OpenAI or others actually run.

concepts.title: Hardware generations
concepts.summary: More memory bandwidth and HBM per chip: the same model costs less per token on Blackwell
concepts.overview: Each new accelerator generation lowers the cost of serving the *same* model. On Blackwell-class hardware a model costs less per token than on the previous generation, mainly because of **more memory bandwidth**, which is usually the real bottleneck for inference, and **more HBM capacity**, so more of the model and more concurrent requests fit on each chip. That makes hardware one of the few levers, along with [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts), that cut the [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) of a frozen model. The chat adds a caveat from the [capacity](#c/capacity) thread. If the new chips are [sold out](#c/blackwell) and [HBM-constrained](#c/hbm-supply), the efficiency exists on paper but can't fully bring costs down. Studies that isolate algorithmic progress divide out hardware price declines, which is how the [~3×/year](#c/e-price-algo) figure is obtained.
concepts.article:
**Hardware generations** are successive families of AI accelerators, such as Nvidia's Hopper and then Blackwell, or new TPU generations. Each one delivers more throughput per chip, per dollar and per watt. For inference economics the key point is that the *same* model, with identical weights, costs less per token on newer hardware. That makes hardware one of the few ways a frozen model gets cheaper over its life.

## Why newer chips cut serving cost

The obvious assumption is that new chips help because they do more arithmetic per second. For inference that is usually not the main reason. [Inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound): generating a token means streaming the active weights and the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) out of HBM, and the arithmetic units wait on that data. Two properties therefore matter most:

- **Memory bandwidth.** More bytes per second out of HBM means more tokens per second for the same model, which directly lowers [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token).
- **HBM capacity.** More memory per chip means more of the model fits on fewer chips, with less cross-chip communication, and more room for KV-caches. More concurrent requests means each pass over the weights serves more users.

Newer chips also bring features that software optimizations exploit. The chat notes that FlashAttention's third version was tuned specifically for Hopper-class hardware, and lower-precision number formats let [quantized](#c/quantization) models run natively.

## Two axes that get conflated

The chat separates two ways newer chips "change the game":

| Axis | Matters for | Main limiter |
|---|---|---|
| Raw FLOPs | Training frontier models | Compute |
| Tokens per dollar per watt | Serving models to users | Memory bandwidth and HBM capacity |

For a subscription-serving constraint like the one behind [Fable 5's gating](#c/fable-gating), the inference axis is the relevant one, and it is gated as much by HBM as by compute.

## The scarcity caveat

Efficiency on a spec sheet only helps if you can get the hardware. In late 2025 Nvidia reported record data-center revenue of $51.2B with [Blackwell sold out](#c/blackwell), and SK Hynix's [HBM](#c/hbm-supply) was sold out for 2026. When the newest generation is supply-constrained, much of the fleet still runs on older chips, and the per-token savings are real but not fully available. This is why hardware progress and [frontier scarcity](#c/frontier-price) can happen at the same time.

## Hardware's share of the cost decline

Hardware is one of three factors that controlled studies separate out of the headline price decline, alongside competition and algorithmic efficiency. The [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper) divides out hardware price declines (and controls for competition) to arrive at ~3×/year for [algorithmic efficiency alone](#c/e-price-algo), against 5–10×/year for frontier price-for-performance overall. So hardware accounts for a meaningful part of the gap, but new, smaller models reaching old quality bars ([cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability)) dominate the headline numbers.

## Limits of the chat's coverage

The chat was candid that it was "thinner here". It had no solid current detail on what comes after Blackwell, on custom silicon such as Google's TPUs or Amazon's Trainium displacing Nvidia, or on inference-specific chips. It offered to research those instead of relying on memory. This entry therefore doesn't describe specific future chips.

## From the chat

- "The same model served on Blackwell-class hardware costs less per token than on the prior generation," mainly through more memory bandwidth and more HBM capacity.
- Memory bandwidth "is usually the actual bottleneck for inference, not raw FLOPs."
- Caveat: "if the new chips are sold out and HBM-constrained, the efficiency exists on paper but isn't fully available to relieve cost."
- The chat distinguished training FLOPs from inference tokens per dollar per watt, and said the latter is what matters for serving capacity.
- It said it lacked reliable detail on the next-generation roadmap and custom or inference-specific silicon.

concepts.title: Distillation
concepts.summary: Train a smaller student on a stronger model's outputs; the artifact is swapped, the capability kept
concepts.overview: Distillation trains a smaller "student" model to imitate a stronger "teacher". The classic form, from Hinton and colleagues in 2015, matches the teacher's output probabilities. For closed teachers, whose weights and distributions are hidden, it means [supervised fine-tuning](#c/sft) on text the teacher generated. For cost, the effect is that the *artifact is swapped* while roughly the same capability is kept. A provider can serve a smaller, cheaper model, and to users it can look as if "the model got cheaper." The chat calls this largely what Epoch's [fixed-capability](#c/fixed-capability) cost curve captures, and the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper) suggests distillation helps explain why declines are fastest at the frontier. It is well documented: TinyGSM got a 125M model to 63.1% on grade-school math using GPT-3.5 data. How much of open models' *reasoning* gains it explains is [contested](#c/c-distill-open).
concepts.article:
**Distillation** is a training technique in which a smaller *student* model learns to reproduce the behavior of a larger or stronger *teacher*. It lets developers keep much of a big model's capability while serving something far cheaper. In inference economics, it is one of the main ways the [cost to reach a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability) keeps falling.

## How it works

The modern form comes from Hinton, Vinyals and Dean's 2015 knowledge-distillation paper. The student is trained to match the teacher's full output probability distribution (its "soft labels"), not just the correct answer, because those distributions carry information about which wrong answers are nearly right.

When the teacher is a **closed model**, that isn't possible. You can't see its weights, hidden states or output distributions. Distillation then becomes output-based: generate a large set of the teacher's responses and fine-tune the student on them. In practice this is [supervised fine-tuning](#c/sft) on a stronger model's outputs, which is why the chat calls it "a souped-up SFT." The same idea underlies [synthetic SFT responses](#c/synthetic-sft) in post-training pipelines.

## Why it matters for cost

Providers don't serve the same giant model forever. They can distill it into a smaller student, or replace it with a new model that reaches the same quality more cheaply. To a user it looks as if the model got cheaper, but the artifact was swapped. Because a smaller model moves fewer bytes per token and fits more requests per GPU, the [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) drops sharply.

This is why distillation matters to the headline trend data. The chat calls the capability-bar-chasing captured by Epoch's curve "largely" this mechanism. The [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s authors suggest greater use of distillation (and [MoE](#c/moe)) may be why prices fall fastest in the highest capability bins, around 31×/year in the top GPQA bin. Distilling a fresh, expensive frontier model into something smaller is a big one-time win, and a years-old cheap model has no equivalent move left.

## Evidence that it works

- **Productized.** OpenAI offers Model Distillation as a product, using outputs of models like GPT-4o and o1-preview to fine-tune cheaper models such as GPT-4o mini.
- **TinyGSM.** 12.3M synthetic math problems generated with GPT-3.5-turbo took a **125M-parameter** model to **63.1%** pass@1 on grade-school math.
- **Open-model lineage.** Alpaca (Llama fine-tuned on ~52K instructions generated by an OpenAI model), Open Orca (GPT-4-distilled outputs), ShareGPT logs, MagicCoder and CodeGemma all relied on outputs from stronger models.
- **Fully open recipes.** [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)'s new synthetic SFT datasets use responses written by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet (for coding).
- **Self-distillation.** DeepSeek distilled [R1](#c/deepseek-r1)'s reasoning into smaller models of its own.

## Contested: reasoning gains
