- It raised the logit lens / early exit as the honest nuance.
- DeepSeek-V3's MTP (`num_nextn_predict_layers: 1`) was described as a training objective whose extra heads "double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference."

concepts.title: Serving system
concepts.summary: What runs the model for many users at once
concepts.overview: The **serving system** is the software and hardware stack that runs a trained model for many users at once, and it is where much of a frozen model's cost reduction happens. It loads the weights onto accelerators (for DeepSeek-V3, all 671B parameters must sit in HBM even though only ~37B are active per token), [batches](#c/batching) requests together, runs the prefill and [decoding loop](#c/decoding), and manages the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). A modern stack, in the chat's summary, runs a GQA or MLA model with [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn) kernels, under [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) memory management, with prefix caching, often KV quantization, low-precision weights (FP8/INT8/INT4) and continuous batching. None of these change the weights, so they make an already-deployed model cheaper over its life. Open stacks like vLLM are well documented, but providers like Anthropic and OpenAI don't publish theirs.

concepts.title: Batching
concepts.summary: Keeping accelerators saturated with many requests
concepts.overview: **Batching** means running many requests through the model at the same time so the accelerator stays busy. During generation each step must stream the model's weights from GPU memory, and for a single request that is a lot of data movement for very little arithmetic, because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). Processing a batch of requests together reuses each weight read across all of them, so throughput (tokens per GPU per second) rises steeply and cost per token falls. The limit is memory: every request in the batch needs its own [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), which is why cache-shrinking tricks ([GQA](#c/gqa), [MLA](#c/mla), [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), KV quantization) translate directly into bigger batches and cheaper tokens. [Continuous batching](#c/cont-batching) goes further, swapping finished requests out and new ones in at every step instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish. The chat listed "better batching" first among the ways a frozen model gets cheaper to serve.

concepts.title: Numeric precision
concepts.summary: FP8 / INT8 / INT4 instead of 16-bit
concepts.overview: **Numeric precision** is how many bits each stored number uses. Models are commonly trained and served in 16-bit formats (BF16/FP16), but weights, activations and the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) can be stored in **FP8, INT8 or INT4**, halving or quartering memory. Since decoding is limited by how fast bytes move out of GPU memory ([inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound)), fewer bytes per parameter means faster tokens as well as more room for batching. The chat listed quantization, "running the model at lower numerical precision, FP8/INT8/INT4, often with negligible quality loss", as a major way a frozen model gets cheaper to serve. DeepSeek-V3 went further: FP8 is native to its training framework, so its config reads `quant_method: "fp8"` and it ships FP8 weights, with a conversion script if you want BF16. Post-hoc compression is covered under [weight quantization](#c/quantization) and [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant).

concepts.title: Decoding loop
concepts.summary: Generating one token at a time, autoregressively
concepts.overview: The **decoding loop** is how a transformer generates text: **one token at a time**. After a **prefill** pass processes the whole prompt in parallel and fills the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), each decode step runs the full stack for just the newest token, reads every cached key and value, gets next-token probabilities from the [output head](#c/output-head), samples one token, appends it, and repeats. Each step depends on the previous one, so steps can't be parallelized within a request, and each must stream the active weights and the whole cache from memory for very little arithmetic. That is why decode is [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), and why long reasoning chains are costly: every thinking token is sequential. [Speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding) has a cheap drafter propose several tokens for the big model to verify at once, and DeepSeek's MTP module can serve as that drafter. [Diffusion LMs](#c/diffusion-lm) abandon strict left-to-right generation altogether.

concepts.title: Query, key, value
concepts.summary: Query = what I'm looking for, key = what I advertise, value = what I hand over
concepts.overview: **Query, key and value** are the three vectors every token produces in each attention head, via three learned projection matrices. The chat's soft-database analogy: the **query** is what the current token is looking for ("I'm a verb, looking for my subject"), each token's **key** advertises what it offers ("I'm a noun, I could be a subject"), and the **value** is the content it hands over if matched. The query is dotted with every earlier key, the scores are scaled and softmaxed into weights, and the output is the weighted blend of values. Crucially, a query is used once and discarded, while keys and values of past tokens are needed by every future token, so only K and V go into the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). That asymmetry is why [GQA](#c/gqa) and [MQA](#c/mqa) cut K/V heads but keep query heads. In DeepSeek-V3 each query/key has 128 content dims plus a 64-dim [RoPE](#c/rope) slice.
concepts.article:
**Query (Q), key (K) and value (V)** are the three roles each token plays inside an [attention head](#c/heads). Every token's vector is multiplied by three separately learned matrices to produce one vector for each role, and the interplay between them is what lets a token gather information from the rest of the sequence.

## The soft database lookup

The chat's analogy is a database lookup where you get a *blend* of results instead of one exact match:

| Vector | Role | Illustration |
|---|---|---|
| **Query** | What the current token is looking for | "I'm a verb, I'm looking for my subject" |
| **Key** | What each token advertises | "I'm a noun, I could be a subject" |
| **Value** | What a token hands over if matched | the actual content it contributes |

In short: *query = what I'm looking for, key = what I advertise, value = what I hand over.*

## How the computation runs

For one head and the current token *t*:

1. Compute `q_t`, and for every earlier token *i*, `k_i` and `v_i`.
2. Score each earlier token: `s_i = q_t · k_i / √d`, where *d* is the head dimension. The scaling keeps scores from growing with dimension.
3. Softmax the scores into weights that sum to 1. A causal mask gives future tokens zero weight.
4. Output `Σ weight_i · v_i`, a blend of values dominated by the best-matching keys.

The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected back to the [residual stream](#c/residual) width.

### A tiny example

Suppose three earlier tokens have scores 2.0, 0.5 and −1.0 against the current query. Softmax gives weights of roughly 0.79, 0.18 and 0.04, so the output is mostly the first token's value with a little of the second's. Nothing is a hard yes/no; every earlier token contributes in proportion to its match.

## Why only K and V get cached

During [decoding](#c/decoding), the query of the current token is used once, for this step, and is never needed again. But the keys and values of every past token are needed by *every future token*. So:

- **K and V are cached** in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), per token, per head, per layer;
- **Q is not.**

This asymmetry drives an entire family of designs:

- [Multi-head attention](#c/mha): one K/V pair per query head, the full cache.
- [Multi-Query Attention](#c/mqa): all query heads share one K/V head, so the cache is about N× smaller.
- [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa): query heads in groups share K/V. With 32 query heads in 8 groups, the cache is 4× smaller.
- [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla): cache a compressed latent from which K and V are reconstructed.

## Position lives in Q and K

Attention on its own ignores order. [RoPE](#c/rope) fixes this by rotating the query and key vectors by position-dependent angles before the dot product, so the score depends on how far apart two tokens are. Values are not rotated. In DeepSeek-V3 each query and key has a 128-dim content part (`qk_nope_head_dim`) plus a separate 64-dim positional part (`qk_rope_head_dim`), while values are 128-dim (`v_head_dim`). That split exists because MLA's compression would otherwise scramble the rotation.

## From the chat

- The chat introduced Q/K/V with the soft-database analogy and the verb/subject example.
- It defined a head as "one complete instance of that whole query-key-value lookup," with its own learned projections.
- It made the key point that "the thing you cache is the keys and values, not the queries," which is why K/V head count, not query head count, sets cache size.
- It noted that head specializations like "subject-verb agreement" are illustrative; real heads are often messier.

concepts.title: Pre-training
concepts.summary: Next-token prediction over trillions of tokens: the expensive phase
concepts.overview: Pre-training is the first and most expensive phase of building a language model. A randomly initialised transformer learns to predict the next token over a huge corpus of mostly web text, measured in trillions of tokens (Llama 4 Maverick about 22T, GLM-5 28.5T), using months of accelerator time. The objective is simple: given the tokens so far, assign high probability to the one that actually comes next. Getting good at that forces the model to absorb grammar, facts, code and patterns of reasoning. The output is a **base model**. It has a lot of latent capability but is not yet an assistant, and asked a question it may simply continue with more questions. [Post-training](#c/post-training) then elicits and directs that capability. How pre-training compute is split between parameters and data is governed by [Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla), and the quality of the corpus ([data curation](#c/c-data-lever)) has turned out to be one of the biggest levers.
concepts.article:
**Pre-training** is the phase in which a language model learns language and world knowledge from scratch by predicting the next token over a vast text corpus. It accounts for the great majority of a model's training compute: trillions of tokens and months of accelerator time. It produces a *base model*, a raw next-token predictor with enormous latent capability but no orientation toward following instructions or holding a conversation. Everything that makes a model feel like an assistant comes afterwards, in [post-training](#c/post-training).

## How it works

The model (for current LLMs, a [decoder-only transformer](#c/transformer)) reads text that has been split into tokens by a tokenizer. At every position it outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token. The loss is the cross-entropy between that distribution and the token that actually came next. Gradients flow back through every layer and all weights are updated. The same step is repeated across the whole corpus, usually in a single pass or close to it.

The objective is deceptively simple. To predict the next token well across web pages, code, papers and books, a model has to internalise syntax, facts, arithmetic, programming idioms and the structure of arguments. In the chat's phrasing, pre-training *builds the capabilities*, and post-training *elicits and directs them*.

Some typical scales from the chat:

| Model | Parameters (total / active) | Pre-training tokens |
|---|---|---|
| [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) | 400B / 17B | ~22T |
| [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) | 744B / ~40B | 28.5T |

## The corpus

Pre-training data is dominated by [filtered web crawl](#c/web-crawl) derived from Common Crawl, with curated sources layered on top: code, academic papers, books, Wikipedia, Q&A sites and math. Building it means [extraction and cleaning](#c/extraction), [deduplication](#c/dedup), [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter) and [decontamination](#c/decontamination). The dominant move is throwing data away. The [DCLM](#c/dclm) benchmark showed that better curation alone, with architecture and training held fixed, could beat the previous open-data state of the art by about 6 MMLU points at half the compute.

## Why it matters

Pre-training sets the ceiling. A widely discussed question (see [RLVR](#c/rlvr)) is whether later reinforcement learning can push a model *beyond* what its base model could already do, or mostly sharpens what was learned here. Either way, the base model's knowledge and raw ability come from this phase.

It is also where most of the compute bill has historically gone. Frontier training compute has grown about 5× per year since 2020 (doubling roughly every 5.2 months), and pre-training compute efficiency has improved about 3× per year. How to spend that compute, bigger model or more data, is the question [Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla) answers: roughly 20 tokens per parameter for a compute-optimal run. Its influence helps explain why frontier models shrank after [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4) and put the extra compute into data.

## Trade-offs and variations

- **Compute-optimal vs. inference-optimal.** Chinchilla minimises training cost for a given quality. Labs that will serve a model billions of times often train a smaller model on far more tokens than 20 per parameter, because it is cheaper to run afterwards.
- **Mid-training / continued pre-training.** The boundary with post-training is fuzzy. Labs often run an intermediate stage heavy in math and code, or extend context length (for example with YaRN), before formal post-training begins.
- **Architecture choices** such as [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) change what "model size" means. Total parameters set memorisation capacity, while active parameters set the per-token cost.
- **Secrecy.** Even open-weight models almost never release their pre-training data, partly for competitive reasons and increasingly for legal ones (copyright and consent scrutiny).

## From the chat

- Pre-training was described as "the expensive, compute-heavy phase": trillions of tokens and months of GPU time, producing a base model that "has read the entire internet but has never been told what they're supposed to *do* with that."
- The chat attributed the post-GPT-4 shrinkage of frontier models partly to Chinchilla: capability that would have come from more parameters came from more and better data on a smaller model.
- On corpora, the chat's headline was "aggressive throwing-away". DCLM and FineWeb-Edu discard the lowest-quality ~90%, and DCLM-Baseline let a 7B model reach 64% MMLU on only 2.6T tokens.
- The chat declined to give a percentage for how much research effort goes into data. It said data work "plausibly rivals or exceeds" architecture and training-code work, and called any specific "X%" figure folklore.
- Flagship recipes remain hidden. Nearly everything concrete about pre-training data comes from open-data projects, and whether closed labs do the same is inference.

concepts.title: Multi-head attention
concepts.summary: Many parallel Q/K/V heads per layer, each learning a different relationship
concepts.overview: **Multi-head attention (MHA)** is the standard attention design from the 2017 Transformer: each layer runs many independent [heads](#c/heads) in parallel, each with its own query, key and value projections, so each can learn a different relationship (loosely, one tracking subject-verb links, another pronoun reference). Outputs are concatenated and projected back into the residual stream. The original Transformer used 8 heads; DeepSeek-V3 has 128 per layer across 61 layers. In plain MHA every query head has its own K/V head, so the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) stores K and V for all of them. That is the most expressive option and the most memory-hungry. The later variants all reduce that cost: [MQA](#c/mqa) shares one K/V head, [GQA](#c/gqa) shares one per group, and [MLA](#c/mla) compresses K/V into a latent.
concepts.article:
**Multi-head attention (MHA)** runs several attention lookups ("heads") side by side in each [layer](#c/layer-stack), each with its own learned projections, and combines their results. It was introduced with the original Transformer in 2017 and remains the conceptual baseline that every later attention variant is measured against.

## How it works

Given the token vectors entering a layer (width *d*), MHA:

1. projects each token into a query, key and value **for every head**, each head using its own three matrices;
2. runs scaled dot-product [attention](#c/attention) separately in each head;
3. concatenates the heads' outputs;
4. applies an output projection to mix them and return a vector of width *d* to the [residual stream](#c/residual).

Heads are typically narrow (head dim is often 64 or 128), so many of them together cost about the same as one wide head. What you gain is several *independent* views of the sequence.

## Why multiple heads

One head has one set of Q/K/V projections, so it tends to learn one kind of relationship. With many heads, each can specialize. The chat's illustrative examples: one head tracking subject-verb agreement, another following which pronoun refers to which noun, another attending to nearby punctuation. Those clean labels are illustrative; real heads are messier and often not neatly interpretable. The principle that different heads learn different relationships holds, though.

Every layer has its **own** fresh set of heads. Layer 3's might do low-level syntactic linking while layer 20's track discourse-level relationships.

## Scale over time

| Model | Heads per layer | Layers |
|---|---|---|
| Original Transformer (2017, base) | 8 | 6 encoder + 6 decoder |
| DeepSeek-V3 | 128 | 61 |

Closed frontier models don't publish head counts.

## The cost: one K/V pair per query head

In plain MHA, query heads and K/V heads come in matched sets: N query heads, N key heads, N value heads. During generation, past keys and values are stored in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), so the cache holds K and V for all N heads, in every layer, for every token. For long contexts and large batches, that cache becomes the dominant memory cost and the main drag on [serving](#c/serving) throughput.

## What came after

MHA's cache cost motivated a sequence of variants:

| Variant | Idea | Cache vs. MHA |
|---|---|---|
| [MQA](#c/mqa) (2019) | All query heads share a single K/V head | ~1/N; quality can dent |
| [GQA](#c/gqa) (2023) | Query heads in groups, one K/V head per group | e.g. ¼ with 32 heads in 8 groups |
| [MLA](#c/mla) (2024) | Cache a compressed latent, reconstruct per-head K/V | ~1/32 in DeepSeek-V3 |
| [DSA](#c/dsa) (2025) | Attend only to top-selected past tokens (on top of MLA) | Less read per step |

All of these keep MHA's many *query* heads, because queries aren't cached, and cut or compress the *key/value* side.

A curiosity: DeepSeek-V3's config lists `num_attention_heads: 128` and `num_key_value_heads: 128`, which looks like plain MHA. It isn't. MLA's compression is expressed through other fields (`kv_lora_rank: 512`). A GQA model like Llama 4 shows `num_key_value_heads` well below `num_attention_heads`.

## From the chat

- The chat explained "multi-head attention" as running multiple Q/K/V heads in parallel in every layer, "each learns to attend to a different pattern," concatenated so the layer gets "many 'views' of the token relationships at once."
- It noted that in standard MHA "there are as many query heads as there are key/value heads," and that is the inefficiency MQA and GQA exploit.
- It warned that tidy head roles are illustrative, not literal.
- It flagged that DeepSeek-V3's equal head counts don't mean plain MHA, because MLA works through separate config fields.

concepts.title: Multi-Query Attention (MQA)
concepts.summary: All query heads share one K/V head: cache shrinks ~N×, quality can dent
concepts.overview: **Multi-Query Attention (MQA)**, proposed by Noam Shazeer in 2019, keeps all N query heads of [multi-head attention](#c/mha) but collapses keys and values to a **single shared K/V head**. Every query still asks its own question, but they all look up against the same keys and values. Since only K and V are stored in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), the cache shrinks by roughly **N×**: with 32 heads, 1/32 of the memory. That means far more concurrent requests or longer contexts per GPU, and less data read per decode step. The catch is expressiveness. Forcing every query to share one K/V view can dent quality, and training can be less stable. That's why [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa), with one K/V head per *group* of queries, became the near-universal compromise. Like GQA, MQA must be built into the model (or converted and briefly retrained); it isn't a serving trick for frozen weights.

concepts.title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
concepts.summary: Query heads in groups, one K/V head per group: most of MQA's savings, little loss
concepts.overview: **Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)** is the compromise between [multi-head attention](#c/mha) (one K/V head per query head) and [MQA](#c/mqa) (one K/V head total). Query heads are split into a few groups, and each group shares one key/value head. With **32 query heads in 8 groups of 4**, you store 8 K/V sets instead of 32, a **4× smaller** [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), while queries still get more variety to look up against than MQA's single set. The chat's summary: "most of MQA's memory savings, little of its quality loss." Introduced in 2023, it is now the near-universal default: [Llama 4](#c/llama4), [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) and [SmolLM3](#c/smollm3) all use it, and in their configs `num_key_value_heads` is much smaller than `num_attention_heads`. It must be baked in at training time (or added by converting and briefly retraining a checkpoint). DeepSeek went further with [MLA](#c/mla).
concepts.article:
**Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)** is an attention design in which the query heads of a layer are divided into groups and each group shares a single key/value head. It sits between standard [multi-head attention](#c/mha) and [Multi-Query Attention](#c/mqa), and since its introduction in 2023 it has become the default attention design for most open LLMs.

## How it works

Start with a layer that has N query heads. Choose G groups (1 < G < N), with N/G query heads per group:

- each query head keeps its own query projection, so it can still ask a distinct question;
- all query heads in a group attend against the **same** key and value vectors, produced by that group's single K/V head;
- only G key/value heads exist per layer, and only they are cached.

### Worked example

| Setup | Query heads | K/V heads | Cache per token per layer | vs. MHA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MHA | 32 | 32 | 32 K + 32 V | 1× |
| **GQA, 8 groups of 4** | 32 | 8 | 8 K + 8 V | **¼** |
| MQA | 32 | 1 | 1 K + 1 V | 1/32 |

With head dimension 128, that's 8,192 cached numbers per token per layer under MHA (32 × 128 × 2), versus 2,048 under this GQA setup. Across a few dozen layers and a 100K-token context, the difference decides whether a request fits on a GPU at all.

## Why it matters

The [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) is the biggest memory consumer in inference, and its size is set by the number of **K/V heads**, not query heads. Queries are used once and discarded. GQA turns down exactly the expensive knob:

- **More concurrency.** A smaller cache per request means more requests batched per GPU, so more tokens per second and lower [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token).
- **Faster decode.** Each generation step reads the whole cache, and a quarter of the bytes means less time waiting on memory, since [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound).
- **Longer contexts** fit in the same memory.

## Why not just MQA?

MQA's single shared K/V head gets the biggest saving but gives every query head the same view to look up against, which can dent quality. GQA keeps several distinct key/value views, one per group, and recovers most of MHA's quality while keeping most of MQA's savings. The number of groups is a dial between the two extremes.

## In practice

GQA is the industry default. From the chat's survey of open models:

| Model | Attention |
|---|---|
| [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) / [Scout](#c/llama4-scout) | GQA |
| [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) | GQA |
| [SmolLM3](#c/smollm3) | GQA, with periodic [NoPE](#c/nope) layers |
| [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) | [MLA](#c/mla) instead |

You can spot GQA in a Hugging Face `config.json`: `num_key_value_heads` is much smaller than `num_attention_heads`.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Architecture, not a serving trick.** GQA changes the model's parameters, so it must be trained in. An existing MHA checkpoint can be converted by merging its K/V heads within each group and then continuing training briefly, but a frozen MHA model can't simply be served as GQA.
- **Still grows with context.** GQA divides the cache by a constant; it doesn't change linear growth with sequence length or the quadratic cost of attention scores. Sparse attention ([DSA](#c/dsa)) and [linear/hybrid attention](#c/linear-attn) target those.
- **Less compression than MLA.** DeepSeek's MLA reaches roughly 32× compression versus MHA, beyond typical GQA ratios, at the cost of extra compute and complexity.

## From the chat

- The chat called GQA "the middle ground that won out" and "now near-universal in modern models because it shrinks the KV-cache substantially with minimal quality loss."
- Worked example from the chat: 32 query heads in 8 groups of 4 gives 8 K/V sets instead of 32, a 4× cache reduction.
- It classed GQA/MQA as needing to be "baked in at training time," unlike FlashAttention or PagedAttention, which work on frozen weights.
- It framed GQA as the kind of small architectural "tweak" that mostly serves inference efficiency rather than quality.
- The attention split among open models is GQA (simple, default: Qwen3, Llama 4) versus MLA (more compression, more complexity: DeepSeek, Kimi K2).

concepts.title: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)
concepts.summary: Cache a compressed 512-dim latent instead of full K/V (~32× smaller)
concepts.overview: **Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)** is DeepSeek's answer to the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) problem, introduced with DeepSeek-V2 in 2024. Instead of sharing K/V heads like [GQA](#c/gqa), it **compresses** each token's keys and values into one small latent vector, caches only that, and reconstructs per-head K and V with lightweight up-projections when needed. DeepSeek-V3's config makes it concrete: `kv_lora_rank: 512` is the cached latent, versus 128 heads × 128 `v_head_dim` = 16,384 for naive full values, **~32× smaller**. Queries get their own compression (`q_lora_rank: 1536`). Because [RoPE](#c/rope) doesn't survive compression, a separate 64-dim positional slice rides alongside ("decoupled RoPE"). MLA keeps more of multi-head attention's expressiveness than GQA but costs extra compute. It is used by DeepSeek-V3/R1/V3.2 and [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2), and [DSA](#c/dsa) builds on it.
concepts.article:
**Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)** is an attention design, introduced by DeepSeek with DeepSeek-V2 in 2024 and carried into DeepSeek-V3, R1 and V3.2, that shrinks the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) by caching a compressed latent representation of each token instead of its full per-head keys and values.

## How it works

In standard [multi-head attention](#c/mha), each token stores a key and a value for every head in every layer. MLA inserts a low-rank bottleneck:

1. **Compress.** Project the token's hidden vector (7,168 in DeepSeek-V3) down to a small latent `c` of dimension `kv_lora_rank` = **512**.
2. **Cache only the latent.** This is what goes into the KV-cache, one 512-dim vector per token per layer, instead of 128 heads' worth of K and V.
3. **Reconstruct.** When attention runs, per-head keys and values are produced from `c` by learned up-projection matrices.

A well-known implementation trick makes step 3 cheap. The up-projections are linear, so they can be folded ("absorbed") into the query and output projections, letting the model attend in latent space without ever materializing full K and V for long contexts.

Queries get similar treatment: `q_lora_rank: 1536` compresses them too, which cuts activation memory during training but doesn't affect the cache.

## The numbers from DeepSeek-V3's config

| Field | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `num_attention_heads` | 128 | Query heads per layer |
| `kv_lora_rank` | 512 | Cached latent size |
| `v_head_dim` | 128 | Per-head value width after reconstruction |
| `qk_nope_head_dim` | 128 | Per-head content part of Q/K |
| `qk_rope_head_dim` | 64 | Per-head positional part ("decoupled RoPE") |
| `q_lora_rank` | 1536 | Query compression |

The chat's comparison: 128 heads × 128 `v_head_dim` = 16,384 numbers for naive full values, versus a 512-dim latent, "~32× smaller… the MLA memory win, in one number." (The 64-dim shared positional key is cached alongside the latent too, a small addition.)

## Decoupled RoPE

[RoPE](#c/rope) rotates keys by position. If you rotate a key reconstructed from a compressed latent, the position-dependent rotation can no longer be absorbed into the projections, which breaks the efficiency trick. DeepSeek's fix is to split each head's query and key into two parts:

- a **content** part (128 dims) that goes through the compression, with no rotation;
- a small **positional** part (64 dims) that carries RoPE and is kept separately.

The chat described this as position riding "in its own 64-dim slice so it survives the compression cleanly."

## MLA vs. GQA

| | [GQA](#c/gqa) | MLA |
|---|---|---|
| How it saves cache | Fewer K/V heads (shared within groups) | Compress all heads' K/V into one latent |
| Typical saving vs. MHA | e.g. 4× (32 heads / 8 groups) | ~32× in DeepSeek-V3 |
| Expressiveness | Groups see identical K/V | Each head gets its own reconstructed K/V |
| Complexity | Simple; supported everywhere | Extra projections, decoupled RoPE, custom kernels |
| Used by | Llama 4, Qwen3, SmolLM3 | [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1), [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2), [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear) |

Note that DeepSeek-V3's config shows `num_key_value_heads: 128`, equal to the query heads. That looks like plain MHA, but the compression is expressed through `kv_lora_rank`, not the K/V head count.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Compute for memory.** MLA pays a compress/decompress cost, which is a good trade when [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound).
- **Must be trained in.** It is an architecture choice, not a post-hoc serving trick.
- **Still a full-attention method.** It shrinks each token's cache entry but still attends to every past token. [DSA](#c/dsa) adds sparsity on top of MLA in DeepSeek-V3.2 to address that.
- **Adoption.** The chat described MLA as newer and less universally adopted than GQA, used mainly in the DeepSeek lineage and Kimi models.

## From the chat

- MLA was described as "DeepSeek's more aggressive take": compress K/V into a smaller shared latent and reconstruct on the fly, keeping more expressiveness than GQA.
- The real config showed `kv_lora_rank: 512` versus 16,384, the ~32× cache saving.
- The chat explained decoupled RoPE: `qk_nope_head_dim: 128` + `qk_rope_head_dim: 64`.
- It placed MLA in the "needs to be baked in at training time" category, alongside GQA/MQA.
- It classed MLA as an efficiency play, "quality-neutral by design," not a source of capability gains.

concepts.title: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)
concepts.summary: A light indexer picks the most relevant past tokens; attend only to those
concepts.overview: **DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)**, introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2 (late 2025), makes each token attend to only a **selected subset** of past tokens instead of all of them. It is a two-stage path. A cheap "lightning indexer", running in low precision with few heads, scores every earlier token against the current one, and full [MLA](#c/mla) attention then runs only over the top-scoring *k*. That cuts attention's main cost from O(L²) to O(L·k). DeepSeek ran it as a controlled experiment: V3.2-Exp added DSA to V3.1-Terminus through continued training, with everything else held fixed, and got essentially identical quality. The chat reported roughly **2–3× faster** long-text processing and **~30–40% less memory** at 128K context, enough to support a 50%+ API price cut. [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) adopted it wholesale (its architecture is literally `glm_moe_dsa`), a case of techniques spreading fast.
concepts.article:
**DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)** is a trainable sparse-attention mechanism that DeepSeek introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp and kept in [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32) (late 2025). Rather than letting every token attend to every earlier token, it cheaply picks the most relevant earlier tokens and runs full attention only over those. It was the *only* architectural change across the whole V3.x line.

## How it works

DSA is a two-stage pipeline in each attention layer:

1. **Lightning indexer.** A deliberately lightweight scorer computes an index score between the current query token and each preceding token. It uses only a few heads and low precision, so scoring the whole history is cheap.
2. **Top-k selection + sparse attention.** The *k* highest-scoring past tokens are selected, and the model's regular attention, [MLA](#c/mla) in DeepSeek's case, runs only over them.

The indexer still looks at every previous token, but it is so light that the expensive part, full attention, now touches only *k* tokens. The chat summarized the payoff as attention cost falling "from quadratic O(L²) to linear O(Lk)", where *k* is small and fixed.

## A controlled experiment

The V3 → V3.2 progression was run to isolate DSA's effect:

| Step | Change |
|---|---|
| V3 → V3.1 | Improved checkpoint |
| V3.1 → V3.1-Terminus | Small improvement |
| V3.1-Terminus → V3.2-Exp | **Add DSA** through continued training, recipe held fixed |
| V3.2-Exp → V3.2 | Same architecture; scaled-up post-training |

The goal was explicitly *not* to improve quality but to minimize the degradation from adding sparsity. The result was parity: "virtually identical output quality."

## Why it matters

Long contexts are where attention's costs explode: score computation grows quadratically, and every decode step reads the entire [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). DSA attacks both. The chat reported:

- roughly **2–3× faster** long-text processing;
- **~30–40% lower memory** at 128K context;
- enough savings to enable a **50%+ API price cut**.

It also composes with MoE. Sparse attention optimizes the attention half of each layer while MoE optimizes the [FFN](#c/ffn) half, so the savings multiply. And it stacks on MLA: MLA makes each cached entry small, DSA reads fewer of them.

## Spread to other models

DSA moved quickly beyond DeepSeek. [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) adopted it wholesale: its technical documentation names the architecture `glm_moe_dsa`, and its report credits DSA with enabling the scale-up to 744B parameters and a 28.5T-token training budget. [GLM-5.1](#c/glm-51) continues the line. The chat compared this to how models adopted RoPE after it was published.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Efficiency, not capability.** DSA was engineered for parity. It makes long context cheaper, not the model smarter. The chat put it in the same "quality-neutral by design" bucket as MLA, GQA and FlashAttention.
- **Must be trained in.** It needs continued training so the model and indexer adapt to sparsity; it isn't a drop-in serving trick.
- **Selection can miss.** A token the indexer ranks low is invisible to full attention for that step. Parity on benchmarks suggests this rarely hurts, but it is a real difference from dense attention.
- **Still new.** The chat described trainable sparse attention at flagship scale as brand new, and whether it becomes as universal as GQA is still open.

## Related approaches

DSA keeps full attention's machinery but sparsifies it. The other main route to cheap long context replaces most attention layers with [linear/hybrid attention](#c/linear-attn) or [state-space layers](#c/ssm), as in [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear), which uses full attention in only 1 in 4 layers.

## From the chat

- DSA was "the single notable *architectural* development across the whole V3.x line," the only change from V3.1-Terminus to V3.2.
- The chat described the two-stage "lightning indexer" plus top-k sparse attention, cutting cost from O(L²) to O(Lk).
- DeepSeek measured parity on purpose; the chat called DSA "the purest example" of an efficiency-only innovation.
- Reported gains: 2–3× faster long text, ~30–40% less memory at 128K, 50%+ price cut.
- GLM-5's `glm_moe_dsa` config was cited as the "smoking gun" that DSA spread to a second frontier-scale flagship within months.

concepts.title: FlashAttention
concepts.summary: Tile attention into SRAM and fuse it into one pass: identical output, far less memory traffic
concepts.overview: **FlashAttention** (Tri Dao and colleagues, 2022) is an [attention kernel](#c/attn-kernel) that computes *exactly* the same result as standard attention but with far less memory traffic. A naive kernel writes the full attention-score matrix to the GPU's big but slow HBM, reads it back for the softmax, writes it again, and reads it again to weight the values. FlashAttention instead **tiles** queries, keys and values into blocks that fit in fast on-chip SRAM and **fuses** scores, softmax and value-weighting into one pass, never materializing the giant matrix. An "online" running softmax gives the correct normalized result block by block. Memory use grows linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, and speed rises because [attention is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). Version 2 improved work partitioning; version 3 targets Hopper-class GPUs. It changes nothing about weights or outputs, so it's a pure serving win that makes frozen models cheaper.
concepts.article:
**FlashAttention** is a GPU implementation of exact [attention](#c/attention) that is designed around the memory hierarchy rather than the arithmetic. Introduced by Tri Dao and colleagues in 2022, it produces mathematically identical outputs to a standard implementation while moving far less data, and it has become the default [attention kernel](#c/attn-kernel) in training and serving stacks.

## The problem: memory traffic, not math

A GPU has two very different kinds of memory:

| Memory | Size | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| **HBM** (high-bandwidth memory) | Large (tens of GB+) | Slow relative to compute |
| **SRAM** (on-chip) | Small | Very fast |

A naive attention kernel for a sequence of length L:

1. computes the L × L score matrix QKᵀ and **writes it to HBM**;
2. **reads it back** to apply the softmax, and **writes** the result;
3. **reads it again** to multiply by V.

For long sequences that intermediate matrix is enormous, and these round trips dominate run time. The arithmetic units sit idle waiting for data. That is the sense in which [attention is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). The chat's framing: almost every optimization "is, at heart, a scheme to move less data or move it less often."

## How it works

FlashAttention combines two ideas.

**Tiling.** Split Q, K and V into blocks small enough to fit in SRAM. Load a block of queries, then stream blocks of keys and values past it, computing partial scores and outputs on-chip.

**Fusion.** Do the score computation, softmax and value-weighting in a single kernel, so the L × L matrix never exists in HBM at all. Only the final output is written back.

The one obstacle is the softmax, which normally needs *all* scores for a row before it can normalize. FlashAttention uses an **online (running) softmax**. As each new block of scores arrives, it keeps a running maximum and running sum, rescales the partial output accordingly, and ends with exactly the correctly normalized result. No approximation is involved.

## What you get

- **Identical outputs.** It is exact attention, not an approximation.
- **Linear memory in sequence length** instead of quadratic, since the score matrix is never stored. This is a big part of why long contexts became practical to train.
- **Faster wall-clock time,** because HBM traffic, the actual bottleneck, drops sharply.

## Generations

The chat described three generations:

- **FlashAttention (2022):** tiling, fusion and online softmax.
- **FlashAttention-2:** better partitioning of work across GPU threads for higher utilization.
- **FlashAttention-3:** tuned for newer Hopper-class hardware features.

## Why it matters for cost

FlashAttention changes *nothing* about a model's weights or outputs. It is a pure serving-efficiency win that applies to an already-trained model. That makes it a clear example of how a frozen model gets cheaper to run over its life, alongside [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant) and [prefix caching](#c/prefix-cache). It is part of the [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) and [algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress) that drive [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) down without retraining.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Doesn't reduce the arithmetic.** Attention is still O(L²) in compute. FlashAttention makes it memory-efficient, not sub-quadratic. Reducing the work itself takes sparse attention like [DSA](#c/dsa) or [linear/hybrid attention](#c/linear-attn).
- **Doesn't shrink the KV-cache.** During decoding the cache still has to be read every step. Shrinking it is the job of [GQA](#c/gqa), [MLA](#c/mla) and quantization.
- **Hardware-specific.** Each generation is tuned to particular GPU features, so kernels need re-engineering as hardware changes.

## In practice

A modern serving stack, in the chat's summary, "typically runs a GQA model, with FlashAttention kernels, under PagedAttention memory management, with prefix caching and often KV quantization on top, plus continuous batching." These techniques stack rather than compete, because each attacks a different bottleneck.

## From the chat

- The chat called FlashAttention "the famous one" and explained it as tiling plus fusion with an online softmax.
- It stressed the result is "mathematically identical output, but with dramatically less memory traffic," with memory scaling linearly instead of quadratically.
- It placed FlashAttention firmly in the "pure serving trick, works on frozen weights" category, "exactly the 'frozen weights get cheaper' mechanism."
- It classed FlashAttention as quality-neutral by design, an efficiency play rather than a capability one.

concepts.title: PagedAttention
concepts.summary: KV-cache in OS-style pages: no wasted reservations, cheap prefix sharing (vLLM)
concepts.overview: **PagedAttention** is the memory-management idea behind the open-source **vLLM** serving engine (2023). It borrows the operating system's virtual-memory trick for the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache). Traditionally each request got one contiguous block of GPU memory sized for the *maximum* possible length, and since most requests stop well short of that, much memory sat reserved but empty (fragmentation). PagedAttention chops the cache into small fixed-size **pages** that can live anywhere, tracked by a per-request block table, and allocates them only as tokens are actually generated. The waste almost disappears, so many more requests fit on the same GPU, which means more tokens per second and lower cost per token. It also makes sharing cheap: requests with the same prefix can point at the same physical pages, which is what makes [prefix caching](#c/prefix-cache) practical. It works on frozen weights; the [attention kernel](#c/attn-kernel) just learns to read scattered pages.
concepts.article:
**PagedAttention** is a technique for storing and accessing the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) in fixed-size, non-contiguous blocks ("pages"), modelled on virtual memory in operating systems. It was introduced in 2023 with **vLLM**, an open-source LLM serving engine, and variants of it are now standard across serving stacks.

## The problem: waste, not size

PagedAttention doesn't make the KV-cache smaller. It stops memory being *wasted* around it. Before it, a serving system typically:

1. received a request without knowing how long the output would be;
2. reserved one **contiguous** chunk of GPU memory big enough for the maximum possible length;
3. filled only part of it before the request finished.

The result was fragmentation: large amounts of memory reserved but empty, plus gaps between allocations too small to reuse. Since the number of requests you can batch is limited by memory, that waste directly lowered throughput.

## How it works

PagedAttention applies the OS paging idea:

- **Pages.** The KV-cache is divided into fixed-size blocks, each holding keys and values for a small number of tokens.
- **Block table.** Each request has a lookup table mapping its logical token positions to physical blocks, which can be anywhere in GPU memory.
- **On-demand allocation.** A new block is allocated only when the previous one fills, so each request wastes at most part of one block.
- **Paged kernel.** The [attention kernel](#c/attn-kernel) is modified to follow the block table and gather keys and values from scattered blocks.

### Example

Two requests arrive. One will produce 300 tokens, the other 3,000, but the server doesn't know that in advance. A contiguous scheme reserves space for the maximum (say 8,000 tokens) for each. With paging, the first request ends up holding just enough blocks for about 300 tokens and the second about 3,000, and everything else stays free for other requests.

## Why it matters

- **More concurrency.** Near-zero waste means many more requests fit in the same memory. More concurrent requests means more tokens per GPU per second, which drives [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) down.
- **Cheap sharing.** When requests share a prefix, such as the same system prompt or document, their block tables can point at the **same physical pages** instead of duplicating them, copying only when they diverge. That is what makes [prefix caching](#c/prefix-cache) cheap to implement, and prefix caching is the mechanism behind API "cached input" discounts.
- **Works on frozen weights.** Nothing about the model changes, so it can be applied to any already-trained model.

## Where it sits

The chat noted PagedAttention "bridges both your categories": it's a kernel-level change *and* a KV-cache memory-management idea. It stacks with the other techniques:

| Technique | Attacks |
|---|---|
| [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn) | HBM ↔ SRAM traffic inside the attention computation |
| **PagedAttention** | Fragmentation / wasted reservation of cache memory |
| [GQA](#c/gqa), [MLA](#c/mla) | Cache size at the source (needs training) |
| [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant) | Bytes per cached number |
| [Prefix caching](#c/prefix-cache) | Redundant recomputation of shared prefixes |
| [Continuous batching](#c/cont-batching) | Idle slots between requests |

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Indirection overhead.** Gathering from scattered blocks is a little less efficient than reading contiguous memory, so paged kernels need careful engineering.
- **Doesn't reduce per-token cache size.** A 100K-token context still needs 100K tokens' worth of keys and values. Shrinking that takes architectural changes or quantization.
- **Undisclosed at closed providers.** The chat noted that providers like Anthropic and OpenAI don't publish their serving stacks, so which variant any of them runs is unknown.

## From the chat

- The chat described PagedAttention as "the vLLM idea," whose problem is "*waste*, not raw size."
- It explained the OS virtual-memory analogy: fixed-size pages in scattered locations, tracked by a lookup table.
- "More concurrency means more tokens served per GPU per second, which is the thing that drives down cost-per-token."
- It highlighted cheap prefix sharing, where two requests with the same system prompt point at the same pages.
- It placed PagedAttention among the pure serving tricks that make a deployed model cheaper without retraining.

concepts.title: KV-cache quantization
concepts.summary: Store keys and values in 8-bit or lower; keys are more sensitive than values
concepts.overview: **KV-cache quantization** stores the cached keys and values in fewer bits: 8-bit, or lower, instead of 16. Going from 16 to 8 bits halves the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), and 4 bits quarters it, so the same GPU memory holds longer contexts or more concurrent requests. Each decode step also reads fewer bytes, which matters because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound). Like weight [quantization](#c/quantization), it trades a little quality for size. One wrinkle the chat flagged: **keys tend to be more sensitive than values**, since keys go into the dot products that decide *which* tokens get attention, and they have a few outlier channels. So schemes often quantize them differently, for example keys per channel and values per token. It needs no retraining, which puts it with [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn) and [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) among the serving tricks that make a frozen model cheaper.
concepts.article:
**KV-cache quantization** reduces the numeric precision of the keys and values stored in a transformer's [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), typically from 16-bit floating point to 8-bit or lower. It is one of the simplest ways to fit longer contexts and bigger batches into the same GPU memory, and it works on an already-trained model.

## How it works

As each new token's key and value vectors are computed, they are converted to a lower-precision format before being written to the cache, along with small scale factors needed to convert them back. When attention runs, the cached values are dequantized, usually inside the [attention kernel](#c/attn-kernel), and used as normal.

| Format | Bits per number | Cache size vs. 16-bit |
|---|---|---|
| FP16 / BF16 | 16 | 1× |
| FP8 / INT8 | 8 | ½ |
| INT4 | 4 | ¼ |

The model's weights are untouched, and so is the computation of the current token's query. Only the stored history is compressed.

## Why it matters

The KV-cache is the biggest memory consumer in inference, growing with context length and batch size. Halving it has two effects:

1. **Capacity.** Twice as many tokens of context, or twice as many concurrent requests, fit in the memory left over after the weights. More concurrency means more tokens per GPU per second and lower [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token).
2. **Bandwidth.** Every decode step reads the whole cache. Fewer bytes read means faster steps, because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound).

## Keys vs. values

The chat flagged that "keys tend to be more sensitive than values, so schemes sometimes quantize them differently." The reason is structural:

- **Keys** feed the query-key dot products that decide which tokens receive attention. Small errors can shift the softmax weights, changing *what* the model looks at. Keys also tend to have a few channels with consistently large magnitudes (outliers), which a single shared scale handles badly.
- **Values** are blended after the weights are fixed, so errors there average out across the weighted sum.

That is why published schemes commonly quantize **keys per channel** (a separate scale for each dimension, absorbing the outlier channels) and **values per token**, or keep keys at higher precision than values.

## Where it sits among other cache techniques

| Technique | Shrinks cache by | Needs retraining? |
|---|---|---|
| [GQA](#c/gqa) / [MQA](#c/mqa) | Fewer K/V heads | Yes |
| [MLA](#c/mla) | Compressing to a latent | Yes |
| **KV quantization** | Fewer bits per number | No |
| [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) | Eliminating wasted reservation | No |

These stack. A GQA or MLA model can additionally have its (already smaller) cache stored in 8-bit, under paged memory management.

## Relation to weight precision

KV quantization is the cache-side sibling of weight [quantization](#c/quantization) and of serving at lower [numeric precision](#c/weights-precision) generally (FP8/INT8/INT4). DeepSeek-V3, for example, ships FP8 weights natively. Weights are fixed and can be carefully calibrated offline, while the cache is produced on the fly for every request, so cache quantization has to be fast and robust to whatever the input produces.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Quality vs. size.** As with any quantization there is a trade-off. 8-bit is widely used; more aggressive 4-bit or lower schemes need more care, especially for keys.
- **Long-context sensitivity.** Small errors in keys can matter more when attention must pick a few relevant tokens out of a very long history.
- **Undisclosed deployments.** The chat noted closed providers don't publish their serving stacks, so whether and how they quantize caches is unknown.

## From the chat

- "The cache doesn't have to be stored at full precision. Storing keys and values in 8-bit (or lower) instead of 16-bit halves (or more) the memory."
- There is a "quality-vs-size tradeoff," as with weight quantization.
- "Keys tend to be more sensitive than values, so schemes sometimes quantize them differently."
- The chat classed KV quantization with FlashAttention, PagedAttention and prefix caching as pure serving tricks on frozen weights, part of why a fixed model's serving cost falls over its life.

concepts.title: Prefix / prompt caching
concepts.summary: Compute a shared prefix's KV-cache once and reuse it — the source of cached-input discounts
concepts.overview: **Prefix caching** (called **prompt caching** in APIs) computes the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) for a shared beginning of a prompt *once* and reuses it across requests. Many requests start identically: the same long system prompt, the same document, the same few-shot examples, or the same agent conversation so far. Since a token's keys and values depend only on the tokens before it, an identical prefix always produces an identical cache, so the server can skip recomputing it and jump straight to the new part. That saves prefill compute and time-to-first-token. [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn)'s shared pages make it cheap: many requests point at the same physical cache blocks. It is the serving mechanism behind **cached-input discounts** on APIs; the chat tied it to the 90%-off cached-input pricing it had seen for Claude. The cache only matches an exact prefix, so static content should go first and changing content last.
concepts.article:
**Prefix caching**, exposed in commercial APIs as **prompt caching**, is a serving technique that reuses the computed [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) of a shared prompt prefix across requests, instead of recomputing it every time. It is one of the simplest serving optimizations and the one most visible to customers, because it appears on price sheets as a discount on "cached input" tokens.

## How it works

In a causal transformer, the keys and values for token *i* depend only on tokens 1…*i*. So if two requests begin with the same 10,000 tokens, those 10,000 tokens produce **bit-for-bit the same** keys and values in every layer, whatever comes after.

A prefix-caching server exploits this:

1. When a request finishes prefill, keep its KV-cache blocks around instead of freeing them immediately.
2. When a new request arrives, find the longest already-cached prefix that matches its beginning exactly.
3. Reuse those blocks, and run prefill only on the new tokens after the match.

With [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), step 3 is nearly free: the new request's block table simply points at the same physical pages, which are shared read-only. Some serving engines index cached prefixes in a tree so partial matches can be found quickly.

## Where prefixes repeat

- **System prompts.** Every request to an app or agent starts with the same instructions.
- **Documents.** Many questions asked about the same long file, codebase or knowledge base.
- **Few-shot preambles.** Fixed examples placed before each query.
- **Multi-turn conversations and agents.** Each new turn re-sends everything so far, and all of it except the newest message was already processed last turn. Agentic coding sessions, which re-send large contexts on every step, benefit heavily.

## Why it matters

- **Less compute.** Prefill over a long prompt is expensive, since attention cost grows with length. Skipping it for the cached portion saves most of that work.
- **Faster responses.** Time to first token drops, because the model starts generating almost immediately.
- **Cheaper tokens.** Providers pass some of the saving on. The chat tied this to "that 90%-off cached-input pricing" it had seen when researching Claude pricing: cached input tokens billed at a fraction of the normal rate.

This connects to the cost thread in the chat about [price vs. serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost). Cached-input pricing is one of the few places where a serving-side efficiency shows up directly and transparently in the price.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Exact prefix only.** The cache matches from the first token onward. Change one token early in the prompt, such as a timestamp in the system prompt, and everything after it misses. Put stable content first and variable content last.
- **Memory pressure.** Cached blocks occupy GPU memory that could hold active requests, so servers evict them after some time or under pressure. APIs typically expose this as a cache lifetime.
- **Only helps prefill.** Generated output tokens are still produced one at a time by the [decoding loop](#c/decoding). Prefix caching cuts input cost, not output cost.

## Where it sits

The chat grouped prefix caching with [FlashAttention](#c/flash-attn), [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn) and [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant) as pure serving tricks that work on frozen weights. Each targets a different bottleneck; prefix caching's target is redundant recomputation. Together with [continuous batching](#c/cont-batching), they're a large part of why a fixed model's [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) falls over its life.

## From the chat

- "If many requests share a common prefix… you compute that prefix's KV-cache once and reuse it across requests instead of recomputing it each time."
- The chat called it "the serving-side mechanism behind the 'prompt caching' discounts you see on APIs," tying it to 90%-off cached-input pricing.
- PagedAttention's page-sharing is "part of what makes it cheap to implement."
- In the chat's first answer, about claude-carbon, cache reads were one of the things that tool's CO₂ estimate handled crudely (counted at full rate), while the token *cost* figures were exact.

concepts.title: Weight quantization
concepts.summary: Run weights at FP8/INT8/INT4, often with negligible quality loss
concepts.overview: Weight quantization stores and computes a model's weights at lower numerical precision, for example **FP8, INT8 or INT4** instead of 16-bit. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), fewer bytes per weight means less data to move per token, a smaller memory footprint and more concurrent requests per GPU, all of which lower [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token). The chat lists it among the core [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that make a frozen model cheaper, "often with negligible quality loss," though some accuracy loss is possible. Related forms appear elsewhere in the graph. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) trains natively in FP8 and ships only FP8 weights (`quant_method: "fp8"`). [KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant) applies the idea to cached keys and values. [QLoRA](#c/qlora) quantizes a frozen base to 4-bit for cheap fine-tuning.
concepts.article:
**Weight quantization** means representing a neural network's weights, and often its activations, with fewer bits than the 16-bit floating point (FP16 or BF16) they are usually trained in. Common targets are **8-bit** (FP8 or INT8) and **4-bit** (INT4). It is one of the standard [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that make an already-trained model cheaper to run, and it modifies the model's [numeric precision](#c/weights-precision).

## How it works

Each weight is mapped from a high-precision value to a lower-precision one using a scale factor, and sometimes an offset, chosen per tensor, per channel or per small group of weights. At inference the low-precision values are either computed on directly by hardware that supports the format, or expanded back ("dequantized") just before use. The main variants are:

- **Post-training quantization.** Quantize a finished model, often using a small calibration dataset to pick scales that minimize error. It needs no retraining, which is why it counts as a frozen-weights optimization.
- **Quantization-aware training.** Simulate low precision during training so the model learns to tolerate it.
- **Native low-precision training.** Train in the low-precision format from the start. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) trains natively in FP8 and publishes only FP8 weights, with a script to convert to BF16.

## Why it cuts cost

Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), the cost of generating a token is dominated by moving weights and cache out of HBM. Halving the bytes per weight (16-bit to 8-bit) roughly halves that traffic for the weights. Going to 4-bit quarters it. The effects compound:

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Fewer bytes read per token | Faster generation on the same chip |
| Smaller model footprint | Fits on fewer GPUs; less cross-chip communication |
| Freed HBM | More room for [KV-caches](#c/kv-cache), so more concurrent requests |
| Native low-precision math on newer chips | Higher arithmetic throughput too |

All of these lower [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token), which makes quantization a key reason a *frozen* model gets cheaper over its life.

## Related forms

- **[KV-cache quantization](#c/kv-quant)**: storing cached keys and values in 8-bit or lower. The chat notes keys tend to be more sensitive than values, so schemes sometimes quantize them differently.
- **[QLoRA](#c/qlora)**: quantizes a frozen base model to 4-bit while training small [LoRA](#c/lora) adapters at higher precision, which brings fine-tuning of large models onto consumer hardware.

## Trade-offs

Lower precision discards information. At 8-bit the quality loss is often negligible for large models. At 4-bit and below, results depend more on the method, the model and the task, and outlier weights or activations need special handling. The chat's phrasing, "often with negligible quality loss," reflects this: often, not always. There is also a hardware dependence. The speed-up is largest when the chip natively supports the format, and a well-established trend is that newer [hardware generations](#c/hardware-gens) add support for ever-lower precisions.

## From the chat

The chat covers quantization only briefly, so this article relies on general, well-established knowledge for the mechanics.

- It listed quantization, "running the model at lower numerical precision, FP8/INT8/INT4, often with negligible quality loss," among the serving optimizations that make a frozen Sonnet-like model cheaper.
- It classed KV-cache quantization as a pure serving trick that works on frozen weights, noting the quality-vs-size trade-off and that keys are more sensitive than values.
- It pointed out that DeepSeek-V3's config shows `quant_method: "fp8"`: FP8 training is native to its framework, so only FP8 weights are provided.
- It described QLoRA as quantizing the frozen base to 4-bit while keeping adapters at higher precision.

concepts.title: Speculative decoding
concepts.summary: A small draft model proposes tokens; the big model verifies them in parallel
concepts.overview: Speculative decoding speeds up generation without changing the output. A small, fast **draft model** proposes several next tokens, and the large model **verifies them in one parallel pass**, accepting the longest correct prefix and resampling where they diverge. Large-model decoding is [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), and checking several tokens costs about as much as generating one, so every accepted guess is nearly free throughput. With the standard acceptance rule, the output distribution matches the big model exactly. The chat lists it among the core [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that lower a frozen model's [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token). It also notes that DeepSeek-V3's [Multi-Token Prediction](#c/mtp) heads, trained to predict several future tokens, "double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference." It modifies the ordinary [decoding loop](#c/decoding).
concepts.article:
**Speculative decoding** is an inference technique that generates text from a large language model faster by letting a cheap *draft* process guess upcoming tokens and having the large *target* model check those guesses in parallel. With the standard acceptance rule, the output is statistically identical to what the target model would have produced alone. That makes it a pure [serving optimization](#c/serving-opts) that works on frozen weights.

## The problem it solves

Ordinary autoregressive generation, the [decoding loop](#c/decoding), produces one token per forward pass of the full model, and each pass has to stream the model's weights from memory. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), a pass that checks five tokens costs about the same wall-clock time as a pass that produces one. The large model spends most of each step waiting on memory, not doing arithmetic. Speculative decoding puts that idle arithmetic to work.

## How it works

1. **Draft.** A small, fast model (or cheap extra prediction heads on the big model) proposes the next *k* tokens one after another. Each draft step is cheap.
2. **Verify.** The large model runs **one** forward pass over the context plus all *k* drafted tokens, producing its own probabilities at each position in parallel.
3. **Accept or reject.** Moving left to right, each draft token is accepted with a probability based on how the target's probabilities compare with the draft's. At the first rejection, a corrected token is sampled from an adjusted distribution and the rest of the draft is discarded.
4. **Repeat** from the new position.

Every step yields at least one token and at best *k*+1, so the speed-up depends on the **acceptance rate**, which is how often the draft agrees with the target. Predictable text, such as code, boilerplate or common phrasing, gets high acceptance.

## Variants

- **Separate draft model**: a smaller model from the same family, sharing the tokenizer.
- **Self-speculation with extra heads**: the model is trained with additional heads that predict tokens further ahead. The chat notes that DeepSeek-V3's [Multi-Token Prediction](#c/mtp) objective, which predicts several future tokens while keeping a causal chain, is primarily a training signal, and that its extra heads "double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference."

## Trade-offs

| Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|
| Lower latency per token | Must run and host a draft model (or train extra heads) |
| More tokens per pass over the weights | Wasted verification work when guesses are rejected |
| Exact output distribution (standard scheme) | Gains shrink when text is unpredictable or batches are already large |

The interaction with batching matters. In a heavily batched server the large model is already busier, so the idle compute that speculative decoding exploits is smaller. How much it saves depends on the workload and the serving setup.

## Relation to cost

Faster generation per request frees accelerator time for other requests, which lowers [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) for the same frozen model. It is one of the techniques behind the chat's answer that a given model does get cheaper to run over its life, through serving work, in lumps. Diffusion language models pursue a related goal, generating several tokens in parallel, through a different architecture ([Diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm)).

## From the chat

The chat treated speculative decoding in only a sentence or two. The mechanics above are standard, well-established material, not from the chat.

- It described it as "a small draft model proposes tokens a big model verifies in parallel," listed among the serving optimizations that make a frozen model cheaper.
- It noted that DeepSeek-V3's MTP heads double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference.
- It gave no numbers on speed-ups or on which providers use it.

concepts.title: Continuous batching
concepts.summary: Swap requests in and out mid-flight to keep accelerators saturated
concepts.overview: Continuous batching, also called dynamic or in-flight batching, is a scheduling technique for LLM servers. Instead of waiting for a whole batch of requests to finish before starting the next, the server **swaps requests in and out at every generation step**: finished sequences leave, and queued ones take their slots. Requests produce very different numbers of tokens, so static [batching](#c/batching) leaves the accelerator partly idle while it waits for the longest one. Continuous batching keeps it saturated. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), each pass over the weights can serve many requests, so higher occupancy directly lowers [cost per token](#c/cost-per-token). The chat lists it among the core [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) that work on frozen weights and pair naturally with [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), which frees memory for more concurrent requests.
concepts.article:
**Continuous batching** (also called *dynamic*, *iteration-level* or *in-flight* batching) is a way of scheduling requests on an LLM inference server so that the batch being processed changes at every token-generation step instead of staying fixed until every request in it finishes. It is one of the most important [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) for throughput, and it works on any frozen model. It modifies plain [batching](#c/batching).

## The problem with static batching

Batching is essential for inference economics. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), one read of the model's weights from HBM can serve many requests at once, so throughput grows with batch size at little extra cost.

With **static batching**, the server gathers a group of requests, runs them together until *all* are done, then starts the next group. LLM requests vary enormously in length. One might need 20 output tokens and another 2,000. Under static batching:

- finished requests leave empty slots that sit idle until the longest request finishes,
- new requests wait in the queue even though capacity is free, which hurts latency,
- the GPU's effective utilization can be low.

## How continuous batching works

The scheduler works at the level of **individual decoding iterations**:

1. At each step, the model generates one token for every active sequence in the batch.
2. Any sequence that has finished (end-of-sequence token or length limit) is removed right away.
3. Waiting requests are admitted into the freed slots, with their prompts processed, then join the ongoing generation.
4. Repeat.

The batch becomes a rolling pool, so the accelerator stays saturated as long as there is demand. The idea was popularized in LLM-serving research and systems around 2022–2023 (the Orca scheduler and then vLLM, among others) and is now standard in production serving stacks.

## Why it needs memory management

Admitting a new request mid-flight requires room for its [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), which grows with every generated token. Reserving a maximum-length contiguous block for each request wastes memory and caps how many can be admitted. That is why continuous batching pairs naturally with [PagedAttention](#c/paged-attn), which stores the cache in small pages allocated on demand, and with cache-shrinking techniques like [KV quantization](#c/kv-quant) and [GQA](#c/gqa). More free memory means more concurrent sequences, which means more tokens per pass over the weights.

## Effects on cost and latency

| Metric | Effect |
|---|---|
| Throughput (tokens/GPU-second) | Rises substantially: fewer idle slots |
| [Cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) | Falls, since the same hardware serves more tokens |
| Queueing latency | Falls: requests start without waiting for a batch to drain |
| Per-token latency | Can rise slightly under heavy load as batches grow |

Providers tune the trade-off between batch size (cheaper per token) and latency (faster per user). Mixing long prompt-processing steps with ongoing generation adds further scheduling complexity, and serving systems use various techniques to balance the two.

## From the chat

The chat mentions continuous batching only in passing. The mechanics and history above are standard, well-established material, not from the chat.

- It named "better batching (continuous/dynamic batching to keep accelerators saturated)" first among the serving optimizations that make a frozen model like a given Sonnet cheaper to run.
- In describing a modern serving stack (GQA model, FlashAttention, PagedAttention, prefix caching, KV quantization), it listed "continuous batching to keep the accelerator saturated" as part of the standard combination.
- It gave no throughput figures and said it couldn't confirm what any specific proprietary provider runs.

concepts.title: RoPE
concepts.summary: Rotate Q/K pairs by position; dot products then depend on relative distance
concepts.overview: **RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding)**, introduced in 2021 (RoFormer), is how nearly every current LLM encodes token order. Instead of *adding* a position vector to each token, it *rotates* the [query and key](#c/qkv) vectors. Each is split into coordinate pairs, and each pair is rotated in its 2-D plane by an angle proportional to the token's position, with different pairs spinning at different **frequencies**. Fast pairs capture fine local distinctions and slow pairs long-range position; the spread is set by a base (`rope_theta: 10000` in DeepSeek-V3). Because both query and key are rotated, their dot product depends only on the *difference* in angle, meaning the **relative distance** between tokens. The weakness is that positions beyond the training length produce unseen angles and quality collapses, which led to [Position Interpolation](#c/pi) and [YaRN](#c/yarn). MLA needs a "decoupled" 64-dim RoPE slice.
concepts.article:
**RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding)** is a [positional encoding](#c/position) scheme, introduced in 2021 in the RoFormer paper, that injects position by rotating query and key vectors rather than adding position vectors to token embeddings. It has become the standard: in the chat's words, it is "the method nearly every current model uses."

## How it works

Take the [query and key](#c/qkv) vectors of a token at position *m* in some head. RoPE:

1. **Splits each vector into pairs** of coordinates: (x₀, x₁), (x₂, x₃), and so on.
2. **Treats each pair as a point in a 2-D plane** and rotates it by an angle *m · θᵢ*, where θᵢ is that pair's frequency.
3. **Uses different frequencies for different pairs.** θᵢ decreases geometrically across the pairs, controlled by a base (`rope_theta`), commonly 10,000, which is the value in DeepSeek-V3's config.

The result: token 1 is rotated a little, token 50 more, token 1,000 more still. Some pairs spin fast (big angle change per step) and others slowly.

| Pair type | Rotation per position | Encodes |
|---|---|---|
| High-frequency | Large | Fine, local distinctions (is this token 1 or 2 back?) |
| Low-frequency | Small | Coarse, long-range position |

Values are not rotated, only queries and keys.

## Why rotation: relative position for free

Attention scores are dot products between a query and a key. Rotate the query by angle *mθ* and the key by *nθ*, and their dot product depends only on the *difference*, (*m − n*)θ. So the score between two tokens depends on how far apart they are, not on where they sit in the sequence. "These two tokens are 5 apart" falls out of the geometry. That relative property generalizes well and is a big reason RoPE displaced absolute position embeddings.

## The long-context problem

RoPE works well within the range seen in training. A model trained on 4,096-token sequences has only ever seen the angles positions 0–4,095 produce. Feed it position 8,000 and the slow, low-frequency pairs reach angles never encountered, so the model is extrapolating and "quality falls off a cliff." Fast pairs are less affected, since they've already cycled through all angles many times during training.

That motivated a family of **context-extension** methods that rescale RoPE after pre-training:

- **[Position Interpolation](#c/pi):** divide all positions by the extension factor. Simple, but it blurs local precision.
- **NTK-aware scaling and [YaRN](#c/yarn):** treat frequencies differently. Leave fast ones alone, squeeze slow ones.

DeepSeek-V3 trains at 4,096 (`original_max_position_embeddings`) and uses YaRN with factor 40 to reach 163,840.

## RoPE and MLA: decoupled RoPE

[MLA](#c/mla) caches a compressed latent and relies on folding its up-projections into other matrices. A position-dependent rotation would break that folding. DeepSeek's workaround is **decoupled RoPE**: each head's query and key get a separate 64-dim slice (`qk_rope_head_dim: 64`) that carries the rotation, alongside the 128-dim content part (`qk_nope_head_dim: 128`) that goes through compression.

## Dropping it: NoPE

Some models skip RoPE in some layers entirely, relying on the causal mask to convey order. See [NoPE](#c/nope). SmolLM3 uses periodic NoPE layers, and Kimi Linear's full-attention blocks use no positional encoding at all.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Bounded by training length** unless rescaled.
- **Extension isn't free.** Stretched contexts are generally used less well at the far end than natively trained ones.
- **Interacts with compression.** Schemes like MLA need special handling.

## From the chat

- RoPE's trick is "geometric: instead of *adding* a position signal to token vectors, it *rotates* them."
- "The dot product ends up depending on the *difference* of their angles… RoPE gives the model *relative* position information for free."
- `rope_theta: 10000` in DeepSeek's config "sets the spread of those rotation frequencies."
- The chat explained why RoPE fails past the trained length (unseen angles on slow pairs), motivating PI and YaRN.
- It noted DeepSeek's decoupled RoPE: position in its own 64-dim slice "so it survives the compression cleanly."

concepts.title: Position Interpolation
concepts.summary: Squeeze positions back into the trained range; blurs local precision
concepts.overview: **Position Interpolation (PI)**, published in 2023, was the first widely used way to extend a [RoPE](#c/rope) model's context window without retraining from scratch. Instead of letting positions run past the trained range, where the rotation angles are unfamiliar and quality collapses, PI **squeezes every position back into range** by dividing by the extension factor. For 8× more context, position 8,000 becomes an "effective position" of 1,000. A short fine-tune on longer sequences then adapts the model.
