It works, but it is a blunt instrument: compressing *all* rotation frequencies uniformly also crowds the fast, high-frequency pairs that encode fine local distinctions, so the model gets worse at telling nearby tokens apart even as it gains reach. That flaw led to NTK-aware scaling and [YaRN](#c/yarn), which squeeze only the slow frequencies. See [positional encoding](#c/position).

concepts.title: YaRN
concepts.summary: Frequency-aware interpolation: keep fast (local) rotations, squeeze slow (long-range) ones
concepts.overview: **YaRN** ("Yet another RoPE extensioN", 2023) stretches a [RoPE](#c/rope) model's context far beyond its training length by treating rotation frequencies differently. High-frequency pairs, which encode local relationships that don't change when a document gets longer, are **left alone**. Low-frequency pairs, the ones that run out of trained range, are **interpolated** (squeezed, as in [Position Interpolation](#c/pi)). A middle band gets a smooth blend. A small **temperature** tweak to attention logits (`mscale`) corrects the sharpness distortion that stretching causes. DeepSeek-V3 is the textbook case: `original_max_position_embeddings: 4096`, `factor: 40`, so 4,096 × 40 = **163,840** tokens, with `beta_fast: 32` / `beta_slow: 1` setting the frequency boundaries. It needs only a short long-context fine-tune, far cheaper than pretraining at 160K. The catch: stretched windows are usually weaker at the far end than natively trained ones.
concepts.article:
**YaRN** ("Yet another RoPE extensioN") is a method for extending the context window of a model that uses [RoPE](#c/rope) positional encoding, published in 2023. It is a refined, frequency-aware form of interpolation that preserves local precision while bringing long-range positions back into the trained range. It is the method [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) uses to go from a 4K training length to a 160K context.

## The problem it solves

RoPE rotates [query/key](#c/qkv) coordinate pairs at a spectrum of frequencies. A model trained on 4,096-token sequences has only seen the angles those positions produce. At position 8,000, the **slow** (low-frequency) pairs reach angles never seen in training, and quality collapses. Pre-training at long lengths from the start is very expensive, because [attention](#c/attention) cost grows with sequence length. So the practical recipe is to *train short, then extend*.

The first extension method, [Position Interpolation](#c/pi), divides every position by the extension factor. That brings slow pairs back into range, but it also compresses the **fast** pairs, which encode fine local distinctions, so the model gets blurrier about nearby tokens. It trades local precision for reach.

## How YaRN works

YaRN's key insight is that not all frequencies need the same treatment:

| Frequency band | Encodes | YaRN treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **High** (fast spinners) | Short-range, local relationships | **Left largely alone**; nearby tokens are still nearby in a longer document |
| **Middle** | Mixed | **Smooth blend** between the two treatments |
| **Low** (slow spinners) | Long-range position | **Interpolated** (squeezed like PI) so they stay in the trained range |

Instead of one global squeeze factor, YaRN applies a graduated correction across the spectrum: compress where you must, preserve where you can. This belongs to the "NTK-aware" family of RoPE scaling methods, and YaRN is its most refined widely used member.

**Temperature correction.** Stretching the effective context slightly distorts the magnitude and sharpness of attention scores. YaRN adds a small scaling of the attention logits to compensate and keep the attention distribution well-behaved. In configs these appear as `mscale` fields.

## Reading DeepSeek-V3's config

DeepSeek-V3's `rope_scaling` block is a textbook YaRN setup:

| Field | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | `"yarn"` | The method |
| `factor` | 40 | Extension multiplier |
| `original_max_position_embeddings` | 4096 | Pre-extension training length |
| `beta_fast` / `beta_slow` | 32 / 1 | Boundaries of the fast (untouched) and slow (interpolated) bands |
| `mscale` fields | — | Attention-temperature correction |

And the arithmetic lines up: **4,096 × 40 = 163,840**, exactly `max_position_embeddings`, the "160K" context. `rope_theta: 10000` sets the base frequency spread that YaRN is rescaling.

## Why it matters

YaRN needs only a short fine-tuning pass on a modest amount of long-context data, and in some cases works reasonably with none, compared with the huge cost of pretraining at 160K. The chat framed this as another instance of the conversation's recurring theme: more capability without proportionally more compute. It is primarily an **efficiency** technique in the chat's classification, quality-neutral by design, the same bucket as [MLA](#c/mla) and [DSA](#c/dsa). Some newer designs sidestep the problem differently by dropping explicit position in some layers ([NoPE](#c/nope)).

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Not a free lunch.** A model stretched 40× generally isn't as good across its full 160K as a model genuinely trained at that length. Use of the far end of the window is often weaker than the headline number suggests.
- **Context claims aren't comparable.** Because of this, advertised context lengths across models don't all mean the same effective capability.
- **Formula details.** The exact per-frequency ramp comes from wavelength thresholds that the betas set; the chat kept to the conceptual level.

## From the chat

- The chat built YaRN up from RoPE: attention is order-blind, RoPE rotates, and rotations beyond the trained length are unfamiliar.
- It contrasted PI's uniform squeeze (which "crowds the high-frequency pairs") with YaRN's "compress where you must (long range), preserve where you can (local detail)."
- It decoded DeepSeek-V3's `rope_scaling` block: factor 40, 4,096 × 40 ≈ 163,840, beta_fast 32 / beta_slow 1, mscale as temperature correction.
- It warned that a 40×-stretched model's far context is usually weaker than a natively trained one's.
- It listed YaRN among the efficiency-first innovations rather than quality drivers.

concepts.title: NoPE
concepts.summary: No positional encoding at all in some layers; the causal mask carries order
concepts.overview: **NoPE** ("no positional encoding") means leaving out explicit position information, with no [RoPE](#c/rope) and no added position vectors, in some or all attention layers. It sounds as if it should fail, since [attention](#c/attention) is order-blind, but in a decoder the **causal mask** already leaks order: a token at position 100 can see 99 predecessors, one at position 5 only four. Research from 2022 onward showed transformers without positional encoding still learn positional information this way, and may generalize better to lengths beyond training because there are no unseen rotation angles to extrapolate. Current use is partial. [SmolLM3](#c/smollm3) combines GQA with **periodic NoPE layers**, and [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear) uses no positional encoding in its full-attention blocks, leaving position to its linear-attention layers, which helps with very long contexts. The chat flagged NoPE as counterintuitive, emerging, and not yet standard in a major dense flagship.

concepts.title: Multi-Token Prediction
concepts.summary: Predict several future tokens in a causal chain; extra heads double as a speculative decoder
concepts.overview: **Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)** trains a model to predict not just the next token but several future tokens. DeepSeek-V3's version keeps a **causal chain**: extra lightweight modules sit after the main model, and each predicts one step further ahead using the previous depth's representation and the actual next token, so the prediction for t₃ builds on t₁ and t₂. That differs from earlier schemes with independent parallel heads. DeepSeek-V3's config sets `num_nextn_predict_layers: 1`, one extra depth. During training it gives a **denser learning signal**, since each position teaches more than one step. At inference the MTP module can be dropped, or reused as a built-in drafter for [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding): it proposes the next-next token, the main model verifies it, and accepted drafts mean more than one token per step. It modifies the [output head](#c/output-head) side of the model.
concepts.article:
**Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)** is a training objective in which a language model learns to predict several future tokens at each position rather than only the next one. DeepSeek-V3 is the best-documented large-scale use, and its design has a second life at inference time as a speculative-decoding drafter.

## Standard next-token prediction

A plain decoder-only [transformer](#c/transformer) produces, at every position, a probability distribution over the next [token](#c/tokenizer) via its [output head](#c/output-head). Training compares that to the true next token. One position, one target, one step of lookahead.

## How MTP works

MTP adds extra prediction targets further ahead. There are two broad styles:

| Style | How | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Parallel heads** | Several independent output heads on the final layer, each predicting t+1, t+2, … directly | Simple; later predictions don't see earlier ones |
| **Sequential (DeepSeek-V3)** | Small extra modules chained after the main model; each takes the previous depth's representation plus the embedding of the actual next token, and predicts one step further | Keeps a **causal chain** across depths |

The chat described DeepSeek's choice as keeping "a causal chain across the prediction depths (predicting t₃ using t₁ and t₂)." Each MTP module is a lightweight transformer block that shares the embedding and output head with the main model, so it adds relatively few parameters.

DeepSeek-V3's config shows the depth: `num_nextn_predict_layers: 1`, meaning one additional future token beyond the normal next-token prediction.

## Why do it: a denser training signal

Every training position now provides more than one supervised target, and the model is pushed to build internal representations that plan a little further ahead. DeepSeek presents it as a way to get a stronger training signal from the same data. It is an auxiliary objective: the main next-token loss is still there.

## Second use: a built-in speculative decoder

At inference, the MTP module can simply be discarded, and the main model works on its own. But it can also serve as a drafter for [speculative decoding](#c/spec-decoding):

1. The main model produces the next token as usual, and the MTP module proposes a guess for the token after it.
2. On the next forward pass, the main model verifies the guess at the same time as computing the following step.
3. If the guess matches what the main model would have produced, it's accepted, and two tokens come out of roughly one step's cost.

Because [decoding](#c/decoding) is sequential and [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound), getting more than one token per weight-read is valuable. DeepSeek reported high acceptance rates for the drafted token, enough to meaningfully speed up generation. The chat's summary: the extra heads "double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference."

## Classification

MTP is one of the few techniques in this map that plausibly helps **both** quality (through the training signal) and efficiency (through faster decoding), which is why its graph attributes list its effect as "both." Most attention and serving tricks are efficiency-only.

## Where it might go

The chat listed "multi-token prediction used as the *primary* objective rather than an auxiliary one" among longer-tail directions it couldn't verify had shipped in any flagship. It placed MTP-as-primary alongside [diffusion LMs](#c/diffusion-lm) as ideas that challenge the one-token-at-a-time assumption of autoregressive models, but held them loosely.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Extra training compute** for the additional modules and losses.
- **Modest depth in practice.** DeepSeek-V3 predicts one extra token; deeper chains get less accurate.
- **Speed-up depends on acceptance.** Drafts that are often wrong waste verification work.

## From the chat

- MTP was listed as one of DeepSeek-V3's three distinctive techniques, alongside [MLA](#c/mla) and [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free).
- The chat emphasized the causal chain across depths, unlike parallel multi-token schemes.
- "This is a training objective for stronger signal, and the extra heads double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference."
- In DeepSeek-V3's config, `num_nextn_predict_layers: 1` "is the Multi-Token Prediction depth."
- MTP as the *primary* objective was flagged as a speculative, unverified frontier direction.

concepts.title: Cross-layer parameter sharing
concepts.summary: Reuse one layer's weights across the stack (ALBERT): saves memory, not compute
concepts.overview: **Cross-layer parameter sharing** reuses the same weights across multiple layers instead of giving each [layer](#c/layer-stack) its own. The cleanest example is **ALBERT** (2019), a BERT variant that used one set of layer weights for *every* layer, which slashed the parameter count. The catch is instructive: it saves **memory, not compute**. You still run the layer N times; it's just the same layer N times. There is a spectrum between fully independent and fully shared: share in groups (layers 1–4, 5–8), share only attention or only the FFN, or share cyclically. Taken to its limit, it becomes **recurrence in depth**: one block looped a variable number of times, as in the Universal Transformer and today's [recurrent-depth reasoning](#c/latent-reasoning). Forced sharing costs expressiveness, and the chat knew of no strong evidence that frontier models use it. A cousin idea shares the cache instead: [cross-layer KV sharing](#c/kv-sharing).

concepts.title: Cross-layer KV-cache sharing
concepts.summary: Adjacent layers share one K/V cache
concepts.overview: **Cross-layer KV-cache sharing** lets adjacent layers use one set of cached keys and values instead of each layer storing its own. Normally the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) is strictly per layer, since each layer's heads produce their own K and V, so a 61-layer model caches 61 layers' worth. If, say, pairs of layers share one cache, cache memory halves, on top of whatever [GQA](#c/gqa) or [MLA](#c/mla) already saves. Published work from 2024, such as Cross-Layer Attention, computes K/V in one layer and reuses them in the next, trading a little quality for memory. Unlike [cross-layer parameter sharing](#c/layer-sharing), which reuses *weights* (ALBERT), this reuses cached *activations*: a different kind of sharing aimed at the same memory bottleneck. The chat described it as real and published but mostly confined to efficiency research and smaller or open models, not a known feature of leading frontier models.

concepts.title: Layer pruning
concepts.summary: Many middle/late layers do little; prune or merge them with modest loss
concepts.overview: **Layer pruning** removes whole layers from a trained model. It works surprisingly often because of how the [residual stream](#c/residual) behaves. Each layer only *adds* an adjustment, and research probing trained transformers finds that **many layers, especially in the middle and later parts of deep models, do surprisingly little**: their updates are close to identity, passing the representation through almost unchanged. Studies have removed or merged a meaningful fraction of layers from large trained models with modest quality loss, sometimes followed by a short "healing" fine-tune. The chat called this emergent redundancy "wasted capacity": parameters and compute spent on layers that contribute little, which is why depth-efficiency research exists. It contrasts with forced similarity ([cross-layer sharing](#c/layer-sharing)), which trades capability for memory. How much can be pruned varies a lot by model, task and how quality is measured. The finding is directionally solid, the exact fractions uncertain.

concepts.title: Linear / hybrid attention
concepts.summary: Full attention in only some layers (Kimi Linear: 1 in 4), cheap linear attention elsewhere
concepts.overview: Standard softmax [attention](#c/attention) compares every token with every earlier token, so compute grows quadratically with context and the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) grows with every token. Linear attention reformulates the operation so each layer carries a fixed-size running summary that is updated once per token: cost becomes linear in length and memory stays constant, at the price of lossy recall. Hybrid attention is the pragmatic compromise. Keep full attention in a minority of layers and use the cheap variant everywhere else. [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear), a 48B model, uses full attention (with [MLA](#c/mla)) in only one layer in four and a linear "Delta Attention" in the rest, and reports competitive quality at significantly higher throughput. The open question in the chat is whether a flagship adopts the approach. Like [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), it is an efficiency play, not a quality play.
concepts.article:
**Linear attention** is a family of replacements for the softmax [attention](#c/attention) at the heart of the [transformer](#c/transformer). It swaps the all-pairs comparison between tokens for a compact running state that is updated once per token. **Hybrid attention** mixes the two: most layers use a cheap linear variant, and a minority keep full attention. As of mid-2026 the hybrid form has shipped in real models, most visibly Moonshot's [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear). Whether it reaches a flagship-scale model is one of the open architecture questions of the next generation.

## How it works

In ordinary attention, each new token's query is scored against the key of every earlier token. The scores go through a softmax and weight a sum of values. That is quadratic in sequence length for a full pass. At generation time every past key and value has to be kept in the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache), which grows without bound and makes long-context decoding [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound).

Linear attention removes the softmax, or approximates it with a kernel feature map, so the computation can be reordered. Instead of comparing the query with every key, the layer keeps a running matrix that accumulates key–value associations. Each new token updates that matrix, and the query reads from it. The per-token cost no longer depends on how long the context is, and the "cache" is one fixed-size state per layer. That is the same shape as a recurrent network, which is why linear attention sits in one family with [state-space models](#c/ssm), RWKV and RetNet.

Newer variants improve how the state is written. Delta-rule designs (the "Delta Attention" in Kimi Linear is one) update the state by correcting what it currently predicts for a key, rather than just adding to it. Gating lets the layer decay old information selectively. These refinements target the classic weakness of linear attention: a fixed-size memory that blurs as it fills.

## Hybrid layouts

Pure linear-attention models tend to lose on tasks that need exact recall of a specific earlier detail. So production designs keep some full attention. In Kimi Linear, one layer in four is full attention (using [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla)) and the other three are linear. Its full-attention blocks also use no positional encoding at all ([NoPE](#c/nope)) and leave positional work to the linear layers, which helps when extending to very long contexts. The same "mostly cheap, a little attention" principle shows up in [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), where Jamba's ablations put the sweet spot at roughly one attention layer per five to seven Mamba layers.

## Why it matters

Long context and long reasoning traces are where attention's cost bites hardest, and those are exactly the workloads that have grown fastest. A hybrid shrinks the KV-cache for most of the stack and raises throughput, so the same hardware serves longer contexts or more users. In the chat's taxonomy it is an efficiency technique, quality-neutral by design. It sits alongside [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa), [GQA](#c/gqa) and KV quantization as ways to hold quality while cutting cost.

## Weaknesses and open questions

- **Scale.** Sub-quadratic attention keeps proving itself at small-to-mid scale. Kimi Linear is a 48B model, not a flagship. The chat cites a source calling a flagship adoption (for example, Kimi's own next flagship) "a decisive data point" for production viability.
- **Recall.** A fixed-size state is a lossy summary. The minority of full-attention layers is there to cover precise lookups, and how few you can get away with is still an empirical question.
- **Competition from sparse attention.** Learned sparse attention such as DSA gets similar long-context savings while keeping exact attention over a selected subset of tokens, and it has already spread to a second flagship ([GLM-5](#c/glm-5)).

## From the chat

- Linear / hybrid attention was described as "the most forward-looking direction" among open-model attention designs, with Kimi Linear (1-in-4 full attention, Delta Attention elsewhere) as the example.
- The chat classed it as an efficiency play, alongside MLA, DSA and GQA, rather than a source of quality gains.
- It was listed as the bleeding-edge idea "closest to landing" in a major open model. The caveat: Kimi Linear is only 48B, so frontier-scale viability is unproven.
- When the user asked about simplifying transformer topology, Claude called hybrids "cheaper wiring," not "simpler wiring." They are the pragmatic answer that is winning in production.

concepts.title: Mixture of Experts
concepts.summary: Split the FFN into many experts; a router sends each token to a few. Capacity of the total, cost of the active
concepts.overview: **Mixture of Experts (MoE)** replaces a transformer layer's single [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) with many parallel FFN blocks, called "experts". A tiny learned [router](#c/router) scores every expert for each token, keeps the top-k, and sums their outputs weighted by those scores. Attention stays dense and shared. This decouples *total* parameters, which set knowledge capacity, from *active* parameters, which set compute per token: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) stores 671B but activates about 37B (8 of 256 routed experts plus 1 shared, in 58 of its 61 layers). Routing is re-decided for every token at every MoE layer, and experts learn low-level token patterns, [not human topics](#c/r-experts). The costs are memory, since every expert must sit in HBM, cross-GPU communication, and the need to keep load balanced. MoE dates to [1991](#c/moe-1991) and became the open-weight default in 2025.
concepts.article:
**Mixture of Experts (MoE)** is a neural-network design in which only part of the model runs for any given input. In modern large language models, it means splitting each transformer layer's [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) into many smaller, parallel "experts" and letting a learned [router](#c/router) send each token to just a few of them. The result is a model with the *capacity* of its total parameter count and roughly the *running cost* of its much smaller active parameter count. By 2025 it had become the default architecture for large open-weight models, including [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Llama 4](#c/llama4), [Qwen3](#c/qwen3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-5](#c/glm-5).

## How it works

A transformer layer has two main parts: attention, where tokens look at one another, and a feed-forward network that processes each token on its own. MoE replaces **only the FFN**. Attention stays dense, and every token still uses all of it. So when a model is described as having "256 experts", that means its FFN block has been split into 256 parallel weight-blocks. It does not mean 256 small models.

In front of the experts sits the router, which is essentially a single learned linear layer. For each token's hidden vector it produces a score for every expert (a dot product with that expert's routing vector) and turns the scores into weights. The token is sent to the top-k experts, and their outputs are combined using those weights and added back into the [residual stream](#c/residual). Routing is decided **fresh for every token, independently, at every MoE layer**. DeepSeek-V3 has 58 MoE layers, so a single token passes through 58 separate routing decisions, and the next token gets its own 58.

## Total vs. active parameters

In a dense model every parameter fires on every token, so compute scales with size. MoE breaks that link:

| Model | Total | Active per token | Routed experts |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V3 | 671B | ~37B | 256 (8 + 1 shared active) |
| Llama 4 Maverick | 400B | 17B | 128 |
| Kimi K2 | ~1T | 32B | 384 |
| GLM-5 | 744B | ~40B | 256 (8 active) |

This is why the phrase "parameter count" became ambiguous after 2023 and why [frontier models could shrink in active size](#c/r-smaller) even as totals climbed. Because active parameters set the arithmetic per token, MoE directly lowers [serving cost per token](#c/cost-per-token) at a given capability.

## What experts specialize in

Inspections of trained routers usually find that experts specialise in **low-level patterns**: token types, punctuation, number-like tokens and structural roles. They rarely specialise in human topics like "chemistry" or "law". The popular picture of a question activating "the chemistry expert" is [appealing but mostly false](#c/m-experts). Routing distributes computational sub-patterns rather than dispatching to topic specialists.

## Trade-offs and limits

- **Load balancing.** Left alone, routing collapses. Experts picked slightly more often early in training get better and are then picked even more, which leaves a few overworked experts and many dead ones. The classic fix is an [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), often combined with an expert-capacity cap that drops or reroutes overflow tokens. DeepSeek later introduced [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) using per-expert bias terms.
- **Memory.** Every expert must be stored. All 671B of DeepSeek-V3's parameters sit in expensive HBM even though most are idle for any given token, which ties MoE to the [memory-bound](#c/memory-bound) nature of inference.
- **Communication.** When experts are spread across GPUs, tokens have to be shipped to wherever their chosen experts live. GLM-5 cut its depth to 80 layers partly to reduce this expert-parallel traffic.
- **Design questions that are still open.** Labs disagree on granularity (many small experts, as in DeepSeek's [fine-grained design](#c/fine-grained), or a few large ones, as in Llama 4) and on whether to keep an always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c). [Qwen3 dropped it](#c/no-shared).

## History

The idea is old. It dates to [Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton in 1991](#c/moe-1991). [Sparse gating in deep networks](#c/sparse-moe) arrived in 2017 (Shazeer et al., up to 137B parameters), the same year as the Transformer. [GShard](#c/gshard) brought it into the Transformer in 2020 at more than 600B parameters, and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) simplified routing to a single expert per token in 2021. What turned the idea into the thing running most open flagships was a decade of [incremental fixes](#c/c-incremental): balancing losses, capacity limits, routing-stability work, shared experts and expert-sharding systems.

## From the chat

- MoE "flips on every single token, and that's not a quirk, it's the whole design". Routing is re-decided per token and per layer.
- The chat corrected the "topic expert" intuition: an expert is just one of N parallel FFN weight-blocks, and specialisation is low-level and "alien to how a human would carve up knowledge".
- MoE is [not a recent breakthrough](#c/r-moe-old). The idea is from 1991 and sparse gating from 2017. Its value came from years of incremental engineering, which is why the chat treated it as evidence that cost declines come mostly from accumulated tweaks.
- The chat declined to attribute Epoch's measured cost drop to MoE alone. MoE is one ingredient in a ~3×/year algorithmic-efficiency slice.
- The routing schemes inside closed models such as Claude and GPT are not disclosed. They are broadly understood to be MoE, but the exact variant isn't known.

concepts.title: Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts
concepts.summary: Jacobs, Hinton, Jordan & Nowlan: the original idea
concepts.overview: **"Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts"** (Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton, *Neural Computation*, 1991) is where the Mixture of Experts idea begins. It proposed training several separate networks (the experts) alongside a gating network that learns, for each input, how much to trust each expert. The experts compete to handle each case, which pushes them to divide the input space among themselves instead of all learning the same thing. In this original form every expert still computed on every input and the gate only reweighted their outputs, so it saved no compute. The step that makes modern [MoE](#c/moe) cheap is sparse top-k gating, which came from [Shazeer et al. in 2017](#c/sparse-moe). The chat used this date to [correct the belief](#c/r-moe-old) that MoE is a recent breakthrough: the core idea is more than three decades old.

concepts.title: Sparsely-gated MoE layer
concepts.summary: Shazeer et al.: sparse gating in deep nets, up to 137B parameters
concepts.overview: The **Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer**, from Shazeer and colleagues at Google in the January 2017 paper "Outrageously Large Neural Networks", is the version of MoE that matters for modern LLMs. A trainable gate picks only the top few of many experts for each input, so compute per example stays roughly fixed while parameter count grows. That enabled models of up to **137 billion parameters** when that was enormous. The layers sat between recurrent (LSTM) layers and were tested on language modelling and machine translation. The paper also ran into the central problem of sparse routing, expert collapse, and added balancing penalties to fight it, the ancestor of the [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss). It appeared the same year as the Transformer. [GShard](#c/gshard) carried the idea into Transformers in 2020, and modern [MoE](#c/moe) descends from it.
concepts.article:
The **Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts layer** was introduced by Noam Shazeer and colleagues at Google in the January 2017 paper *"Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer."* It took the [1991 mixture-of-experts idea](#c/moe-1991), made the gating **sparse** so that only a few experts run for each input, and put it inside a deep network. That broke the rule that more parameters means proportionally more compute, and it let the authors train models of up to **137 billion parameters**. Nearly every modern [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) LLM descends from this layer.

## How it works

The layer holds a large pool of expert networks, each a simple feed-forward block, and a gating network. For each input the gate computes a score per expert and keeps only the top-k, setting the rest to zero. Only the selected experts run, and their outputs are combined using the gate's weights. The paper added tunable noise to the gate scores before the top-k selection. The noise encourages exploration and helps spread load.

Since most experts are skipped for any given input, total parameters can grow by orders of magnitude while computation per example grows only a little. The paper called this "conditional computation" and presented it as the way past the compute limits of dense models.

## Architecture

The experiments predate the Transformer's dominance. The MoE layers were placed between stacked LSTM layers and applied to language modelling and machine translation. The design pattern is still the same one used today: a learned [router](#c/router) in front of a pool of [feed-forward](#c/ffn) experts.

## The balancing problem

The paper identified the failure mode that still shapes MoE design. Left to itself, the gate tends to converge on a few favourite experts. They get more training, so they improve, so they get picked more, and the rest of the pool is wasted. The authors added extra loss terms that penalise uneven expert usage. This is the ancestor of the [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), which was later refined and eventually replaced in DeepSeek's case by [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free).

## Why it matters

The 2017 paper came out the same year as the Transformer. From there the path runs through [GShard](#c/gshard) (2020), which put sparse MoE into the Transformer at more than 600B parameters, and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) (2021), which simplified routing to one expert per token. It then leads to the fine-grained, shared-expert designs of [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) and its peers. The key idea, that capacity can grow faster than cost, is the reason the total-versus-active split exists at all.

## Trade-offs and limits

Sparse gating makes computation cheap, but not memory or communication. Every expert still has to be stored, and on multi-device hardware tokens must be sent to wherever their chosen experts live. Training stability and load balance also needed years of further work. The chat's point was that the breakthrough came in 2017 but most of the value arrived later, through a long tail of [incremental engineering](#c/c-incremental).

## From the chat

- The chat dated "the version that matters for modern LLMs—sparse, gated, dropped into deep nets" to 2017, with the Shazeer et al. paper enabling models of up to 137B parameters.
- It noted that the paper is the same age as the Transformer, which means MoE's key innovations came well before the inference-price data window that Epoch measures (roughly April 2024 onward).
- It used the paper as the main example that "breakthrough vs. tweak" is a false binary. The idea came in 1991 and 2017, but almost none of the value was realised until later fixes made it trainable and servable.

concepts.title: GShard
concepts.summary: MoE folded into the Transformer, past 600B parameters
concepts.overview: **GShard** (Lepikhin et al., Google, 2020) brought sparse [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) into the Transformer and scaled it past **600 billion parameters**, using multilingual machine translation as the test bed. It replaced the feed-forward block in every other Transformer layer with an MoE layer, routed each token to its top two experts, and put a cap on how many tokens each expert could take per batch, sending overflow onward without expert processing. Just as important was the systems side: GShard was an automatic sharding approach that spread experts across many accelerators, the start of the expert-parallel training that every large MoE now depends on. It sits between the [2017 sparsely-gated layer](#c/sparse-moe) and the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch), which cut routing to a single expert per token in 2021.

concepts.title: Switch Transformer
concepts.summary: Simplified routing to one expert per token; toward trillion-parameter models
concepts.overview: The **Switch Transformer** (Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer, Google, 2021) simplified [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) routing to its limit: each token goes to **exactly one** expert (top-1) rather than two or more. That roughly halves routing computation and communication and makes each expert's batch smaller and more predictable. The authors paired it with an expert *capacity factor* (a buffer on how many tokens each expert accepts, with overflow passed through untouched), a simplified [load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), and stability tricks such as computing the router in higher precision. It pushed sparse models toward a trillion parameters, with a 1.6T-parameter model, and reported large pre-training speedups over dense T5 baselines at equal compute. Later designs went the other way on granularity: DeepSeek's [fine-grained experts](#c/fine-grained) route each token to many small experts instead of one large one.
concepts.article:
The **Switch Transformer**, published by William Fedus, Barret Zoph and Noam Shazeer at Google in 2021, showed that sparse [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) routing could be made radically simpler. Where earlier designs sent each token to its top two or more experts, Switch sends each token to **exactly one**. The paper argued that this top-1 "switch" routing keeps model quality while cutting routing cost, communication and implementation complexity, and it used the approach to push sparse Transformers toward trillion-parameter scale.

## How it works

Switch follows the standard MoE pattern: the [feed-forward network](#c/ffn) in a Transformer layer is replaced by a pool of experts, and a learned [router](#c/router) scores each expert for each token. Switch keeps only the single highest-scoring expert and scales its output by the router's probability, so the router still gets a gradient.

Top-1 routing has several practical benefits:

- **Less computation in the router** and fewer expert calls per token.
- **Smaller expert batches**, because each token occupies one slot and not two.
- **Simpler communication** when experts are spread across devices.

## Capacity and balancing

Hardware needs fixed tensor shapes, so each expert gets a fixed *capacity*: the number of tokens it can accept per batch, set by a **capacity factor** multiplied by an even share of the batch. Tokens routed to an expert that is already full overflow and pass through the layer unprocessed via the residual connection. A capacity factor above 1 gives some slack at the cost of wasted compute.

To keep routing balanced, Switch uses a simplified [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss). It penalises the product of the fraction of tokens each expert receives and the router probability assigned to it, pushing both toward uniform. The paper also addressed training instability with selective precision: the router runs in float32 while the rest of the model uses bfloat16. It also used smaller initialisation and more dropout inside experts during fine-tuning.

## Scale and results

The paper scaled to a **1.6-trillion-parameter** model and reported substantial pre-training speedups over dense T5 baselines trained with the same compute per token. Those results cemented the point that sparse models could turn extra parameters into quality without extra per-token arithmetic.

## Why it matters

Switch is the step between [GShard](#c/gshard) (2020, top-2 routing past 600B parameters) and the modern open-weight MoE era. It established the vocabulary later work took for granted: capacity factors, token dropping, router precision and a simple balancing loss.

## Trade-offs and limits

Top-1 routing gives each token only one expert's view per layer, and dropped tokens mean some computation is skipped. Later designs moved the other way on granularity. DeepSeek's [fine-grained experts](#c/fine-grained) split capacity into many small experts and route each token to several (8 of 256 in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3)), plus an always-on shared expert. That arrangement gives the router finer-grained combinations to choose from. [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) sits nearer the Switch end, with few large experts active per token. The capacity and dropping machinery was also partly superseded: DeepSeek-V3 reports dropping no tokens, relying on [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) instead.

## From the chat

- The chat described Switch as the 2021 step that "simplified routing to a single expert per token and pushed toward trillion-parameter models".
- It listed "the top-1 simplification" among the incremental fixes that together turned MoE from a clever idea into the architecture behind most frontier models.
- The chat noted that router top-k is "usually 1 or 2" in the classic picture. Modern fine-grained designs like DeepSeek-V3 use 8 routed experts, and the gap shows how far the field moved after Switch.

concepts.title: Auxiliary load-balancing loss
concepts.summary: Penalize lopsided routing so experts don't collapse into a few favourites
concepts.overview: The **auxiliary load-balancing loss** is an extra training penalty that stops a [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) [router](#c/router) from collapsing onto a few favourite experts. Without it, training falls into a feedback loop: experts picked slightly more often early on get more gradient updates, improve, get picked even more, and leave the rest of the pool dead, wasting most of the model's capacity. The loss grows when routing is lopsided. In the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) form it multiplies each expert's share of tokens by its average router probability, pushing both toward uniform. It usually comes with an expert-capacity cap that drops or reroutes overflow tokens. The tension is that pushing too hard for balance can erase useful specialisation and hurt quality. That penalty is what DeepSeek's [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) was designed to avoid. The idea traces back to the [2017 sparsely-gated MoE paper](#c/sparse-moe).

concepts.title: Auxiliary-loss-free balancing
concepts.summary: Per-expert bias terms balance load without the loss's quality penalty (DeepSeek)
concepts.overview: **Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** is DeepSeek's alternative to the [auxiliary balancing loss](#c/lb-loss), and it shipped in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) (December 2024). Each expert gets a bias term that is added to its router score *only when choosing the top-k experts*. After each training step the bias goes down for overloaded experts and up for underused ones, so traffic evens out. The gating weights that combine expert outputs still come from the unbiased token-expert affinity. Balancing is therefore done by a simple controller, without a gradient-carrying loss that fights the language-modelling objective, and DeepSeek reports it avoids the quality penalty such losses impose. In the public V3 config it shows up as `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` ("no aux" meaning no auxiliary loss) with `scoring_func: "sigmoid"`.
concepts.article:
**Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** is a technique for keeping [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) routing balanced without adding a penalty term to the training loss. DeepSeek researchers introduced it in 2024 and used it at scale in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) (December 2024). It replaces the conventional [auxiliary load-balancing loss](#c/lb-loss) with per-expert bias terms that steer which experts get chosen. The aim is to keep all experts in use without the quality loss an auxiliary loss can cause.

## The problem it solves

An MoE [router](#c/router) left alone tends to collapse. A few experts win early, get more training, and end up handling most tokens while the rest sit idle. The standard remedy is an auxiliary loss that penalises uneven routing. That loss sends its own gradients into the router and the model, and those gradients pull against the actual language-modelling objective. Set the penalty weight too low and the load stays unbalanced. Set it too high and quality suffers, because the router is pushed away from the experts that suit each token best.

## How it works

The method separates *which experts are selected* from *how their outputs are weighted*:

1. The router computes an affinity score between the token and each expert. In DeepSeek-V3 this uses a sigmoid rather than a softmax.
2. A per-expert **bias** is added to these scores, but **only for top-k selection**. The token goes to the 8 experts with the highest biased scores.
3. The **gating weights** used to combine the selected experts' outputs come from the original, unbiased affinities.
4. After each training step, each expert's bias is nudged by a fixed small amount: down if the expert was overloaded, up if it was underloaded.

This amounts to a feedback controller placed next to the model, not a term inside the loss. No balancing gradient flows through the network, so the model's parameters are shaped only by the real training objective, while the biases quietly move traffic around.

DeepSeek-V3's technical report says it also kept a very small sequence-level balance loss as a backstop against extreme imbalance within a single sequence. The main mechanism is still the bias. The report also describes routing with no token dropping during training or inference, which older capacity-capped designs like the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) relied on.

## In the config

The public DeepSeek-V3 `config.json` exposes the technique directly: `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` ("noaux" meaning no auxiliary loss) and `scoring_func: "sigmoid"`. DeepSeek-V3 combines it with [fine-grained and shared experts](#c/fine-grained): 256 routed experts, 8 active per token, plus 1 shared expert.

## Why it matters

Load balancing is one of the long-running engineering problems that decided whether MoE was practical. Auxiliary-loss-free balancing is a good example of the [incremental fixes](#c/c-incremental) that unlocked MoE's value years after the idea itself. It adds nothing at inference, costs almost nothing in training, and removes a trade-off between hardware efficiency and model quality.

## Trade-offs and limits

The bias update is a hand-tuned controller with its own step-size hyperparameter. Because balance is enforced over batches, individual sequences can still be lopsided, which is why a small complementary loss was kept. The approach also assumes the router's affinity scores are worth protecting from interference, meaning some useful specialisation exists. That specialisation is [low-level rather than topical](#c/r-experts).

## From the chat

- The chat described it as DeepSeek's answer to the balancing problem: "adjusting per-expert bias terms to balance load without the performance penalty of an auxiliary loss, while keeping the actual gating based on pure token-expert affinity."
- When it walked through DeepSeek-V3's real `config.json`, it tied `scoring_func: "sigmoid"` and `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` to this technique, reading "noaux" as literally "no auxiliary loss".
- It placed the technique in the wider balancing tension: balance the load enough to use every parameter, but not so hard that you destroy the useful specialisation the router has learned.

concepts.title: Fine-grained + shared experts
concepts.summary: Many small experts plus an always-on shared one (DeepSeek)
concepts.overview: **Fine-grained plus shared experts** is DeepSeek's MoE layout, introduced in its DeepSeekMoE work in 2024 and used in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3). Instead of a few large experts, capacity is cut into **many small ones**. V3 has 256 routed experts, each with an intermediate width of only 2048, smaller than the 7168-wide hidden state, where a dense FFN would usually be several times wider. Each token activates 8 of them. With more, smaller experts to pick from, the router has far more possible combinations. On top of that sits one **[shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c)** that every token always uses. It captures common, general-purpose processing so the routed experts don't each have to relearn it. [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and GLM-4.5 kept this pattern. [Llama 4](#c/llama4) went the other way with few large experts, and [Qwen3 dropped the shared expert](#c/no-shared), so the question is still open.
concepts.article:
**Fine-grained plus shared experts** is a way of organising a [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) layer that DeepSeek popularised with its DeepSeekMoE work in 2024 and carried into [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) and [V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32). It makes two changes to the classic design. First, **fine-grained segmentation**: split the expert capacity into many small experts and activate several per token, not a few large ones. Second, **shared-expert isolation**: set aside one or more experts that every token always uses. The layout has spread widely. [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and GLM-4.5 both use it.

## How it works

In a classic MoE such as the [Switch Transformer](#c/switch), each expert is a full-size FFN and a token goes to one or two of them. Fine-grained MoE keeps the parameter budget but divides it into smaller pieces. Concretely, in DeepSeek-V3:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Hidden size (`hidden_size`) | 7168 |
| Dense FFN intermediate (first 3 layers) | 18432 |
| Expert intermediate (`moe_intermediate_size`) | 2048 |
| Routed experts | 256 |
| Routed experts per token | 8 |
| Shared experts | 1 |

A token entering an MoE layer is scored by the [router](#c/router). It goes to 8 of the [256 routed experts](#c/experts), and each of those computes 7168 → 2048 → 7168 with its own weights. Their outputs, plus the shared expert's, are summed back into the [residual stream](#c/residual). That is why "9 active experts" sometimes appears in write-ups: 8 routed plus 1 shared.

The notable detail is the width. In a dense transformer the FFN's middle layer is usually several times *wider* than the hidden size, as with V3's own dense layers at about 2.6×. The experts here are deliberately *narrower* than the hidden size, and that is the design choice.

## Why many small experts

Picking 8 of 256 gives vastly more possible expert combinations than picking 1 or 2 of 8 or 16. The router can put together a more specific mix for each token, and each expert can specialise more narrowly. The active compute is similar to a coarser design with the same active parameter count, but the model's knowledge is split into finer pieces.

## Why a shared expert

Some processing is needed by almost every token. Without a shared expert, many routed experts would each learn a redundant copy of these basics, which wastes capacity. An always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) handles the common part, so the routed experts can concentrate on what varies.

## Adoption and divergence

This is where open-model designs split in 2025:

- **Kept both ideas:** DeepSeek-V3/V3.2, Kimi K2 (384 routed experts, an even sparser configuration) and GLM-4.5.
- **Fewer, larger experts:** [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4) uses 128 experts with 2 active per token at an 8192 width, and alternates MoE and dense layers.
- **Dropped the shared expert:** [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) removed it. The chat called this [one of the unsettled questions in MoE design](#c/no-shared).

## Trade-offs and limits

More, smaller experts mean more routing decisions, more small matrix multiplications that are harder to run efficiently, and heavier all-to-all communication when experts are spread across GPUs. GLM-5, which also uses 256 experts, reduced its layer count to 80 partly to limit expert-parallel traffic. The shared expert's value is also disputed: Qwen3's results suggest a strong model can do without it.

## From the chat

- The chat introduced shared experts as "a newer refinement... DeepSeek popularized": always-on experts that capture general processing, so routed experts don't "redundantly relearn the basics".
- It pointed out that DeepSeek's expert intermediate width (2048) is *smaller* than the hidden size (7168), "backwards from a normal FFN and... the whole point of fine-grained MoE."
- It framed the DeepSeek-versus-Llama 4 contrast as two MoE philosophies: many small experts against few large 8192-wide ones.
- It corrected a typo in the user's question: the hidden size is 7168, not 716.

concepts.title: Dropping the shared expert
concepts.summary: Qwen3 removed it — an unsettled MoE design question
concepts.overview: **Dropping the shared expert** is the MoE design choice [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) made in April 2025. Its MoE layers have only routed experts, with no always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c). DeepSeek's [fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained) layout had made a shared expert look standard: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45) all kept one, arguing that it absorbs common processing so routed experts don't each relearn the basics. Qwen3 removing it, while still ranking at the top of its size classes, suggests the shared expert may not be necessary, or that its benefit can be recovered through other choices such as expert count and training setup. The chat called this "one of the genuinely unsettled questions in MoE design right now," and for now it stands as a live experiment, not a settled result.

concepts.title: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
concepts.summary: Keep predicting tokens, but on curated examples of the behaviour you want
concepts.overview: Supervised fine-tuning is the first stage of [post-training](#c/post-training). The model keeps doing exactly what it did in pre-training, predicting the next token, but now on a curated dataset of prompts paired with ideal responses: thousands to millions of "here's a question, here's a good answer" demonstrations. This teaches the *format* of being an assistant, meaning that questions get answers, instructions get followed and conversations take turns. It does most of the work of turning a base model into something that behaves like a helper. Its limit is that the model can only imitate what it is shown, and good demonstrations are expensive to write. Increasingly they are [generated by stronger models](#c/synthetic-sft). Tülu 3's new SFT responses came from GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which makes SFT the main channel for [distillation](#c/distillation). Later stages ([reward modeling](#c/reward-model), RL) build on the SFT model.
concepts.article:
**Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**, also called *instruction tuning*, is the first stage of [post-training](#c/post-training). It keeps the same learning mechanism as [pre-training](#c/pretraining), next-token prediction with a cross-entropy loss, but swaps the raw web corpus for a curated dataset of *examples of the behaviour you want*: prompts paired with high-quality responses. It is the step that makes a base model act like an assistant at all.

## How it works

Each training example is a prompt (possibly a multi-turn conversation) plus a target response, formatted with the chat template the model will use at inference. The loss is usually computed only on the response tokens, so the model learns to *produce* good answers rather than to predict the user's words. Training runs for relatively few steps, at a learning rate well below pre-training's, so the model's knowledge is redirected rather than overwritten.

What the model learns is mostly behavioural:

- that a question should be followed by a helpful answer rather than by more questions;
- that instructions and format constraints should be obeyed;
- the turn-taking structure of a conversation;
- style, tone, and the refusal patterns written into the demonstrations.

SFT can be done as full fine-tuning or with [LoRA](#c/lora). LoRA is extremely common for SFT specifically, especially outside the frontier labs.

## Where the data comes from

Datasets range from thousands to about a million examples. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)'s SFT mixture has 939,344 samples drawn from many sources, including FLAN v2, CoCoNot and WildChat. Prompts come from three buckets: paid annotators, real user logs, and model-synthesized prompts (for example persona-driven generation for diversity). Responses are increasingly [synthetic](#c/synthetic-sft). All of Tülu 3's *new* SFT responses were written by GPT-4o, or by Claude 3.5 Sonnet for coding, because those gave the best results. Regenerating completions for existing datasets through that pipeline even improved downstream [DPO](#c/dpo) performance. Everything is [decontaminated](#c/decontamination) against evaluation benchmarks.

Closed frontier labs cannot do this for their flagship models, because there is no stronger model to copy. They rely more on paid human experts and on their own earlier models.

## SFT as distillation

Training on a stronger model's outputs is output-based [distillation](#c/distillation). It is the only form available when the teacher is a closed API, since you cannot see its weights or probabilities. Much of the 2023–2024 open-model wave (Alpaca, which fine-tuned Llama on about 52K model-generated instructions; Open Orca; ShareGPT-trained models) was SFT-as-distillation. TinyGSM showed how strong the effect can be: 12.3M synthetic math problems from GPT-3.5-turbo got a 125M-parameter model to 63.1% on grade-school math. DeepSeek likewise distilled [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1)'s reasoning into smaller models via SFT on its traces.

## Limitations

- **Imitation ceiling.** The model can only be as good as its demonstrations. It never sees what a *better* answer would look like.
- **Cost and coverage.** High-quality human demonstrations are expensive and cannot cover every situation.
- **Forgetting.** Push too hard (high learning rate, too many steps) and fluency or knowledge degrade.

These limits motivate the next stages. [Reward modeling](#c/reward-model) turns cheaper *comparisons* into a training signal, and reinforcement learning ([RLHF](#c/rlhf), [RLVR](#c/rlvr)) lets the model explore and be rewarded for outputs better than any in the SFT set.

## In practice

Real pipelines rarely run SFT once. Labs interleave SFT and RL over several rounds, and they often run an SFT "cold start" on curated reasoning traces before large-scale RL. For someone adapting an open model to a domain, SFT with LoRA is the default and often the only step.

## From the chat

- The chat called SFT the stage that "does most of the heavy lifting in converting a base model into something that behaves like an assistant at all". The mechanism is the same as pre-training, and only the data differs.
- It named SFT's core limitation: the model "can only imitate the demonstrations it's shown", which is why RL can in principle exceed it.
- It called distillation "essentially a souped-up SFT," and noted that for the instruction-following quality of 2023–2024 open models, "a great deal of it, openly" came from frontier outputs.
- It highlighted the Tülu 3 admission that its synthetic SFT responses were written by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet. This is where the open recipe and the frontier recipe genuinely diverge.

concepts.title: Reward modeling
concepts.summary: Learn from comparisons which response is better
concepts.overview: Reward modeling rests on a simple observation: it is much easier to say which of two answers is better than to write the ideal answer yourself. So after [SFT](#c/sft), labs collect *comparison* data. Humans, or increasingly [an LLM judge](#c/llm-judge), see two responses to the same prompt and pick the preferred one. A separate network, usually initialised from the SFT model with a scalar output head, is trained to give the preferred response a higher score. Once trained, it can score any new response, and that turns fuzzy human taste into a number [RLHF](#c/rlhf) can optimise. It is also RLHF's weak point. A learned reward model is a noisy, gameable proxy, and a policy optimised hard against it can learn to please the scorer without actually being better. [DPO](#c/dpo) avoids training one at all, and [RLVR](#c/rlvr) swaps it for a deterministic checker where correctness can be verified.
concepts.article:
**Reward modeling** is the [post-training](#c/post-training) stage that turns *preferences* into a trainable signal. Instead of showing the model ideal answers, as [SFT](#c/sft) does, you show a judge pairs of answers and record which one is better, then train a **reward model** to predict those judgments. The reward model then acts as an automated critic that can score any response. It supplies the "human feedback" in [RLHF](#c/rlhf).

## Why comparisons

The motivating insight is asymmetric difficulty. Writing a perfect response to a hard prompt is slow and expensive, while comparing two candidate responses is fast and needs less expertise. Comparisons also capture qualities that are hard to demonstrate but easy to recognise: tone, helpfulness, appropriate caution, concision. Because they rank the model's *own* outputs, they tell it about the region of behaviour it actually occupies.

## How it works

1. **Collect prompts** and sample several responses per prompt, from the model being trained and often from a pool of other models.
2. **Label preferences.** An annotator marks which response is preferred, producing (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples. Classic RLHF used human annotators. Open pipelines such as [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) now lean heavily on [LLM-as-a-judge](#c/llm-judge), and Qwen2 describes a human–automation hybrid.
3. **Train the reward model.** Typically this is a copy of the SFT model with its output head replaced by a single scalar. The standard objective (a Bradley–Terry-style pairwise loss) pushes the chosen response's score above the rejected one's.
4. **Use it.** The reward model scores fresh generations during reinforcement learning, or filters and ranks samples.

Post-training data therefore has two main ingredients, demonstrations for SFT and preference pairs for this stage. For the 8B Tülu 3 model the preference set was roughly 250–300K pairs.

## Trade-offs and failure modes

- **Proxy, not truth.** The reward model only approximates what the labellers wanted. The chat called it "a noisy, gameable proxy": a policy optimised against it can learn to satisfy the reward model without being right. This is *reward hacking*, and it is why RLHF usually adds a penalty for drifting too far from the SFT model.
- **Label noise and bias.** Humans disagree and have systematic tastes (for example, preferring longer answers). LLM judges bring biases of their own.
- **Coverage.** A reward model is only reliable near the distribution it was trained on. As the policy improves, its outputs can drift out of that region.
- **Extra machinery.** A separate network has to be trained, stored and run during RL.

## Alternatives and successors

- **[DPO](#c/dpo)** skips the explicit reward model and optimises the policy directly on preference pairs.
- **[RLVR](#c/rlvr)** replaces the learned model with a deterministic verifier (unit tests, answer checking) wherever correctness is objective, which removes the proxy problem in those domains.
- **Process rewards and rubric-based rewards** are active research directions for extending verifier-like signals to domains without ground truth, such as scoring intermediate reasoning steps rather than only final answers.

## In practice

Preference-data construction is empirical and expensive. Tülu 3's ablations found that including on-policy responses (from the model being trained) helped, that scaling the number of unique prompts helped, and that using new prompts rather than reusing SFT prompts helped. How much human judgment remains in frontier labs' preference data is not disclosed.

## From the chat

- The chat described reward modeling as moving from "imitate good examples" to "learn what's *better*," motivated by comparing being easier than writing.
- It stressed that preferences can train a separate reward model or be "used more directly". The latter is the DPO route.
- It called the learned reward model's weakness central to why [RLVR](#c/rlvr) mattered: "a learned reward model is a noisy, gameable proxy … A verifier isn't a proxy; it checks ground truth."
- It flagged the shift toward LLM judges as real but not total, and said the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge is now "load-bearing for the whole preference-data pipeline."

concepts.title: RLHF
concepts.summary: Optimize against a learned reward model of human preference
concepts.overview: RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) is the post-training method that made chat assistants work, and it was popularised by OpenAI's InstructGPT and ChatGPT around 2022. It builds on [SFT](#c/sft) and a trained [reward model](#c/reward-model) that scores responses the way human raters would. The model then generates responses, the reward model scores them, and a reinforcement-learning algorithm (classically PPO, with a separate critic network) updates the model toward higher-scoring outputs. A penalty keeps it from drifting too far from the SFT model. Unlike imitation, RL lets the model be rewarded for answers better than any demonstration. Its weakness is that the reward is a learned, gameable proxy. That led to two successors: [DPO](#c/dpo), which skips the reward model, and [RLVR](#c/rlvr), which replaces it with a checker for math and code.
concepts.article:
**Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)** is a [post-training](#c/post-training) technique that optimises a language model against a learned model of human preferences. It was the method that turned instruction-tuned models into the helpful, conversational assistants of 2022 onward, with OpenAI's InstructGPT and ChatGPT the best-known examples. It remains the standard way to shape subjective qualities like helpfulness, tone and harmlessness.

## How it works

RLHF sits at stage 3 of the classic pipeline:

1. **[SFT](#c/sft)** gives a model that already behaves roughly like an assistant.
2. **[Reward modeling](#c/reward-model).** Humans compare pairs of responses, and a reward model is trained to predict which one they prefer.
3. **RL optimisation.** The SFT model (now the *policy*) generates responses to prompts. The reward model scores each one, and a policy-gradient algorithm updates the policy to make high-scoring responses more likely.

The classic algorithm is **PPO** (Proximal Policy Optimization). PPO uses a separate *critic* or value network to estimate how good each step is, and it clips updates to keep training stable. Two further ingredients are standard:

- a **KL penalty** against the frozen SFT (reference) model, so the policy cannot drift into strange text that happens to score well;
- the **reward model itself**, kept frozen during RL.

During training that is up to four models in memory: policy, reference, reward model and critic. This is part of why RLHF is expensive and fiddly.

## Why it matters

RL goes beyond imitation. SFT can only copy its demonstrations, but RL lets the model explore its own outputs and be rewarded for ones better than anything in the demonstration set. So RLHF can in principle exceed the quality of the human-written examples. It is also where much fine-grained behaviour gets shaped: tone, helpfulness, refusals, harmlessness. The chat noted that safety and alignment behaviour lives predominantly in post-training.

## Trade-offs and failure modes

- **Reward hacking.** The reward model is a learned proxy, and optimising hard against it finds its blind spots, such as responses that *look* good to the scorer without being correct. The KL penalty mitigates this but does not remove it.
- **Cost.** The critic roughly doubles memory and compute relative to the policy alone, and the whole setup has many hyperparameters.
- **Subjective signal.** Human preference is well suited to style and helpfulness but a poor signal for correctness in math or code, where raters may not be able to tell.

## What it led to

Two lines of work each removed a piece of RLHF:

| Successor | What it removes | Idea |
|---|---|---|
| [DPO](#c/dpo) (2023) | The separate reward model and RL loop | Optimise the policy directly on preference pairs |
| [RLVR](#c/rlvr) (2025) | The *learned* reward | Use a deterministic checker where correctness is objective |
| [GRPO](#c/grpo) (2024) | The critic network | Use a group of samples' average reward as the baseline |

For reasoning models, RLVR with GRPO has become the dominant stage-3 technique. RLHF-style preference optimisation remains the tool for open-ended qualities where no verifier exists.

## From the chat

- The chat placed RLHF and RLVR as "both *Stage 3* techniques" that "differ in where the reward comes from". RLHF's learned reward is "good for subjective qualities like helpfulness and tone, but a noisy, gameable proxy."
- It explained that PPO "needs a separate 'critic' or value network … that roughly doubles the memory and compute". Removing that critic is GRPO's main contribution.
- It presented DPO as RLHF's "known alternative", simpler and popular in open models, and said whether it matches full RL at scale is debated.
- It noted the shift from human raters to [LLM judges](#c/llm-judge) in open pipelines, which means that for many open models the "human" in RLHF is increasingly a model.

concepts.title: DPO
concepts.summary: Optimize directly on preference pairs, no separate reward model
concepts.overview: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization, 2023) gets most of the benefit of [RLHF](#c/rlhf) without training a separate [reward model](#c/reward-model) or running a reinforcement-learning loop. Its key result is mathematical. The optimal policy under RLHF's KL-regularised objective can be written in closed form, so the reward is *implied* by the policy itself. That allows training directly on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples with a simple classification-style loss. The loss raises the model's likelihood of the chosen response relative to a frozen reference model, and lowers it for the rejected one. No sampling happens during training and no critic is needed, so DPO is cheap, stable and easy to run. It became very popular in open models, for example in the [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) recipe. Whether it matches full online RL at frontier scale is debated.
concepts.article:
**Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** is a [post-training](#c/post-training) method, introduced in 2023, that aligns a model to preference data without an explicit [reward model](#c/reward-model) or a reinforcement-learning loop. It combines stages 2 and 3 of the classic [RLHF](#c/rlhf) pipeline into one supervised-style training step. That makes it much simpler to run, and it has become a staple of open-model post-training.

## How it works

RLHF optimises a policy to maximise a learned reward while a KL penalty keeps it close to a reference model, usually the [SFT](#c/sft) model. DPO's authors showed that this objective has a closed-form optimal solution. The reward can be written in terms of the ratio between the policy's probability of a response and the reference model's. Substituting that back into the standard pairwise preference loss leaves a loss that depends only on the policy and the reference, so no separate reward network is needed.

In practice, for each (prompt, chosen, rejected) triple:

1. compute how much more likely the chosen response is under the policy than under the frozen reference;
2. compute the same for the rejected response;
3. push the first up relative to the second, through a logistic loss scaled by a temperature β that sets how far the policy may move from the reference.

That is the whole procedure. There is no generation during training, no critic, and no reward model to train or keep in memory.

## Why it matters

- **Simplicity and cost.** Two models (policy and frozen reference) instead of RLHF's four, and a training loop that looks like fine-tuning.
- **Stability.** Fewer moving parts and hyperparameters than PPO-based RLHF.
- **Accessibility.** A team that can do SFT can do DPO, often with [LoRA](#c/lora). That largely explains its spread through open models.

The chat described it as "a lighter-weight Stage 2+3 combined," "simpler and popular in open models."

## Trade-offs

- **Offline data.** Standard DPO learns from a fixed set of preference pairs rather than sampling fresh outputs and scoring them. If those pairs come from other models, the signal may not match the policy's own mistakes. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)'s ablations found that including *on-policy* responses (from the model being trained) in the preference data improved results.
- **Bounded by the preferences.** Like RLHF it inherits the biases of whoever labelled the pairs, increasingly an [LLM judge](#c/llm-judge).
- **Not for verifiable reasoning.** For math and code, where correctness can be checked, online RL with a verifier ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) has become the dominant approach for reasoning models.
- **Scale question.** Whether DPO matches full online RL at the frontier is openly debated. Frontier labs' exact recipes are undisclosed.

## In practice

A common open recipe is SFT, then DPO on preference pairs, then (for reasoning) RLVR on [verifiable problems](#c/verifiable-problems). That is the shape of Tülu 3, which found that regenerating SFT completions through its synthetic pipeline improved DPO performance, and that scaling unique prompts and using prompts not seen in SFT helped. Many variants that tweak the loss have followed, but the basic method remains the default.

## From the chat

- The chat introduced DPO as RLHF's "known alternative" that "skips training a separate reward model and optimizes the model directly on preference pairs."
- It said DPO is "simpler and popular in open models," and that "whether it matches full RL at scale is debated". This is presented as an open question, not a settled one.
- The Tülu 3 findings (on-policy data, more unique prompts, new prompts rather than reused SFT prompts) were cited as examples of how much ablation building good preference data takes.

concepts.title: RLVR
concepts.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards: a checker, not a learned judge
concepts.overview: RLVR (reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards) replaces [RLHF](#c/rlhf)'s learned [reward model](#c/reward-model) with a deterministic checker. It runs the code against unit tests, compares the math answer with ground truth, or checks a format constraint, and gives a binary pass/fail reward. Because the checker verifies correctness itself, there is no noisy proxy for the model to game. That makes it especially effective in math and code, and it has become the dominant post-training paradigm for reasoning models. [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1) was the landmark case: RL on correct answers alone produced long chains of thought and a spontaneous "aha moment" of self-reflection. [GRPO](#c/grpo) made it affordable. Two questions remain open: how to extend it to domains with no verifier, and whether it [creates new reasoning or mainly sharpens](#c/c-rlvr-new) what the base model could already do.
concepts.article:
**Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR)** is a [post-training](#c/post-training) method in which a model is optimised against a *deterministic verifier* rather than a learned judge. The model attempts a problem, a program checks whether the result is correct, and the model is reinforced toward attempts that pass. Since early 2025 it has become the dominant technique for training reasoning models, and it underlies much of the test-time-compute paradigm, in which models "think" at length before answering.

## How it works

RLVR is a stage-3 (reinforcement learning) technique, like [RLHF](#c/rlhf). What changes is where the reward comes from:

| | RLHF | RLVR |
|---|---|---|
| Reward source | Learned [reward model](#c/reward-model) of human preference | Rule-based checker |
| Signal | Continuous score, noisy | Usually binary: correct or not |
| Gameable? | Yes, it is a proxy | Much less, since it checks ground truth |
| Best domains | Tone, helpfulness, style | Math, code, checkable constraints |

A typical loop samples a batch of [verifiable problems](#c/verifiable-problems), generates several reasoning traces per problem, scores each final answer with the verifier, and updates the policy. The standard update algorithm is [GRPO](#c/grpo), which compares each attempt with the group's average and so needs no critic network. That cost saving is a large part of why reasoning training spread so quickly across labs.

## Why it matters

The striking result came from [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1). Optimising only for correct final answers made the model *learn to reason at length*. Extended chain-of-thought, self-reflection ("wait, let me reconsider") and branching emerged during training without being taught, which researchers called an "aha moment." RLVR teaches a model to *use* inference-time thinking productively.

It also drove visible capability jumps. [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32)'s rise to GPT-5-comparable performance came from "a scalable RL framework and scaled-up post-training compute," and its Speciale variant reached gold-medal level at the 2025 IMO and IOI. Competition math and coding are the showcases because they are the most verifiable domains.

## Failure modes

- **Length bias.** Naive RLVR tends to make reasoning chains ever longer, sometimes without improving them.
- **Exploration collapse.** If every sampled attempt at a problem is wrong, the group has no variation and there is no learning signal. This is severe on hard or unfamiliar problems.
- **Reward hacking.** The model may find ways to satisfy the checker without genuine reasoning (for example, exploiting weak tests), so reward design matters.

The [GRPO variants](#c/grpo-variants) (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VAPO and others) are mostly patches for these problems. Data work matters too: curated verifiable datasets balanced toward medium difficulty, [decontaminated](#c/decontamination) against benchmarks, often with curricula of increasing difficulty.

## The contested question

Does RLVR create genuinely new reasoning ability? A careful [coverage study](#c/rlvr-study) found that across PPO, GRPO and others, RLVR *increases the likelihood* of correct samples but *decreases coverage* of solvable problems. The model gets better at sampling answers it could already produce, but gains no capability beyond the base model. The same work found that [distillation](#c/distillation) *can* transfer new reasoning patterns, and that current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and "remain far from optimal." Other work reports broader gains. The chat treated this as "a serious, credible critique rather than settled fact," with the truth depending on what counts as "new." See [the claim](#c/c-rlvr-new).

## The open frontier

The hard problem is **extending verifiable rewards beyond cleanly checkable domains**, such as essays, legal analysis, or agents over 50 tool calls. Candidate approaches include learned verifiers, rubric-based rewards and process rewards that score intermediate steps. Agentic RL, training models to use tools over long horizons, is probably the biggest current frontier. Frontier labs' exact RL recipes are undisclosed.

## From the chat

- The chat called RLVR "the dominant post-training paradigm for reasoning models" and a "clean departure" from RLHF. It swaps a noisy, gameable proxy for a verifier that "checks ground truth."
- It described R1's "aha moment" as the landmark demonstration: self-reflection "fell out of optimizing for correct answers over long reasoning chains."
- It gave real weight to the finding that RLVR sharpens rather than expands ability, but labelled it one research line, not consensus. It also noted that the alphabet of variants "may matter less than the marketing implies."
- It named extension to soft domains as the unresolved problem, and agentic RL as the area where its knowledge was least current.

concepts.title: GRPO
concepts.summary: Score a group of attempts and reinforce the above-average ones; no critic model
concepts.overview: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is the reinforcement-learning algorithm that made [RLVR](#c/rlvr) cheap enough to spread across labs. It was introduced in DeepSeek's 2024 math work and used for [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1). Standard PPO, the RLHF workhorse, runs a separate critic or value network next to the model to estimate how good each step is, which roughly doubles memory and compute. GRPO drops the critic.
