- The chat called V3 "the most thoroughly documented" open model and pulled the exact shape from the real `config.json` instead of relying on secondhand articles. That corrected earlier roundup figures: 61 layers, with the first 3 dense.
- It explained "9 active experts" as 8 routed plus 1 shared, and walked through why the 2048 expert width is smaller than the 7168 hidden size.
- It worked out MLA's memory saving from the config: a 512-dim cached latent against 16,384 for naive K/V, about 32× smaller.
- On openness: the architecture and inference are fully open, the training components partly so, and the data is not released. The chat said this is broadly the same for Llama 4, Qwen3 and Kimi K2.

concepts.title: DeepSeek-R1
concepts.summary: RLVR elicited reasoning, including an 'aha moment'

attributes.notes: RLVR elicited reasoning, including an 'aha moment'

concepts.overview: **DeepSeek-R1** (January 2025) is DeepSeek's reasoning model, built on the same **671B-total / 37B-active** MoE backbone as [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3): 61 layers, [MLA](#c/mla), 256 routed experts with 8 + 1 shared active. The architecture is unchanged. What's new is post-training. R1 showed that [RLVR](#c/rlvr), reinforcement learning against automatically checkable rewards for math and code, optimised with [GRPO](#c/grpo), can elicit long chain-of-thought reasoning, including a reported "aha moment" where the model spontaneously began to reflect on and revise its work. It reached this largely without distilling from a closed frontier model, which [cuts against the claim](#c/c-distill-open) that open reasoning gains mostly come from copying. DeepSeek then [distilled](#c/distillation) R1's reasoning into smaller open models. Whether RLVR creates [genuinely new ability](#c/c-rlvr-new) or sharpens latent ability is still debated.
concepts.article:
**DeepSeek-R1** is an open-weight reasoning model released by DeepSeek in January 2025. It became the landmark demonstration that **reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards** ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) can teach a large language model to reason step by step, producing long chains of thought and even spontaneous self-correction, without human-written reasoning traces for every step. Its architecture is the [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) backbone unchanged. Everything new about R1 is in [post-training](#c/post-training).

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Total / active parameters | 671B / ~37B |
| Layers | 61 |
| Experts | 256 routed, 8 + 1 shared active per token |
| Attention | [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla) |
| Base | DeepSeek-V3 |

Because the backbone is identical to V3, R1's jump in reasoning shows clearly that capability can come from training alone, with no architectural change.

## How it was trained

The central method is RLVR. Instead of rewarding the model with a learned reward model that stands in for human preferences, as in [RLHF](#c/rlhf), RLVR uses deterministic checks: does the math answer match the ground truth, does the code pass its tests. A verifier checks ground truth directly and isn't a proxy, so it is much harder to game than a learned reward model, and it works best in domains like math and code where correctness can be checked mechanically.

The optimiser is [GRPO](#c/grpo) (Group Relative Policy Optimization), from DeepSeek's earlier math work. For each problem the model samples a group of attempts, the verifier scores them, and each attempt is judged against the group's average. Better-than-average attempts are reinforced and worse ones suppressed. This removes the separate critic network that PPO needs, which cuts memory and compute a lot and is a major reason reasoning training spread so quickly across labs.

DeepSeek also reported an experimental variant, R1-Zero, trained by RL directly on the base model. The released R1 added a small amount of curated "cold-start" data and further stages to improve readability and general behaviour.

## The "aha moment"

The most discussed result was emergent behaviour. During RL training the model began, without being told to, to pause, re-examine its work and change approach mid-solution. DeepSeek called this an "aha moment". Nobody taught the model to write "wait, let me reconsider". The behaviour emerged from optimising for correct final answers over long reasoning chains. This is the mechanism behind the test-time-compute paradigm: RLVR teaches a model to make productive use of thinking at inference time.

## Distillation

DeepSeek then showed that R1's reasoning could be [distilled](#c/distillation) into much smaller open models, which were trained on R1's outputs. The direction matters. That is a lab distilling its *own* model downward, not copying a closed frontier model. The flagship case is closer to "RL produced reasoning, then distillation propagated it downward" than to "open models faked reasoning by copying GPT", which [challenges the idea](#c/c-distill-open) that distillation from closed models drives open reasoning gains.

## Reception and caveats

R1 made RLVR plus GRPO the default recipe for reasoning post-training and set off a wave of [GRPO variants](#c/grpo-variants) (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VAPO and others) aimed at length bias, exploration collapse and training stability. One of these, GSPO, specifically addresses stability problems when training MoE models.

Whether RLVR creates new reasoning ability is disputed. One careful study found that RLVR raises the probability of correct samples but narrows the set of problems a model can solve at all. On that reading it sharpens abilities the base model already had, and distillation is what transfers genuinely new patterns. R1's "aha moment" is the strongest evidence [on the other side](#c/c-rlvr-new). The truth probably depends on how "new" capability is defined.

## From the chat

- The chat described R1 as the landmark RLVR demonstration: "RLVR training can elicit sophisticated reasoning including an 'aha moment' where models spontaneously develop self-reflection."
- It explained GRPO's importance as mostly about cost, since dropping the critic network made reasoning training affordable.
- It corrected its own earlier claim that "a chunk" of open reasoning gains came from distillation. R1's headline result came largely *without* a frontier-distillation crutch, and DeepSeek distilled its own model downward.
- It flagged the RLVR-doesn't-create-new-ability study as "a serious, credible critique rather than settled fact."

concepts.title: DeepSeek-V3.2
concepts.summary: Only architectural change: sparse attention; capability came from scaled RL

attributes.notes: Only architectural change: sparse attention; capability came from scaled RL

concepts.overview: **DeepSeek-V3.2** (late 2025) keeps the [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) backbone: **671B total, 37B active**, 61 layers, 256 routed experts with 8 + 1 shared active, and [MLA](#c/mla). Its single architectural change, relative to V3.1-Terminus, is **[DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)](#c/dsa)**, added through continued training. A cheap "lightning indexer" scores earlier tokens, and full attention runs only over the selected top few, cutting attention cost from O(L²) to O(Lk). DeepSeek held the recipe fixed to isolate DSA, and the aim was parity, not a quality gain. It reports roughly 2–3× faster long-context processing, 30–40% less memory at 128K and a 50%+ API price cut, with nearly identical quality. The capability jump to GPT-5-comparable levels, with the V3.2-Speciale variant reporting IMO/IOI gold-medal performance, came from scaled RL post-training. Those comparisons are DeepSeek's own. V3.2 is the clearest example that [architecture wins are now mostly efficiency](#c/c-arch-efficiency).

concepts.title: Llama 4 Maverick
concepts.summary: Fewer, larger experts; MoE every other layer; ~22T tokens

attributes.notes: Fewer, larger experts; MoE every other layer; ~22T tokens

concepts.overview: **Llama 4 Maverick** (Meta, April 2025) was Meta's first MoE generation: **400B total, 17B active**, 128 experts, 1M-token context, trained on about 22 trillion tokens. It takes a different MoE approach from DeepSeek. It uses **fewer, larger experts**, with 2 active per token at an 8,192 width against DeepSeek's 8 of 256 at 2,048, and it **alternates MoE and dense blocks** every other layer, where DeepSeek makes nearly every layer MoE. For attention it uses the standard [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa), not MLA. The chat called it the "conservative, classic MoE" reference point against DeepSeek's more aggressive design. It is natively multimodal and ships with a smaller sibling, [Llama 4 Scout](#c/llama4-scout). A later benchmark (Stanford HELM's IFEval) showed IBM's much smaller hybrid [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4) trailing only Maverick among open models.
concepts.article:
**Llama 4 Maverick** is an open-weight [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model released by Meta in April 2025, alongside its smaller sibling [Llama 4 Scout](#c/llama4-scout). It was Meta's first MoE generation, after the dense Llama 1–3 line. Maverick has **400 billion total parameters with 17 billion active per token**, 128 experts and a 1-million-token context window, and was trained on about 22 trillion tokens. The chat described its design as the "conservative, classic MoE" counterpoint to [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3).

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Meta |
| Released | April 2025 |
| Total / active parameters | 400B / 17B |
| Experts | 128 |
| Active experts per token | 2, each 8,192 wide |
| MoE placement | Alternating MoE and dense layers |
| Attention | [Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)](#c/gqa) |
| Context | 1M tokens |
| Training data | ~22T tokens |

## A different MoE philosophy

Open MoE models in 2025 split on **expert granularity**. DeepSeek cut its FFN capacity into [many small experts](#c/fine-grained): 256 of them at a 2,048 intermediate width, with 8 routed plus 1 shared active per token. Llama 4 went the other way, with fewer and larger experts: 2 active per token at an 8,192 width. Meta's own description says each token goes to a shared expert plus one of the 128 routed experts. Either way, each Llama 4 expert is a much bigger slice of FFN.

The second difference is **where MoE appears**. DeepSeek-V3 makes every layer MoE except the first three. Llama 4 alternates MoE and dense blocks every other layer, so half its layers carry an ordinary dense FFN.

On attention, Llama 4 uses the industry-standard [GQA](#c/gqa), which shrinks the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) by sharing key/value heads across groups of query heads. It does not use DeepSeek's [MLA](#c/mla), which compresses more but is more complex.

## Why it matters

Maverick is a useful control case. It is a big, well-resourced MoE model that took the simpler path on every axis: coarser experts, a partly dense stack and default attention. Comparing it with DeepSeek-V3, [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) makes the design space clear. On the FFN side everyone converged on MoE but disagreed on granularity and shared experts. On the attention side the split is GQA (Llama 4, Qwen3) against MLA (DeepSeek, Kimi K2). The chat regarded its specs, like DeepSeek's, as the most trustworthy in the comparison because they come from real technical reports.

Maverick also serves as a benchmark reference. In Stanford HELM's IFEval instruction-following results, IBM's hybrid [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4)-H-Small beat every open-weight model except Maverick, a model more than twelve times its size (the chat quotes 402B for Maverick in that context).

## Trade-offs and limits

Few large experts give the router fewer combinations per token than fine-grained designs, and interleaving dense layers limits how far total capacity can grow for a given active budget. Maverick's sparsity ratio (17B of 400B, about 4%) is broadly similar to DeepSeek-V3's (37B of 671B, about 5.5%). Kimi K2 pushed further, to 32B of about 1T. As with every MoE model, all 400B parameters must be held in memory to serve it.

## Reception and caveats

The launch drew criticism when it emerged that the version at the top of the LMArena leaderboard was an experimental chat-tuned variant, not the released model. This fed a wider scepticism about vendor-reported benchmarks. The chat gives no benchmark figures for Maverick, and none are given here.

## From the chat

- The chat called Llama 4 "Meta's first MoE generation" and gave its specs: 400B total, 17B active, 128 experts, 1M context, ~22T tokens, April 2025.
- It set Llama 4 against DeepSeek as "a genuinely different MoE philosophy": fewer, larger experts (2 active at 8,192) against many small ones (2,048), and MoE every other layer against almost every layer.
- It described Llama 4's use of GQA as "the safe default".
- It noted that Llama 4's config would show `num_key_value_heads` well below `num_attention_heads`, unlike DeepSeek's MLA setup, where the two are equal.

concepts.title: Llama 4 Scout
concepts.summary: The small sibling with a huge context

attributes.notes: The small sibling with a huge context

concepts.overview: **Llama 4 Scout** (Meta, April 2025) is the smaller sibling of [Llama 4 Maverick](#c/llama4): a **109B-parameter** [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model whose standout feature is a **10-million-token context window**, ten times Maverick's 1M and far beyond most open models of its time. It uses the same family design, with [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa) for a smaller KV-cache and Meta's coarser MoE with fewer, larger experts. Per Meta it has 17B active parameters across 16 experts, and it was sized to run on a single high-end GPU host. At multi-million-token lengths the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) and attention cost dominate everything else, which is why techniques like GQA, [NoPE](#c/nope)-style positional changes and sparse or linear attention matter so much at that scale. How well Scout actually uses its full 10M context is less established than the headline number.

concepts.title: Qwen3
concepts.summary: Dropped the shared expert
concepts.overview: **Qwen3** (Alibaba, April 2025) is an open-weight model family widely regarded as the top open family in each size class. It includes dense models and MoE models, with the flagship **Qwen3-235B-A22B** (235B total, 22B active, 128 experts with 8 active per token) and a smaller 30B-A3B. For attention it uses the standard [GQA](#c/gqa). Its notable MoE decision is a subtraction: it [dropped the shared expert](#c/no-shared) that [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45) all kept, which makes it a live test of whether the always-on expert is needed. The family also introduced switchable thinking and non-thinking modes in one model. The weights are open, but the training data and full training pipeline are not.
concepts.article:
**Qwen3** is a family of open-weight language models released by Alibaba's Qwen team in April 2025. It spans small dense models up to large [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) models, and it earned a reputation as the best open family in each size class. Its architectural significance is a deliberate **subtraction**: unlike the DeepSeek-style MoE designs of the time, Qwen3's MoE models have **no shared expert**.

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Alibaba (Qwen team) |
| Released | April 2025 |
| MoE flagship | Qwen3-235B-A22B (235B total, 22B active) |
| Smaller MoE | Qwen3-30B-A3B |
| Experts (flagship) | 128, 8 active per token |
| Shared expert | None |
| Attention | [Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)](#c/gqa) |
| Also | Dense models at smaller sizes |

The "A22B" naming states the active parameter count directly, which reflects how central the [total-versus-active split](#c/r-smaller) had become by 2025.

## Dropping the shared expert

DeepSeek's [fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained) design pairs many small routed experts with one always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) that handles processing nearly every token needs, so the routed experts don't each relearn it. By 2025 [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3), [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) and [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45) all kept a shared expert.

Qwen3 [removed it](#c/no-shared). Its MoE layers use only routed experts, still fine-grained, with 8 of 128 active in the flagship. Qwen3 ranked at the top of its size classes anyway, which is evidence that the shared expert is at least not essential. The chat described the question as "one of the genuinely unsettled questions in MoE design right now." The field hasn't settled it.

## Attention

Qwen3 uses GQA, the standard choice that shrinks the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) by having groups of query heads share key/value heads. It does not use DeepSeek's [MLA](#c/mla), which compresses more but is more complex. In the 2025 landscape this puts Qwen3 with [Llama 4](#c/llama4) on attention, and with DeepSeek on fine-grained experts.

## Training and modes

Qwen3 models support a hybrid **thinking / non-thinking** mode. The same model can reason at length before answering or respond directly, so users can trade test-time compute for speed. This fits the wider 2025 shift in which capability gains came mainly from [post-training](#c/post-training) and reasoning RL, not from architecture changes. On post-training data, the chat cited the Qwen team's earlier (Qwen2) description of a hybrid pipeline: human annotation combined with automated data synthesis, with LLM judges used more and more for scale.

## Why it matters

Qwen3 is a clean natural experiment. It is a top-tier MoE family that removed a component its peers treated as standard, and it didn't pay an obvious price. With its strong results across sizes, that made it a default base for many open fine-tunes and derivative models.

## Trade-offs and caveats

Without a shared expert, the routed experts must cover common processing among themselves, which may make routing and balancing matter more. Whether dropping it helps, hurts or is neutral at a given scale hasn't been cleanly isolated in public. The chat also cautioned that its internal Qwen3 numbers leaned partly on third-party comparison write-ups. The headline counts are solid, but finer details such as exact layer and head counts should be checked against the model card.

## From the chat

- The chat called Qwen3 "widely regarded as the top-tier open-weight family by size class."
- Its highlighted MoE decision was dropping the shared expert, described as "a live experiment in whether the always-on shared expert is actually necessary."
- It placed Qwen3 on the GQA side of the attention split, with Llama 4, against MLA in DeepSeek and Kimi K2.
- It cautioned that the finer Qwen3 specs came partly from secondhand roundups and deliberately gave no layer or head counts.

concepts.title: Kimi K2
concepts.summary: The sparsest: 1T total, 32B active
concepts.overview: **Kimi K2** (Moonshot AI, July 2025) is the sparsity standout of the open MoE landscape: **about 1 trillion total parameters with only 32B active** per token (roughly 3%), spread over **384 experts**. That pushes the "huge total, small active" ratio further than almost any other open model. It borrows from the DeepSeek lineage, using [Multi-head Latent Attention](#c/mla) instead of GQA and keeping DeepSeek's [fine-grained + shared expert](#c/fine-grained) layout, with 8 routed experts plus a shared one per token. Moonshot trained it with its MuonClip optimizer and positioned it for agentic and tool-use work. The chat flagged that its specs came partly from comparison roundups, not a first-party report it could verify, so the exact figures are well attested but secondhand. Its sibling [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear) tests linear attention at smaller scale.
concepts.article:
**Kimi K2** is an open-weight [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model released by the Chinese lab Moonshot AI in July 2025. At about **one trillion total parameters with only 32 billion active per token**, it is the sparsest of the major open flagships. It stores roughly 30 times more parameters than it uses on any given token. Architecturally it follows [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) closely, and the chat called it "the scale standout" of the 2025 open landscape.

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Moonshot AI |
| Released | July 2025 |
| Total / active parameters | ~1T / 32B |
| Routed experts | 384 |
| Active experts per token | 8 routed + 1 shared |
| Shared expert | Yes |
| Attention | [Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)](#c/mla) |

Compared with DeepSeek-V3 (256 experts, 671B total, 37B active), K2 adds more experts and more total capacity while cutting active parameters slightly. That is the MoE bet in its purest form: grow knowledge capacity, keep per-token cost flat.

## Design lineage

K2 shows how quickly open-model techniques spread. It takes two defining DeepSeek choices:

- **[MLA](#c/mla)** compresses keys and values into a small cached latent, giving a much smaller [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) than the standard [GQA](#c/gqa) used by Llama 4 and Qwen3.
- **[Fine-grained + shared experts](#c/fine-grained)**: many small routed experts plus an always-on [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c). [Qwen3](#c/qwen3) dropped the shared expert, but K2 kept it.

Moonshot's main training change was the optimizer. It trained K2 with **MuonClip**, a variant of the Muon optimizer with a mechanism to keep attention logits from blowing up. Moonshot presented this as the key to stable pre-training at trillion-parameter scale.

## Why it matters

K2 is the extreme data point on the sparsity axis. It shows that a model can be pushed to a trillion parameters while its per-token arithmetic stays comparable to models a third its size, which is exactly why [frontier size and serving cost came apart](#c/r-smaller). It was also positioned for agentic use (tool calling and multi-step tasks), the area where post-training was moving fastest in 2025–26.

## Trade-offs and limits

Extreme sparsity keeps compute cheap but not memory. All ~1T parameters must be held in accelerator memory to serve the model, which makes it expensive to host even though each token is cheap to compute. With 384 experts, all-to-all communication and load balancing are also harder when experts are spread across many GPUs.

## The Kimi Linear direction

Moonshot also released [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear), a much smaller 48B model that uses full attention (MLA) in only one of every four layers and a cheaper linear "Delta Attention" in the rest, with no positional encoding in its full-attention layers. The chat pointed to whether Moonshot adopts that approach for its next flagship (K3) as a decisive test of whether [linear attention](#c/linear-attn) works at production scale.

## From the chat

- The chat called K2 "the scale standout": 1T total, 32B active, 384 experts, pushing the sparsity ratio "further than almost anyone."
- It noted that K2 borrows MLA "from the DeepSeek lineage rather than using GQA" and keeps the shared expert.
- It warned that K2's specs came partly from comparison roundups, not a first-party report it could verify: "well-attested-but-secondhand."
- It raised the future K3 flagship as the test of whether Kimi Linear's hybrid attention reaches flagship scale.

concepts.title: Kimi Linear
concepts.summary: Linear attention in 3 of 4 layers, no positional encoding

attributes.notes: Linear attention in 3 of 4 layers, no positional encoding

concepts.overview: **Kimi Linear** (Moonshot AI, 2025) is a **48B-parameter** MoE model with about 3B active. It is Moonshot's test of [linear / hybrid attention](#c/linear-attn). Only **one in four layers** uses full attention, and those use [MLA](#c/mla). The other three use a linear "Delta Attention" (Kimi Delta Attention) whose cost grows linearly with sequence length and whose state doesn't grow the way a [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) does. Its full-attention blocks drop explicit positional encoding entirely ([NoPE](#c/nope)) and leave position to the linear layers, which helps when extending to very long contexts. It reports competitive quality at much higher throughput. It is still a mid-sized model, though, and whether the approach holds at flagship scale, for instance in Moonshot's next flagship after [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2), was flagged as one of the decisive open questions for linear attention.

concepts.title: GLM-4.5
concepts.overview: **GLM-4.5** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, July 2025) is a **355B-total, 32B-active** [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model and the direct predecessor of the [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) line. In MoE design it sided with DeepSeek: like [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) and [Kimi K2](#c/kimi-k2) it **kept a shared expert**, while [Qwen3 dropped it](#c/no-shared), which is why the chat cites it in the shared-expert debate. It was released as open weights and aimed at reasoning, coding and agentic use, the direction the whole GLM family has followed since. The family then moved fast: GLM-4.6 in September 2025, then 4.7, then GLM-5 in February 2026, which roughly doubled the size to 744B total and 40B active. The chat gives few further architectural details for GLM-4.5 itself.

concepts.title: GLM-5
concepts.summary: Imports DSA; 80 layers to cut expert-parallel traffic; 'slime' async RL; trained on Huawei Ascend

attributes.notes: Imports DSA; 80 layers to cut expert-parallel traffic; 'slime' async RL; trained on Huawei Ascend

concepts.overview: **GLM-5** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, February 2026) is an open-weight, MIT-licensed MoE flagship: **744B total, ~40B active**, with 256 experts and 8 active per token (about 5.9% sparsity), trained on 28.5T tokens and scaled up from GLM-4.5's 355B/32B. It takes [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa) wholesale from [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32), and its architecture is literally named `glm_moe_dsa`. It reduces depth to **80 layers** to cut expert-parallel communication. Its main novelty is post-training, an asynchronous RL system called **slime** that decouples generation from training for large-scale agentic RL. Reports say it was trained on about 100,000 Huawei Ascend chips with no Nvidia hardware, which was initially unconfirmed. It [self-reports](#c/vendor-claims) 77.8% on SWE-bench Verified, about 3 points behind Claude Opus 4.6. Context is 200K in, about 128K out.
concepts.article:
**GLM-5** is an open-weight [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) language model released by Zhipu AI (Z.ai) in February 2026. It is the flagship of a fast-moving family (GLM-4.5, 4.6, 4.7, then 5, 5-Turbo, [5.1](#c/glm-51) and [5.2](#c/glm-52)), and it is the one with a real technical report. Its construction shows two trends of the period clearly: architecture techniques spreading quickly between labs, and the most novel engineering moving from the transformer to the post-training pipeline.

## Architecture

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Developer | Zhipu AI (Z.ai) |
| Released | February 2026 |
| Total / active parameters | 744B / ~40B |
| Experts | 256, 8 active per token (~5.9% sparsity) |
| Layers | 80 |
| Attention | [DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)](#c/dsa) |
| Pre-training data | 28.5T tokens |
| Context | 200K input, up to ~128K output |
| License | MIT, open weights |

It grew from [GLM-4.5](#c/glm-45)'s 355B total and 32B active, roughly doubling total parameters while adding only about 8B active.

## Importing DeepSeek Sparse Attention

GLM-5 did not build its own long-context mechanism. It adopted [DSA](#c/dsa), introduced months earlier in [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32), and its architecture identifier, `glm_moe_dsa`, says so openly. DSA uses a cheap "lightning indexer" to score earlier tokens and runs attention only over the most relevant ones, bringing attention cost down from quadratic toward linear in sequence length. The report presents DSA as what made scaling to 744B parameters and 28.5T tokens affordable. Coverage compared the adoption to how models took up [RoPE](#c/rope) once it was published.

## Depth traded for communication

GLM-5 uses 256 experts but cuts its layer count to 80 in order to **reduce expert-parallelism communication**. In a large MoE, experts sit on different GPUs and every MoE layer sends tokens across the network to reach them. Fewer layers mean fewer of these exchanges. It is a concrete case of the depth–width–expert-count trade-off being settled partly by serving and systems constraints, not by model quality alone.

## Post-training: slime

As the chat put it, "the post-training story is the headline, not the architecture." GLM-5's main engineering contribution is **slime**, an asynchronous RL infrastructure. Standard RL for LLMs runs generate, score and update steps one after another, so at 744B scale GPUs sit idle in one phase while another runs. Slime separates generation from training so both run continuously. It is aimed at **agentic** training: runs reportedly produce 3,000–6,000 messages (about 60–100M output tokens) to train long-range planning and tool use. It builds on the [RLVR](#c/rlvr) wave, extended to long-horizon agent trajectories where rewards are harder to define.

## Hardware

Several sources report that GLM-5 was trained on about **100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B** chips using the MindSpore framework, with no Nvidia hardware. That is significant given Zhipu's placement on the US Entity List. One careful source noted the training hardware was not officially confirmed at first, so the claim is plausible and widely repeated but should be treated with some caution.

## Benchmarks and caveats

Zhipu reported **77.8% on SWE-bench Verified**, 62% on BrowseComp, first place on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and reduced hallucination. More balanced coverage put it about 3 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 on SWE-bench Verified and about 9 points behind on Terminal-Bench 2.0: competitive with the closed frontier on agentic coding, and leading among open models, but not on top. These are mostly self-reported [vendor claims](#c/vendor-claims), and independent verification was still pending.

## From the chat

- The chat anchored on GLM-5 over newer versions because it has "a real technical report (the arXiv source)". Details for 5.1 and later came only from thin secondary sources.
- It called the DSA adoption "the clearest illustration of the 'techniques diffuse fast' point": one lab's late-2025 innovation became a second flagship's backbone within months.
- It highlighted the 80-layer choice as a "real systems-level architecture decision" driven by expert-parallel communication cost.
- It trusted the report's construction facts (744B/40B, 256 experts top-8, DSA, 80 layers, slime, 28.5T tokens) but wanted independent confirmation of the hardware claims and benchmark comparisons.

concepts.title: GLM-5.1
concepts.summary: Claims 94.6% of Claude Opus 4.6's coding score (self-reported)

attributes.notes: Claims 94.6% of Claude Opus 4.6's coding score (self-reported)

concepts.overview: **GLM-5.1** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, late March 2026) is an incremental update on the [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) base. By the available accounts it keeps the same shape: a **744B-total, ~40B-active** [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) with 256 experts, 8 active per token, and [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa). Its headline claim is that it scores **94.6% of Claude Opus 4.6's coding score**. That figure is self-reported and not independently verified, and the chat found it only in a single SEO-oriented blog that itself flagged the numbers as unverified [vendor claims](#c/vendor-claims). It arrived alongside GLM-5-Turbo during a period when the GLM family was releasing new versions every few weeks. It was later followed by [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52), which added a 1M-token context. Beyond these points the chat had little verified detail on what changed from GLM-5 to 5.1.

concepts.title: GLM-5.2
concepts.summary: High/Max reasoning presets; benchmark claims disputed

attributes.notes: High/Max reasoning presets; benchmark claims disputed

concepts.overview: **GLM-5.2** (Zhipu AI / Z.ai, released June 13, 2026) adds a **1-million-token context** over [GLM-5.1](#c/glm-51), about 5× the GLM-5 line's 200K, with up to 131,072 output tokens. It also adds two reasoning-effort presets, **High** and **Max**, with Max recommended for coding. It launched on every GLM Coding Plan tier, with MIT-licensed open weights to follow. Coverage contradicts itself. [Early reports (June 13–15)](#c/glm52-early) said no benchmarks were published at all. [Later reports (June 16–17)](#c/glm52-late) claimed it [beats GPT-5.5 on long-horizon coding](#c/c-glm52) at one-sixth the cost, and even that it beat Claude Fable 5 in blind tests. Treat these as unverified vendor claims. Parameter count is reported as 753B, against 744B for 5.1, which could be a real change or loose reporting. With no technical report, how the 1M context was achieved is unknown.

concepts.title: SmolLM3
concepts.overview: **SmolLM3** (Hugging Face, 2025) is a small, fully open **3B-parameter dense** model. It appears in this landscape for its attention design, not its size. It uses [Grouped-Query Attention](#c/gqa) with **periodic [NoPE](#c/nope) layers**: roughly every fourth layer drops rotary positional encoding and relies on the causal mask alone to convey token order, while the other layers keep [RoPE](#c/rope). The aim is better behaviour when extending to long contexts, since layers without explicit positions don't hit unfamiliar position values past the training length. Hugging Face also published its training recipe in unusual detail. The chat mentions it only briefly, as a small-model example of NoPE alongside [Kimi Linear](#c/kimi-linear), and notes that removing positional encoding had not yet become standard in any major flagship.

concepts.title: Jamba
concepts.summary: Largest Mamba hybrid family
concepts.overview: Jamba is AI21's family of [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids), first released in March 2024 and the largest Mamba-based hybrid family in the literature, scaling up to 398B total parameters. About 7/8 of its layers are [Mamba](#c/mamba) blocks and the rest are attention, and it also uses [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe). Its ablations produced a notably specific design rule. More attention (up to 1:1) raised benchmark quality but cut throughput, and a ratio of about one attention layer per five to seven Mamba layers sat on the Pareto frontier. Published scores put it roughly level with Mixtral and Llama-2 70B on common-sense and reading tasks. It shows known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code. A 2026 [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper) found that the 52B Jamba-1.7-Mini collapsed under hidden-state-poisoning triggers that did not affect pure transformers.

concepts.title: Nemotron-H
concepts.summary: Swapped most attention for Mamba for throughput

attributes.notes: Swapped most attention for Mamba for throughput

concepts.overview: Nemotron-H is NVIDIA's hybrid model family. It replaced most of a transformer's attention layers with [Mamba](#c/mamba) (Mamba-2) blocks, explicitly to raise inference throughput, and kept a few attention layers for precise recall, the standard [hybrid](#c/hybrids) recipe. The base models come in 8B and 56B sizes, and NVIDIA took them through real post-training to strong instruction-following and long-context results rather than stopping at base-model benchmarks. NVIDIA describes the family as showing that hybrids can be state-of-the-art in capability while offering faster inference. The chat flagged that as a vendor claim, favourably selected. A 2026 [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper) reported that the hidden-state-poisoning weakness it found in Mamba hybrids extends to Mamba-2-based models like Nemotron. That single early result doesn't show up in capability benchmarks.

concepts.title: Granite 4.0
concepts.summary: H-Small beat open models 12× its size on IFEval

attributes.notes: H-Small beat open models 12× its size on IFEval

concepts.overview: Granite 4.0 is IBM's late-2025 enterprise model family built on a Mamba–attention [hybrid](#c/hybrids). The chat called it the most telling hybrid data point because it makes a size-efficiency claim, which is the whole point of the architecture. IBM reports that Granite-4.0-H-Small outperformed every open-weight model on Stanford HELM's IFEval instruction-following benchmark except Llama 4 Maverick, a 402B model more than twelve times its size. IBM also reports that it keeps pace with much larger models on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v3. Its defining practical feature is much lower GPU memory use than comparable transformers, the payoff of the fixed-size [Mamba](#c/mamba) state. Caveat: these are vendor-reported results on domains (instruction following, tool calling) where the model looks especially good, so they support [Hybrids match transformers at large scale](#c/c-hybrid-parity) without settling it.

concepts.title: Mercury Coder
concepts.summary: First commercial dLLM: ~1,100 tokens/s on H100

attributes.notes: First commercial dLLM: ~1,100 tokens/s on H100

concepts.overview: Mercury Coder, from Inception Labs, launched in February 2025 as the first commercially available [diffusion language model](#c/diffusion-lm). Instead of emitting code one token at a time, it refines blocks of tokens in parallel. Inception reports Mercury Coder Mini at about 1,109 tokens/s and Mercury Coder Small at 737 tokens/s on H100s, 5–10× faster than comparable autoregressive models, with coding quality on par. Mercury Coder Mini (1.3B) is open under Apache 2.0. The follow-up Mercury 2 (February 2026) is reasoning-capable. Inception reports 1,009 tokens/s on one Blackwell GPU, 91.1 on AIME 2025 and 67.3 on LiveCodeBench. The chat highlighted Mercury's pitch that long chains of thought become cheap when filled in parallel. All of these figures are vendor-reported and partly postdate the model's knowledge cutoff. See [the parity claim](#c/c-diffusion-parity).

concepts.title: Gemini Diffusion
concepts.summary: ~1,479 tokens/s, coding parity with 2.0 Flash Lite

attributes.notes: ~1,479 tokens/s, coding parity with 2.0 Flash Lite

concepts.overview: Gemini Diffusion is Google's experimental [diffusion language model](#c/diffusion-lm), announced at Google I/O in May 2025. It generates about 1,479 tokens per second, roughly 5× faster than Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite. On coding benchmarks Google reports near-parity with that autoregressive sibling: HumanEval 89.6% vs 90.2%, and MBPP 76.0% vs 75.8%. The chat called this "the single most important data point" for diffusion LMs, because it is a like-for-like comparison inside one lab. It also marks a frontier lab taking the paradigm seriously. Caveats: the numbers are Google's own, the parity is shown on coding, a structured domain, and the comparison is to a small, fast model rather than a frontier one. It is key evidence for, but not proof of, the contested [parity claim](#c/c-diffusion-parity). Compare [Mercury Coder](#c/mercury).

concepts.title: Epoch AI
concepts.summary: Trend data from disclosures and prices; the most neutral source in the chat
concepts.overview: Epoch AI is an independent research organization that tracks AI trends such as compute, model size, training runs and inference prices, using public disclosures, revenue data and published prices. The chat relied on it more than any other source and called it one of "the most neutral". It is not selling chips, real estate or models. Its figures in the chat: AI chip compute stock growing **3.4×/year** ([e-stock](#c/e-stock)), frontier training compute **5×/year** ([e-train](#c/e-train)), pre-training efficiency **~3×/year** ([e-pretrain-eff](#c/e-pretrain-eff)), inference price at fixed capability falling **9–900×/year** ([e-price-all](#c/e-price-all)), and the parameter-count history, including the post-GPT-4 shrink. Its limits, which it flags itself: price trends built from current list prices are inflated by frozen proprietary prices, the fastest rates are recent and may not last, and closed-model parameter counts are estimates. See [the ~100×/year claim](#c/c-100x).

concepts.title: Inference price-trend paper (arXiv 2511.23455)
concepts.summary: Controls for frozen list prices and competition
concepts.overview: The inference price-trend paper (arXiv **2511.23455**) is an academic study of how fast the price of reaching a given benchmark score falls, designed to control for the confounds in headline figures. The chat drew on it (partly through an alphaXiv summary) for three results. First, frontier price-for-performance falls about **5–10× per year** once frozen list prices are accounted for ([e-price-frontier](#c/e-price-frontier)). Second, isolating algorithmic efficiency, by dividing out hardware price declines and controlling for competition using open models, gives **~3× per year** ([e-price-algo](#c/e-price-algo)). Third, declines are fastest at high capability: **31×/year** in the top GPQA-Diamond bin against **1.7×/year** in the bottom ([e-price-top](#c/e-price-top)). The authors suggest distillation or MoE may explain the gap. It therefore both [challenges the ~100×/year headline](#c/c-100x) and [supports faster declines at the frontier](#c/c-frontier-fastest).

concepts.title: Open-model price analysis (LessWrong)
concepts.summary: Open weights avoid proprietary list-price games
concepts.overview: This is a LessWrong analysis of how fast algorithmic progress lowers inference prices. Its key methodological move is to use **open-weight models**. Proprietary developers "tend not to change the inference price of older models," so their frozen list prices sit next to cheap new models and inflate apparent declines. Open weights are served by many competing hosts, which avoids those list-price games. The analysis finds open-model prices at fixed capability falling a fairly steady **7–28× per year, geometric mean ~11.8×** ([e-price-open](#c/e-price-open)), and fairly **uniform across quality levels**. It therefore [challenges the ~100×/year headline](#c/c-100x) and complicates the claim that [declines are fastest at the frontier](#c/c-frontier-fastest). The same piece also notes that across studies prices dropped more for top models. It is a blog-hosted analysis, not peer-reviewed; the chat treats it as a clean independent read.

concepts.title: Nvidia / Jensen Huang
concepts.summary: Sells the chips: '$1 trillion in demand… we are going to be short'
concepts.overview: Nvidia, and its CEO Jensen Huang, is the dominant seller of AI accelerators, taking the overwhelming majority of accelerator spend. That makes it both an essential source and an **interested party**. The chat drew several things from Nvidia. There were its audited results: record fiscal Q3 2026 data-center revenue of $51.2B, with [Blackwell sold out](#c/blackwell). There was its GTC framing that computing demand grew ~**1,000,000× in two years** ([e-demand](#c/e-demand)), made up of ~10,000× per request and ~100× usage. And there were Huang's escalating forecasts, from $500B of high-confidence demand through 2026 to at least **$1 trillion through 2027**, along with "we are going to be short." The chat called the trillion-dollar figures "the most interest-conflicted" in the discussion, noting that Nvidia sells the chips, while accepting that the direction is corroborated elsewhere. It [supports](#c/c-squeeze) the view that frontier scarcity lasts into 2027–28.

concepts.title: SemiAnalysis
concepts.summary: Memory share of spend; chips as the binding constraint
concepts.overview: SemiAnalysis is a semiconductor and AI-infrastructure research firm whose estimates get re-reported widely. In the chat it is the source for the claim that **memory could be ~30% of hyperscaler AI spending in 2026, up from ~8% in 2023–24** ([e-hbm](#c/e-hbm)), and, in the chat's words, for "a SemiAnalysis-type read" that chip production became "a binding constraint on the pace of the AI compute buildout" in late 2025 and early 2026. This graph also attributes the **+36% 2026 capex** figure to it ([e-capex](#c/e-capex)). The chat itself quoted that figure from secondary coverage based on company guidance. The chat classes SemiAnalysis with McKinsey and Bloomberg Intelligence as the few analyst shops behind many widely echoed numbers. Its percentages are therefore "directional analyst estimates, not hard facts," and repeated citations shouldn't be counted as independent confirmation. See [HBM supply](#c/hbm-supply).

concepts.title: McKinsey
concepts.summary: ~70 → ~220 GW of data-center supply in five years
concepts.overview: McKinsey is a management consultancy whose data-center projections the chat called "the one to anchor on" for the longer horizon. Its figure is that global data-center supply could grow from about **70 GW today to about 220 GW within five years**, with around **75% of the growth driven by AI** ([Data centers: ~70 → ~220 GW](#c/dc-growth), [e-dc](#c/e-dc)). That is roughly a tripling, or about 26% a year compounded. It is a capacity forecast, not a measurement, and it doesn't account explicitly for the [slips](#c/slip) already pushing 2026 projects into 2028. The chat groups McKinsey with SemiAnalysis and Bloomberg Intelligence as analyst shops whose numbers get echoed across many outlets. It is less interested than a chipmaker, but its percentages are still best read as directional. [JLL](#c/jll)'s ~14% CAGR is a more conservative comparison point.

concepts.title: JLL
concepts.summary: Real-estate outlook: inference overtakes training in 2027
concepts.overview: JLL is a commercial real-estate firm whose data-center outlook supplied the chat's view of the long-run workload mix. By its estimates, AI was about a quarter of data-center workloads in 2025, mostly training. [Inference overtakes training in 2027](#c/inference-shift), and AI could be half of all workloads by 2030. It also expects nearly 100 GW of new capacity between 2026 and 2030, the sector growing at a **~14% CAGR** ([e-dc-jll](#c/e-dc-jll)), and a buildout needing up to $3 trillion by 2030. The chat classes JLL as having a position, since real-estate analysts benefit from the buildout. JLL does name a real fragility in its own bull case: the inference supercycle depends on inference applications that "don't yet exist at scale." Its growth rate is noticeably lower than [McKinsey](#c/mckinsey)'s.

concepts.title: Accuris / Tech Insider
concepts.summary: Slips, cancellations, transformer lead times
concepts.overview: Accuris (an electronics-component supply-chain analysis firm) and Tech Insider (a trade publication) are the chat's main sources on the physical side of the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity). Accuris reported that **30–50% of planned 2026 AI data-center capacity is projected to slip to 2028** because of interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks ([slip](#c/slip)). It also reported that HBM now uses ~23% of DRAM wafer capacity, and that the spending is "funded, contracted, and under construction." Tech Insider reported transformer lead times stretching from 12–18 to **36–48 months**, gave a starker estimate that ~50% of planned US 2026 data centers could be delayed or cancelled, and placed the shift to electrical gear as the bottleneck around May 2026. These are analyst and trade sources, and they [support](#c/c-squeeze) the view that frontier scarcity lasts into 2027–28. The chat found them useful because they describe hard physical lead times, not demand projections.

concepts.title: Stanford teaching model
concepts.summary: Supply/demand scenarios — explicitly a toy, not a forecast
concepts.overview: The Stanford teaching model is a course page (Stanford MSE 435) that sets out supply-and-demand scenarios for AI compute. It **explicitly calls itself a pedagogical toy, not a forecast**, and the chat cited it only "for the framework, not predictions." Its scenarios: through 2025–26, TSMC expands capacity while data-center power struggles to keep up. If demand growth slows to ~100% a year, supply might catch up and the gap close (the "AI winter" case, where investment returns get harder). An energy breakthrough would move the bottleneck to memory bandwidth. If everything improves equally, no single chokepoint remains and margins compress across the stack. Because it sketches a way supply could catch up, it serves as a [counterpoint](#c/c-squeeze) to the view that scarcity lasts until 2027–28. It is academic and has no commercial stake. See [capacity constraint](#c/capacity).

concepts.title: RLVR coverage study
concepts.summary: RL raises the odds of correct samples but narrows what's solvable
concepts.overview: This is an academic study that tested reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) across algorithms including PPO and [GRPO](#c/grpo). Its deflating finding: RLVR **increases the likelihood of correct samples but decreases coverage of solvable problems**. It makes a model better at producing high-reward answers it could already produce, but doesn't give it abilities beyond the base model's reach. It contrasts this with [distillation](#c/distillation), which can transfer genuinely new reasoning patterns from a stronger teacher, and it notes that current RLVR algorithms perform similarly to one another and remain far from optimal. It [challenges](#c/c-rlvr-new) the claim that RLVR creates new reasoning ability. The chat later cautioned that it is one paper's framing, and that it doesn't measure how much of any model's reasoning came from distillation.

concepts.title: Tülu 3 (Ai2)
concepts.summary: The rare fully open post-training recipe
concepts.overview: Tülu 3, from the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), is the rare project that open-sourced an *entire* post-training recipe: model weights, datasets, a data-curation and evaluation toolkit, training code and a reproduction guide. Its 405B version competes with GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku and DeepSeek-V3, so the chat treats it as a frontier-relevant view into what closed labs do. Its most cited disclosure is that all of its new **synthetic SFT datasets contain responses written by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet** (the latter for coding), because those gave the best responses. That makes it direct evidence that [distillation from closed models](#c/c-distill-open) is part of open post-training, at least for SFT data. It is an independent, fully transparent source. See [synthetic SFT responses](#c/synthetic-sft) and [post-training](#c/post-training).

concepts.title: DCLM benchmark
concepts.summary: Fixed model, only the data curation varies
concepts.overview: DCLM (DataComp for Language Models) is a benchmark in which the model architecture and training setup are **held fixed and only the data-curation strategy varies**. It turns data selection into a competition over which curation method gives the best model for the same compute. The chat argued that the benchmark's very existence shows where the field's attention has moved: "You don't build a whole competitive testbed around a variable unless it's where the action is." Its headline result is that **DCLM-Baseline beat the prior open-data state of the art by ~6 MMLU points while using half the compute**, which [supports](#c/c-data-lever) the claim that data curation is the biggest lever. DCLM-Baseline also illustrates heavy [deduplication](#c/dedup) and [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter). It is an academic source, and its evidence is controlled by design.

concepts.title: Vision-language specialist study
concepts.summary: Specialists beat the all-task model on 5 of 7 tasks
concepts.overview: This is a vision-language instruction-tuning study the chat cited as direct evidence that specialists can beat a generalist on their own tasks. The researchers split the training data by task and compared one model tuned on everything against task experts tuned only on their relevant subsets. **On 5 of 7 downstream tasks, the all-data model was outperformed by the task expert.** The chat paired it with an expert-LM paper that explains the mechanism, negative task transfer, and reports a +10.4% mean accuracy gain from selecting relevant experts at inference. It [supports](#c/c-specialists) the specialist claim. The chat's caveats: this evidence comes mostly from SFT and smaller-scale or vision-language settings, very large models seem to absorb diverse tasks with less interference, and one careful study is not established law. See [Specialize, then merge](#c/merging).

concepts.title: Hybrid robustness paper (2026)
concepts.summary: Mamba components carry a new robustness weakness
concepts.overview: This is a 2026 security paper finding that Mamba–Transformer [hybrids](#c/hybrids) inherit a new **robustness vulnerability** from their [Mamba](#c/mamba) components. Under certain hidden-state-poisoning triggers, even the 52B Jamba-1.7-Mini hybrid collapses on a robustness benchmark while pure Transformers do not, and the weakness extends to Mamba-2-based hybrids such as [Nemotron-H](#c/nemotron-h). It [challenges](#c/c-hybrid-parity) the claim that hybrids match transformers at large scale. Quality parity on capability benchmarks doesn't rule out trade-offs those benchmarks can't see. The chat asked readers to hold it loosely: "early research, one paper, on a specific attack class", something "to watch rather than a settled verdict." It is an academic source with no evident commercial stake.

concepts.title: 'No Free Lunch' dLLM survey (2026)
concepts.summary: Diffusion speedups vs autoregressive, compared carefully
concepts.overview: This is a May 2026 survey titled "A Comparative Survey of Inference Acceleration for DLLMs against AR-LLMs: No Free Lunch." It compares the speed-ups claimed for [diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm) against autoregressive models under careful conditions. The chat hadn't read it in depth, and said the title alone signals its thesis: the parallel-generation speed advantage isn't free, and the quality/speed/compute triangle has costs that headline tokens-per-second figures obscure. It therefore [challenges](#c/c-diffusion-parity) the claim that diffusion LMs match autoregressive quality at 5–10× the speed, most of whose support comes from vendors' own benchmarks. The chat called it "probably the most intellectually honest next stop" and "the corrective to all the vendor benchmarks." The paper postdated the chat's knowledge, so it was relaying the source, not confirming it.

concepts.title: Vendor announcements
concepts.summary: Benchmarks published by the model's own developer
concepts.overview: Vendor announcements are benchmark results and capability claims published by a model's own developer, such as launch posts, technical reports and marketing. The chat treated them as **self-reported**: often real, but not independently verified. Examples in the chat include NVIDIA's framing that [Nemotron-H](#c/nemotron-h) hybrids are state-of-the-art with faster inference, Meta's results for BLT and LCM ("matches Llama 3", partly at 8B scale), and Gemini Diffusion's and Mercury's coding benchmarks. They [support](#c/c-hybrid-parity) the claim that hybrids match transformers at scale, but the chat wanted independent replication before accepting general parity. Its pattern for weighing them: note the scale tested, the domains covered (often just coding and math) and who ran the evaluation, and compare against independent critiques such as the [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper).

concepts.title: GLM-5.2 launch coverage (June 13–15)
concepts.summary: No official benchmark numbers at release
concepts.overview: This is the first wave of reporting on Zhipu's (Z.ai's) [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52), written **June 13–15, 2026** around its release. It was emphatic that Zhipu published **no official benchmark scores** at launch: no SWE-bench Verified, no LiveCodeBench, no HumanEval. One outlet called this unusual for a release of that scale and said the numbers "should be treated as marketing promises until independent verification arrives." It did confirm concrete additions: a one-million-token context (about 5× the GLM-5 line's 200K), High and Max reasoning-effort modes, and rollout across all GLM Coding Plan tiers with MIT-licensed open weights to follow. It [challenges](#c/c-glm52) the later claim that GLM-5.2 beats GPT-5.5 on long-horizon coding. It is analyst and press coverage, and the chat judged it the more careful wave.

concepts.title: GLM-5.2 later coverage (June 16–17)
concepts.summary: Suddenly claims wins over GPT-5.5, sourcing unclear
concepts.overview: This is the second wave of [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52) coverage, from **June 16–17, 2026**, which suddenly carried strong benchmark claims. It described GLM-5.2 as a 753-billion-parameter open-weights model that **beats GPT-5.5 on multiple long-horizon coding benchmarks at one-sixth the cost**. One outlet added that it scored above Claude Opus 4.7 and, in some human blind tests, outperformed Claude Fable 5. It [supports](#c/c-glm52) the GLM-5.2 coding claim, but the chat was skeptical. The claims appear only in the newest, partly aggregated coverage. They contradict the "no benchmarks at launch" reporting from two days earlier ([early coverage](#c/glm52-early)). They read like vendor launch framing. And the chat couldn't verify the comparison models. It treated the blind-test claim as "unverified marketing" pending independent evaluation.

concepts.title: Inference cost at fixed capability falls ~100×/year
concepts.overview: **Claim:** the cost of reaching a *fixed* level of LLM capability falls about 100× per year, halving roughly every two months. The source is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch), measuring the cheapest model that clears a given benchmark bar across all models at their current list prices. The spread is wide: 9× to 900× per year depending on the milestone, with the fastest drops in the most recent year. Two independent analyses push back. The [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper) controls for confounds and finds 5–10× per year for frontier price-for-performance, and only about 3× per year from algorithmic efficiency alone. The [LessWrong open-model analysis](#c/open-price) argues that proprietary vendors rarely cut old models' list prices, which inflates the all-models figure. Open-weight models show a cleaner 7–28× per year. **Status: contested.** A steep decline is real, but ~100× is the upper, confounded end; 5–12× is the more defensible "real" figure. See [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability).

concepts.title: Price declines are fastest at the capability frontier
concepts.overview: **Claim:** inference prices fall fastest for the most capable models and slowest at the low end. The main evidence is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper): models in the top GPQA-Diamond bin fell 31× per year, against 1.7× per year for the bottom bin. Its authors suggest different mechanisms at the top, such as heavier use of [distillation](#c/distillation) and MoE. The explanation is headroom. A newly reached high bar is at first cleared only by one expensive model, so the first cheap match is a huge multiplier. Old low bars have already had their cost wrung out. The main counterweight is the [open-model analysis](#c/open-price), which finds open-weight prices falling fairly uniformly (7–28× per year) across quality levels, and notes that proprietary list-price quirks can distort the picture. Epoch also cautions that the steepest recent rates may not persist. **Status: emerging.** It is also the correction to the intuition that [higher bars take longer to catch](#c/m-harder).

concepts.title: Frontier capacity stays scarce until ~2027–28
concepts.overview: **Claim:** frontier inference capacity stays scarce, and priced or rationed accordingly, until roughly 2027–28. Support comes from the supply side. [Nvidia](#c/nvidia)'s Jensen Huang sees at least $1 trillion of demand through 2027 and says "we are going to be short," though he sells the chips. [Accuris](#c/accuris) and Tech Insider report HBM sold out for 2026, high-voltage transformer lead times of 36–48 months, and 30–50% of planned 2026 data-center capacity slipping to 2028. The counter is conditional, not contrary. The [Stanford teaching model](#c/stanford-toy), explicitly a pedagogical toy, shows that if demand growth slows to about 100% per year, supply catches up and the gap closes. Claude's own read, flagged as reasoning rather than reporting: premium capacity eases around 2027–28 only if frontier demand decelerates. If reasoning and agentic demand keeps compounding, the squeeze could last longer. **Status: contested** — a forecast, not a measurement. See [Capacity constraint](#c/capacity).

concepts.title: Sustained cost declines come mostly from incremental work
concepts.overview: **Claim:** the large, sustained declines in AI cost come mostly from accumulated incremental engineering, punctuated by occasional big ideas that open new room for that grind. The chat's main example is [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe). The idea dates to 1991 and sparse gating to 2017, but almost none of its value arrived then. It came from a decade of fixes: [load-balancing losses](#c/lb-loss), expert-capacity limits, top-1 routing, routing stability, shared experts and systems work for sharding. The second argument is the shape of the curve. [Algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress) improves on a smooth ~3× per year exponential, not a staircase, which is what you'd expect from many small wins. Claude flagged this as its own synthesis, not a claim Epoch makes. Looking forward, it could flip if a paradigm shift such as test-time compute dominates the next phase. **Status: emerging.** Breakthroughs reset the ceiling; incremental work delivers the savings.

concepts.title: Recent architecture wins are efficiency; quality came from post-training
concepts.overview: **Claim:** the notable architecture innovations of recent years mostly buy efficiency, meaning the same quality at lower cost, while the big 2025 quality jumps came from post-training with RL and test-time compute. The cleanest evidence is [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/deepseek-v32). Its only architectural change from V3.1-Terminus was [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/dsa), whose stated goal was to *minimize degradation*, not gain quality. DeepSeek held the recipe fixed and measured parity, with roughly 2–3× faster long-text processing. The capability jump to GPT-5-comparable results came instead from a scalable RL framework and scaled-up [post-training](#c/post-training). The same sorting applies to MLA, GQA, KV quantization, FlashAttention and YaRN: all are engineered to preserve quality while cutting cost. [MoE](#c/moe) sits in between, buying quality per unit of inference cost. [GLM-5](#c/glm-5) fits the pattern: DSA imported for efficiency, with RL infrastructure as the headline. **Status: emerging.** The GPT-5 comparisons are DeepSeek's own.

concepts.title: RLVR creates genuinely new reasoning ability
concepts.overview: **Claim:** reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards ([RLVR](#c/rlvr)) gives models genuinely new reasoning ability, not just better use of what the base model could already do. The strongest evidence for it is [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1). RL on a base model produced an "aha moment" in which self-reflection, backtracking and long chains of thought emerged without being taught, and many groups report similar emergence. Against it, a careful [coverage study](#c/rlvr-study) across PPO, [GRPO](#c/grpo) and others found that RLVR raises the probability of correct samples but *narrows* the set of problems the model can solve at all. It sharpens sampling toward answers the base model could already produce, while [distillation](#c/distillation) can transfer genuinely new patterns. The same study found current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and remain far from optimal. **Status: contested.** The chat's read is that the truth is probably in between, and it depends on what counts as "new" and on how capable the base model already was.

concepts.title: Distillation from closed models drives open reasoning gains
concepts.overview: **Claim:** a meaningful share of open models' reasoning gains comes from [distilling](#c/distillation) closed frontier models, meaning training on their outputs. Parts of this are well documented. Distillation from closed models works (TinyGSM trained a 125M model to 63.1% on grade-school math using GPT-3.5 data), and it was pervasive in the 2023–24 open wave: Alpaca, Open Orca, ShareGPT. [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3), the best-documented open post-training recipe, generated its synthetic SFT responses with GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The *reasoning*-specific version is weaker. [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1) got its reasoning from [RLVR](#c/rlvr) on its own base model and then distilled that into smaller siblings. No reliable figure for "what share is distillation" exists, because labs don't disclose post-training data and using competitor outputs often breaks terms of service. **Status: contested.** It is plausible and certainly true for chat behaviour, but unmeasured for headline reasoning gains. See [the retraction](#c/r-distill).

concepts.title: Specialists beat a generalist on their own turf
concepts.overview: **Claim:** a model post-trained only on one domain's data beats a generalist trained on everything, on that domain. It is a real, named effect: *negative transfer* or *task interference*. A [vision-language study](#c/vl-study) found that task experts trained on the relevant subset beat the all-data model on 5 of 7 tasks. An expert-LM paper reported +10.4% mean accuracy from picking task experts over a multi-task baseline. Labs' practice points the same way: several open reasoning models [specialize, then merge](#c/merging) by weight-averaging. Positive transfer pushes the other way. Math training improved coding, data-poor tasks free-ride on data-rich ones, and one study found transfer is asymmetric: code and math are "safe donors," factuality is an "intrusive" one. Most specialist-wins evidence is from SFT and smaller or vision-language settings, and very large models seem to absorb diverse tasks with less interference. **Status: contested.** It likely holds more for small models and narrow budgets.

concepts.title: Data curation is the biggest lever
concepts.overview: **Claim:** data curation (sourcing, cleaning, [deduplication](#c/dedup), [model-based quality filtering](#c/quality-filter), mixing, [decontamination](#c/decontamination)) is the single biggest lever on model quality, and probably the largest share of effort. The key evidence is the [DCLM benchmark](#c/dclm). It holds architecture and training fixed, varies only the curation, and found that keeping just the top ~10% of Common Crawl by a small classifier let a 7B model reach 64% MMLU on 2.6T tokens, beating the prior open-data best by about 6 MMLU points at half the compute. That field-wide benchmarks now compete on curation is itself a signal. Post-training reports (Motif, [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3)) name dataset construction as the hardest part, and teams reuse existing mixtures rather than build their own. Against it: no rigorous effort-share figure exists ("80% is data" is folklore), and the evidence is from open-data projects, not closed flagships. **Status: emerging.**

concepts.title: Hybrids match transformers at large scale
concepts.overview: **Claim:** [Mamba–Transformer hybrids](#c/hybrids) match pure transformers' quality at large scale, with better efficiency. For it: [Jamba](#c/jamba) scales to 398B and is competitive on standard and long-context benchmarks. [Granite 4.0](#c/granite-4)'s H-Small beat every open model on IFEval except one twelve times its size. Nemotron-H is described as state-of-the-art with faster inference. Much of this is [vendor-reported](#c/vendor-claims) on favourable benchmarks. Against it: Jamba shows known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code, so parity is average rather than uniform. A 2026 [robustness paper](#c/robustness-paper) found that hybrids collapse under hidden-state-poisoning triggers that don't affect pure transformers, one early paper on one attack class. No hybrid leads the overall frontier, which remains transformer-based as far as is known. **Status: emerging.** It is a Pareto win (comparable quality, less memory, more speed), not yet a strict capability tie everywhere.

concepts.title: Diffusion LMs match autoregressive quality at 5–10× speed
concepts.overview: **Claim:** [diffusion language models](#c/diffusion-lm) reach the quality of autoregressive models while generating 5–10× faster. For it: [Gemini Diffusion](#c/gemini-diffusion) roughly matches Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite on code (HumanEval 89.6% vs 90.2%, MBPP 76.0% vs 75.8%) at about 5× the speed. [Mercury Coder](#c/mercury) reports coding parity at 5–10× the throughput of comparable AR models, and Mercury 2 posts strong AIME and LiveCodeBench scores. All of these numbers are the vendors' own, and all are in code and maths, structured domains. Against it: the May 2026 ["No Free Lunch" survey](#c/no-free-lunch) compares dLLM inference acceleration with AR models under controlled conditions and finds that the speedups come with trade-offs the headline tokens/s hide. Structural issues remain around variable-length output and KV-caching. No dLLM claims to be the best model overall. **Status: contested.** The claim holds for coding on vendor benchmarks, and general parity is unproven.

concepts.title: GLM-5.2 beats GPT-5.5 on long-horizon coding
concepts.overview: **Claim:** Zhipu's [GLM-5.2](#c/glm-52), released June 13, 2026, beats GPT-5.5 on several long-horizon coding benchmarks at about one-sixth the cost. The evidence conflicts across time. [Launch coverage from June 13–15](#c/glm52-early) says no official scores were published at release, with no SWE-bench Verified, LiveCodeBench or HumanEval, and treats the numbers as marketing promises. [Later coverage from June 16–17](#c/glm52-late) carries strong claims: 753B open weights beating GPT-5.5, and even outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 and, in some blind tests, Claude Fable 5. That wave appeared only in aggregated coverage and contradicts the earlier reports. Its sourcing is unclear and vendor-flavoured, and it landed during a charged moment tied to US restrictions on American models abroad. There is no technical report yet. What is confirmed about 5.2 is a 1M-token context and High/Max reasoning modes. **Status: contested.** Wait for independent evaluation.

concepts.title: Each layer predicts a token, and the guesses get blended
concepts.overview: **Myth:** every layer of a transformer guesses the next token, and the model blends those guesses. It is a natural picture. "Deep" suggests many parallel judgments, ensembles of voters are a familiar way to improve predictions, and interpretability tools like the logit lens *can* read rough early guesses from middle layers. In reality the layers form a sequential pipeline. Each layer transforms one vector per token and adds its adjustment to the [residual stream](#c/residual), and only after the last layer does the [output head](#c/output-head) turn that vector into a probability distribution. There is exactly one prediction. It is "an assembly line, not a panel of voters." Early exit and logit lens are diagnostic or optimization tricks, not how normal inference works. See [the correction](#c/r-layers).

concepts.title: Layers refine one vector in sequence; only the last one predicts
concepts.overview: In a standard [decoder-only transformer](#c/transformer), a token enters as an embedding vector and passes up the [layer stack](#c/layer-stack). Each layer applies attention, the only place tokens exchange information, then a feed-forward network that works on each token independently. Both are wrapped in residual connections, so each layer *adds an adjustment* to a running representation, the [residual stream](#c/residual), rather than replacing it. Early layers tend to capture local, surface patterns, and later ones more abstract, long-range structure. Only the final layer's output goes through the unembedding [output head](#c/output-head) to become a next-token distribution. Every layer also has its own independently learned query, key and value heads and its own FFN, which is why depth adds representational power rather than repetition. It is also why the [KV-cache](#c/kv-cache) is stored per layer.

concepts.title: The 100×/year means a given Sonnet gets 100× cheaper
concepts.overview: **Myth:** Epoch's "inference cost falls ~100× per year" means a specific model, say a particular Sonnet, gets 100× cheaper to run each year. It is an easy reading. The headline is phrased as "the cost of inference," and prices of named models do sometimes drop. But the metric fixes *capability*, not the model. It tracks the cheapest model that clears a given benchmark bar, and that model changes over time: a task that needed GPT-4-class compute in 2023 might be handled by something Haiku-sized later. See [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability). A frozen set of weights does get cheaper to serve, through [serving optimizations](#c/serving-opts) like batching, quantization and better kernels, and through [new hardware generations](#c/hardware-gens). That happens at a far more modest pace and in lumps. And the [price you pay](#c/price-vs-cost) is a business decision only loosely tied to either.

concepts.title: Higher capability bars take cheap models longer to catch
concepts.overview: **Myth:** as benchmark bars rise, it should take cheap models longer and longer to catch up, so cost declines should be slowest at the top. It sounds airtight, since harder capability seems harder to reproduce cheaply. The data shows the opposite. In the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper), the top GPQA-Diamond bin fell 31× per year and the bottom bin only 1.7×. See [Price declines are fastest at the capability frontier](#c/c-frontier-fastest). The reason is headroom. A newly reached bar is at first cleared only by one expensive model, so the first cheaper model to match it is a huge multiplier, often via [distillation](#c/distillation) or MoE. Old low bars have already had their cost wrung out. The user's instinct does survive in another form: the steepest drops are recent, and Epoch warns they may not persist.

concepts.title: claude-carbon's token cost is lossy
concepts.overview: **Myth:** the "lossy" caveat on the claude-carbon tool means its token *cost* figures are unreliable. That's a reasonable worry when a tracking tool warns about lossiness and you only care about dollars. But the caveat is about its carbon estimates. The token counts and dollar costs come straight from Claude Code's own JSONL transcripts, the same data that ccusage, the built-in `/cost` command and the status line read, so they are equally accurate across all of them. The lossy part is converting tokens into grams of CO₂. That relies on extrapolated per-model emission factors, counts cache reads at full rate, and assumes average grid carbon intensity, because Anthropic doesn't publish per-model energy data. See [the correction](#c/r-carbon). For [serving cost](#c/cost-per-token) and energy more broadly, only estimates exist.

concepts.title: Token cost is exact; only the CO₂ estimate is lossy
concepts.overview: For tracking what Claude Code sessions cost, the token counts and dollar figures are exact. Every tool reads the same local transcripts (`~/.claude` JSONL logs), so claude-carbon, ccusage (the standard answer, with per-day, per-session and per-project breakdowns and a live mode), the built-in `/cost` command and the status line all agree. On Pro/Max subscriptions `/cost` shows tokens but not dollars, since those plans aren't billed per token. What is genuinely lossy is claude-carbon's conversion of tokens into CO₂. It uses extrapolated emission factors for models without published data, counts cache reads at full rate, and assumes grid-average carbon intensity. That won't be "fixed," because Anthropic doesn't publish per-model energy data. Treat the carbon figure as order-of-magnitude. See [the misconception](#c/m-carbon) and, for why per-token [serving cost](#c/cost-per-token) is itself opaque, [Price ≠ serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost).

concepts.title: Experts are topic specialists (a 'chemistry expert')
concepts.overview: **Myth:** in a [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) model, each expert is a topic specialist. A chemistry question goes to the "chemistry expert," a coding question to the coding one. The name invites this, and it matches how human teams divide work. In reality an expert is just one of many parallel [feed-forward](#c/ffn) weight blocks inside a layer. The [router](#c/router) is a small linear layer that scores every expert with a dot product against the token's current vector and sends the token to the top few. That decision is re-made for every token at every MoE layer, so neighbouring words can go to entirely different experts. When researchers inspect trained routers, specialization is mostly low-level and syntactic (punctuation, numbers, structural roles), not human topics. See [the correction](#c/r-experts).

concepts.title: Experts specialize in low-level token patterns, re-chosen every token at every layer
concepts.overview: MoE routing is fine-grained and mechanical. At each MoE layer, a small [router](#c/router) computes a score for every expert as a dot product between the token's current vector and each expert's learned routing vector. A softmax turns the scores into weights, and the token goes to the top-k experts, whose outputs are combined by those weights. The decision is made fresh for every token at every layer: a 60-layer model makes 60 routing decisions per token, and the active set churns constantly. Inspected routers show experts specializing in low-level, often syntactic or positional patterns rather than topics. Training needs [load balancing](#c/lb-loss) to stop a few experts from winning everything, and designs like DeepSeek's [shared expert](#c/shared-expert-c) handle common processing. The payoff is that the full pool of [routed experts](#c/experts) sets capacity, while only the few active ones set per-token cost.

concepts.title: Capacity is all about GPUs
concepts.overview: **Myth:** AI capacity is simply a matter of how many GPUs exist. It's natural, because Nvidia dominates the headlines and accelerators are the most expensive visible component. In reality the [binding constraint](#c/capacity) has kept moving. Through 2024 and early 2025 it was [power](#c/power): Microsoft reportedly held chips it couldn't plug in. By late 2025 it swung back to chip supply. By around May 2026 it was [transformers and switchgear](#c/electrical-gear), with high-voltage transformer lead times of 36–48 months. [HBM memory](#c/hbm-supply) is the underappreciated one. It was sold out for 2026 and is heading toward about 30% of hyperscaler AI spend, up from about 8%. On top of that, 30–50% of planned 2026 data-center capacity is projected to slip to 2028. At least four constraints bind in turn, so buying more GPUs alone doesn't add capacity.

concepts.title: Frontier models keep getting bigger
concepts.overview: **Myth:** frontier models keep getting bigger in parameter count. It was true for years. GPT-1 to GPT-3 grew about 1,000× in two years, and GPT-3 to GPT-4 (an estimated 1.8T) another ~10×. Extrapolation would put today's models near 10 trillion. But in 2023 the trend reversed. Epoch estimates GPT-4o at about 200B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet at about 400B, roughly an order of magnitude smaller than GPT-4. These are estimates: Anthropic has never published a parameter count.
