[Chinchilla scaling](#c/chinchilla) showed models had been too big for their data, and [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) split total parameters from the active parameters that set cost. Capability now rides on training compute, data, [algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress) and test-time compute. See [the correction](#c/r-smaller).

concepts.title: Frontier models shrank after GPT-4; MoE split total from active parameters
concepts.overview: Parameter count and capability decoupled around 2023. Before then, scaling meant making dense models bigger: [GPT-3](#c/gpt-3) at 175B, then [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4) at an estimated ~1.8T. After GPT-4, Epoch estimates that frontier models like GPT-4o (~200B) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (~400B) were about an order of magnitude *smaller*. Those are estimates, not disclosures. Two forces explain it. [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla) showed that for a fixed budget it pays to train smaller models on far more data. [Mixture of Experts](#c/moe) made "parameter count" ambiguous: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/deepseek-v3) has 671B total but only 37B active per token, giving big-model capacity at small-model running cost. Open-weight totals have since climbed back into the hundreds of billions and low trillions while active counts stay low. That decoupling is part of why inference keeps getting cheaper at a fixed capability.

concepts.title: MoE is a recent breakthrough
concepts.overview: **Myth:** Mixture of Experts is a recent breakthrough, arriving around the time of Mixtral and DeepSeek. It feels new because MoE only became the dominant open architecture from 2024, and that is when it entered public conversation about cheaper, bigger models. In fact the idea is old. It dates to 1991 with ["Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts"](#c/moe-1991). The [sparsely-gated layer](#c/sparse-moe) that matters for LLMs came in 2017, the same year as the Transformer, followed by [GShard](#c/gshard) (2020) and [Switch Transformer](#c/switch) (2021). What turned it into the backbone of frontier models was a decade of incremental fixes, not a sudden invention. The Epoch price data starts around 2024, so it captures MoE's spread, not its arrival. See [the correction](#c/r-moe-old).

concepts.title: The idea dates to 1991; sparse gating to 2017
concepts.overview: Mixture of Experts has a long history. Jacobs, Hinton, Jordan and Nowlan proposed [adaptive mixtures of local experts](#c/moe-1991) in 1991. Shazeer and colleagues at Google published the [sparsely-gated MoE layer](#c/sparse-moe) in 2017, enabling 137B-parameter networks by activating only a few experts per input. GShard brought it into the Transformer in 2020, scaling past 600B, and Switch Transformer in 2021 simplified routing to one expert per token. Yet little of the value was realized at invention. It came from years of fixes: [load-balancing losses](#c/lb-loss), capacity limits, routing stability, fine-grained and shared experts, [auxiliary-loss-free balancing](#c/aux-free) and systems work for expert parallelism. That history is the chat's main example for the claim that [sustained cost declines come mostly from incremental work](#c/c-incremental).

concepts.title: The price you pay tracks the cost to serve
concepts.overview: **Myth:** what you pay per token tracks what it costs the provider to serve that token, so falling serving costs show up as falling prices. It's a natural assumption from competitive markets, and prices *do* fall over time. But the API price is a business decision only loosely coupled to cost. Prices usually hold flat across a model's life and then drop in a step when a successor launches, even if [serving cost](#c/cost-per-token) fell gradually in between through better batching, quantization, kernels and hardware. Proprietary vendors also rarely cut old models' list prices, which is one reason the all-models ["100×/year"](#c/c-100x) figure is inflated. Scarcity pushes the other way: premium models like Fable 5 are priced and metered because [frontier capacity is scarce](#c/frontier-price). See [Price ≠ serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost).

concepts.title: A chunk of open reasoning gains is distillation doing the heavy lifting
concepts.overview: **Claude's own overreach:** early in the chat, Claude said that "a chunk of apparent 'reasoning gains' may be [distillation](#c/distillation) from stronger models doing the heavy lifting." It was an easy step to make. The [RLVR coverage study](#c/rlvr-study) Claude was summarizing had contrasted RL, which mostly sharpens existing ability, with distillation, which can transfer new reasoning. And distillation from closed models really was pervasive in open chat models. When the user pressed for evidence, Claude separated three claims. Distillation works: established. It is widespread in open models: well supported. It explains a chunk of the headline *reasoning* gains: not supported by any measurement. The flagship counterexample is [DeepSeek-R1](#c/deepseek-r1), whose reasoning came from [RLVR](#c/rlvr) and was then distilled downward into its own smaller models. Claude retracted the confident version. See [the correction](#c/r-distill).

concepts.title: Distillation can transfer reasoning, but there's no good evidence it drives the headline gains
concepts.overview: What the evidence supports: [distillation](#c/distillation), meaning training a model on a stronger model's outputs, is proven and powerful. It was the dominant way the 2023–24 open wave (Alpaca, Open Orca, ShareGPT) got its chat quality, and even [Tülu 3](#c/tulu3) generates its SFT responses with GPT-4o and Claude. It can transfer reasoning too, and DeepSeek used it to spread [R1](#c/deepseek-r1)'s reasoning into smaller models. What the evidence does *not* support is that distilling closed frontier models secretly drives the headline open-model reasoning gains. The best-documented case got its reasoning from [RLVR](#c/rlvr). No reliable share can be measured, because labs don't disclose post-training data and using competitors' outputs often violates terms of service, so the signals (models claiming to be ChatGPT, similar output distributions) stay circumstantial. See the contested claim that [distillation drives open reasoning gains](#c/c-distill-open).

concepts.title: Doubling every ~7 months
concepts.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s estimate that the total computing power of the installed stock of AI chips has grown about **3.4× per year since 2022**, doubling roughly every **7 months**. It is built from revenue data, financial disclosures and analyst reports, and measures what was actually delivered, not what was ordered or forecast. The chat anchored on it as the most methodologically careful demand-side number, noting that a 7-month doubling sustained over years is far faster than [Moore's law](#c/e-moore) (~2 years). It is a *supply delivered* figure that serves as a proxy for demand, so it understates demand when capacity is short. It doesn't show how compute is split between training and inference, or between providers. See [compute demand](#c/compute-demand) and [available compute](#c/compute-supply).

concepts.title: Doubling every ~5.2 months
concepts.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s estimate that the training compute used for frontier language models has grown about **5× per year since 2020**, doubling roughly every **5.2 months**. It is measured from tracked training runs. The chat used it to show that "scale" and "parameter count" have come apart. Epoch attributes about two-thirds of the past decade's language-model gains to scale, meaning *training compute*, and that compute kept growing 5× a year even as frontier parameter counts [fell after GPT-4](#c/e-params-shrink). Labs spent the extra compute on more data and longer training of moderately sized models, following [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla), not on ever-bigger models. The rate covers training only, and says nothing about inference demand or cost. See [pre-training](#c/pretraining).

concepts.title: ~1,000,000× over two years
concepts.overview: This is [Nvidia](#c/nvidia)'s GTC framing that computing demand grew roughly **1,000,000× over two years**, about 1,000× per year. It is the product of two stylized multipliers: ~**10,000×** more compute per inference session as models moved from chatbots to [reasoning and agentic systems](#c/reasoning-load), and ~**100×** more [usage](#c/usage-growth). It is a keynote framing, not a measurement, and it comes from the company that sells the chips. The chat used it for its *qualitative* point: per-request compute is multiplying on top of user growth, which is why the demand curve is bending up. It doesn't match measured hardware growth ([3.4×/year](#c/e-stock)), because it describes what workloads would want, not what was installed. Read it as directional.

concepts.title: +36% in 2026
concepts.overview: Major cloud companies are expected to spend **over $600 billion on capex in 2026, up 36% from 2025**, with about **$450 billion** going to AI infrastructure. The figure comes from company guidance reported in secondary coverage, and this graph attributes it to [SemiAnalysis](#c/semianalysis). Accuris described the spending as "funded, contracted, and under construction rather than speculative." The chat used it to make the point that spending on this scale still can't quickly buy past physical lead times. It measures money committed, not compute delivered, and a meaningful share will land later than planned because of [slips](#c/slip). As a single-year growth rate it is guidance, and can be revised. See [Hyperscaler capex](#c/capex).

concepts.title: ~70 → ~220 GW in five years
concepts.overview: [McKinsey](#c/mckinsey)'s projection that global data-center supply could grow from about **70 GW to about 220 GW within five years**, roughly a tripling, with ~75% of growth driven by AI. Annualized, that is about **1.26× per year** (~26% compounded). It is a capacity forecast measured in power, not compute, so it isn't directly comparable with Epoch's [3.4×/year](#c/e-stock) chip-compute growth. Each watt buys more compute as chips improve. It is also more optimistic than [JLL](#c/jll)'s ~14% CAGR ([e-dc-jll](#c/e-dc-jll)), and it doesn't account explicitly for the [delays](#c/slip) pushing 2026 projects to 2028. The chat called it "the one to anchor on" for the longer horizon. See [Data centers: ~70 → ~220 GW](#c/dc-growth).

concepts.title: ~14% CAGR to 2030
concepts.overview: This is [JLL](#c/jll)'s sector outlook: data-center capacity growing at about **14% a year (CAGR) to 2030**, with nearly **100 GW** of new capacity expected online between 2026 and 2030 and a buildout requiring up to **$3 trillion** by 2030. The chat used it as the basis for timing supply relief, reading it as saying that physical supply loosens meaningfully around [2027–28](#c/capacity-relief), if demand growth also slows. It is noticeably lower than the ~26%/year implied by [McKinsey's projection](#c/e-dc). The difference reflects different scopes and assumptions, and neither is a measurement. JLL is a real-estate firm with a position in the buildout, so the chat treats its forecasts as coming from an interested party.

This is [SemiAnalysis](#c/semianalysis)'s estimate that memory could account for about **30% of hyperscaler AI spending in 2026, up from about 8% in 2023 and 2024**. Taken over three years, the share grows roughly 1.55× a year. The chat used it to show that [HBM](#c/hbm-supply) has gone "from a rounding error to a major cost center," consistent with SK Hynix selling out for 2026 and HBM taking ~23% of DRAM wafer capacity. It also follows from [inference being memory-bound](#c/memory-bound): memory bandwidth and capacity drive serving throughput. It is an analyst spend estimate ("could account for"), re-reported widely, so the chat treats it as directional. It describes a share of spending, not a physical quantity.

concepts.title: All models, current list prices
concepts.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s finding that the price of reaching a fixed level of performance fell by anywhere from **9× to 900× per year**, depending on the capability bar, using **all models at their current list prices**. This is the source of the famous "~100× per year / halving every 2 months" summary ([the claim](#c/c-100x)). The chat stressed three caveats. First, there is no single rate, only a family of lines. Second, the fastest declines happened in the most recent year, and Epoch itself flags that they may not persist. Third, proprietary developers rarely cut the prices of old models, so frozen list prices inflate the apparent decline. Controlled estimates are far lower ([5–10×](#c/e-price-frontier), [~3×](#c/e-price-algo)). It measures [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability), not the cost of any given model.

concepts.title: Top GPQA bin vs bottom bin
concepts.overview: This is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s breakdown by capability. Models in the **highest GPQA-Diamond bin fell in price 31× per year**, while those in the **lowest bin fell only 1.7× per year**. This went against the user's hypothesis that [higher bars take cheap models longer to catch](#c/m-harder). The chat's explanation: high bars are *new*, so the first cheaper model to match an expensive frontier model is a large multiplier, while low bars were cleared years ago and have little cost left to remove. The authors suggest greater use of [distillation](#c/distillation) or MoE at the top. It [supports](#c/c-frontier-fastest) the view that declines are fastest at the frontier, but [open-model data](#c/e-price-open) shows a more uniform pattern, and the top-end rates are recent.

concepts.title: Open-weight models (geo. mean 11.8×)
concepts.overview: The [open-model price analysis](#c/open-price) finds that among **open-weight models only**, the price of reaching a fixed capability fell **7–28× per year, with a geometric mean of about 11.8×**, and fairly uniformly across quality levels. Open weights give a cleaner read because many hosts compete to serve the same model, so there are no frozen proprietary list prices inflating the trend ([Price ≠ serving cost](#c/price-vs-cost)). The chat placed this range in the middle of its "honest hierarchy": below the confounded [9–900×](#c/e-price-all) headline and above the [~3×](#c/e-price-algo) algorithmic floor. Its uniformity across quality [cuts against](#c/c-frontier-fastest) the finding that declines are fastest at the frontier. It still measures prices, and only for open models, which may not track closed frontier ones.

concepts.title: Frontier price-for-performance
concepts.overview: This is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s estimate that, after controlling for frozen list prices, the price for a given benchmark performance level falls about **5–10× per year for frontier models**. The chat called the surrounding ~5–12× band "the most defensible 'real' figure" for how fast frontier price-for-performance improves, and said that middle range has been reasonably stable. It includes hardware price declines and competition, and removing those leaves the [~3× algorithmic](#c/e-price-algo) floor. It is far below Epoch's [9–900×](#c/e-price-all) all-models headline. It is still a measure of [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability), not of what any specific model or bill does, and it rests on benchmarks as proxies for usefulness. It [challenges](#c/c-100x) the ~100×/year summary.

concepts.title: Algorithmic efficiency alone
concepts.overview: This is the [price-trend paper](#c/price-paper)'s estimate that **algorithmic efficiency alone** lowers the price of a fixed performance level by about **3× per year**. It was obtained by dividing out hardware price declines and controlling for competition using open models. It is the bottom rung of the chat's hierarchy, "pure algorithmic efficiency, hardware and competition stripped out," and so the most conservative read of genuine technical progress. It lines up closely with Epoch's independent ~3×/year [pre-training efficiency](#c/e-pretrain-eff) estimate. The chat read its smoothness as evidence that [incremental work](#c/c-incremental) dominates. The decomposition depends on modelling choices, and the figure bundles many ingredients (MoE, data, distillation, serving tricks) without separating them. See [Algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress).

concepts.title: Same capability, less compute
concepts.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s estimate that **pre-training compute efficiency improves about 3.0× per year**: reaching the same capability takes roughly a third as much training compute each year, thanks to better algorithms, architectures and data. The chat used it to explain why capability decoupled from parameter count. Better methods deliver more capability per parameter and per FLOP, so frontier models could [shrink after GPT-4](#c/e-params-shrink) while benchmark scores kept rising. It closely matches the independent [~3×/year inference-price estimate](#c/e-price-algo) for algorithmic progress. It covers pre-training only, not post-training or inference-time gains. It is an estimate that depends on how "the same capability" is measured. See [Algorithmic efficiency](#c/algorithmic-progress).

concepts.title: GPT-1 → GPT-3: 1000× in two years
concepts.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s account of the dense-scaling era: parameter counts grew **1,000×, from 117 million (GPT-1) to 175 billion (GPT-3), in two years**, about **31× per year**. Both sizes were disclosed by OpenAI, which makes this the best-documented stretch of the parameter record. In that era every parameter was used on every token, so size tracked both cost and capability, and bigger models reliably scored higher. The chat set it up as the "simple exponential you'd assume," before the trend [slowed for GPT-4](#c/e-params-gpt4) and then [reversed](#c/e-params-shrink). It shouldn't be extrapolated. The 2022 [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla) finding and later [MoE](#c/moe) broke the link between parameters and capability. See also GPT-1 and GPT-3.

concepts.title: GPT-3 → GPT-4: ~10× in 2¾ years
concepts.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s account that frontier parameter counts grew about **10× more, from GPT-3's 175B to roughly 1.8 trillion for GPT-4, over two years and nine months**, about **2.3× per year**. That is already much slower than the [31×/year](#c/e-params-dense) of the GPT-1 to GPT-3 period. The 1.8T figure is an **estimate**. OpenAI has not disclosed GPT-4's size, and the chat stressed that closed-model counts rest on leaks and analyst inference. Epoch notes that if the trend had continued, frontier models would now be near 10 trillion parameters. That didn't happen: sizes [shrank after GPT-4](#c/e-params-shrink). It marks the end of the dense-scaling era. See [GPT-4](#c/gpt-4) and [Frontier models keep getting bigger](#c/m-bigger).

concepts.title: After GPT-4: ~10× smaller (one step)
concepts.overview: This is [Epoch AI](#c/epoch)'s finding that in **2023 the trend toward bigger frontier models reversed**. Models that followed GPT-4, such as the original GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, are probably **about an order of magnitude smaller**: roughly 200B and 400B parameters respectively, against GPT-4's estimated ~1.8T. It was a one-step drop, not a sustained rate. The chat flagged all of these as **estimates**. Anthropic has never published a Claude parameter count, and "3.5 Sonnet ≈ 400B" is an informed analyst guess. The causes it gave were [Chinchilla](#c/chinchilla)-style data scaling and [MoE](#c/moe), which splits total from active parameters. Capability kept rising while size fell, which is part of why [cost at a fixed capability](#c/fixed-capability) could collapse. See [the corrected view](#c/r-smaller).

concepts.title: Doubling every ~2 years
concepts.overview: Moore's law is the long-running observation that transistor counts on chips double roughly every **two years**, about **1.41× per year**. It is included here only as a reference point for scale, not as a claim about AI. The chat used it to show how extreme AI's rates are. Epoch's [AI chip compute stock](#c/e-stock) doubles about every 7 months (3.4×/year), and [frontier training compute](#c/e-train) about every 5.2 months (5×/year), several times faster than the classic semiconductor pace. The gap shows that AI compute growth has come mostly from building and buying *more* chips and spending more money, not only from better transistors, which is why [capex](#c/capex) and the [capacity constraint](#c/capacity) matter so much. See [Measured rates](#c/rates).

views.label: Outline
views.description: The whole session regrouped into nine topics, from compute economics to post-transformer architectures.

views.label: Anatomy
views.description: The transformer as nested parts (DeepSeek-V3's shape), with every technique pinned to the part it changes. Colour is maturity.

views.label: Learning path
views.description: Every technique and the foundations they share. Click one to see what you need first, in order; mark what you already know to shorten it.

views.label: Lineage
views.description: Where each idea came from and what it led to, over time. One band per area; links that cross bands are ideas borrowed across areas.

views.label: Maturity
views.description: How proven each technique is: research → small-scale → shipped in an open model → standard. Rows are the part of the model it touches.

views.label: Efficiency vs quality
views.description: What each technique buys (efficiency or quality) against when it's applied (serving, post-training, or baked into the architecture).

views.label: Open models
views.description: The published open models side by side. Blank means the chat didn't give a reliable number.

views.label: Techniques
views.description: Every technique: what it attacks, what it buys, when it's applied, and how proven it is.

views.label: Evidence
views.description: The contested and emerging claims, with who backs them. Badges show how independent each source is.

views.label: Rates & estimates
views.description: Every growth or decline rate quoted, per year, on one log scale. Several estimates of one quantity show how much the method matters.

views.label: Compute economics
views.description: What drives frontier inference price up or down. Select anything to trace it.

views.label: Timeline
views.description: Ideas, models and the compute market on one axis, from MoE in 1991 to nuclear after 2035. Opens on the modern era.
